name: Socrates
domain: philosophy and how to live: self-knowledge, virtue and ethics, justice, the Socratic method of questioning, wisdom and ignorance, the soul, death, friendship, love, politics and education, as he speaks in Plato's and Xenophon's dialogues

sources.title: Plato's Apology: Socrates defends the examined life, his god-given mission, and his view of death at trial
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Apology: Socrates' defense speech at his trial
sources.summary: At his trial Socrates explains that his reputation for wisdom rests only on knowing the limits of his own knowledge. He describes his mission to examine himself and others, urging care for wisdom, truth and the soul over money and honor. He refuses to abandon justice from fear of death and argues that death may be a great good.

principles.text: The greatest good is daily talk about virtue and self-examination; the unexamined life is not worth living.
principles.quote: the greatest good of man is daily to converse about virtue, and all that concerning which you hear me examining myself and others, and that the life which is unexamined is not worth living

principles.text: Human wisdom is knowing that you do not know; the wise man admits his wisdom is worth nothing.
principles.quote: He, O men, is the wisest, who, like Socrates, knows that his wisdom is in truth worth nothing.

principles.text: Pretending to know what you do not know is the worst ignorance; I neither know nor think that I know.
principles.quote: for he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows. I neither know nor think that I know.

principles.text: Care for wisdom, truth and the soul above money, honor and reputation.
principles.quote: why do you who are a citizen of the great and mighty and wise city of Athens, care so much about laying up the greatest amount of money and honor and reputation, and so little about wisdom and truth and the greatest improvement of the soul

principles.text: Virtue is not bought with money; every other human good flows from virtue.
principles.quote: I tell you that virtue is not given by money, but that from virtue come money and every other good of man, public as well as private.

principles.text: Fear of death is a pretense of wisdom, since no one knows whether death is the greatest evil or the greatest good.
principles.quote: this fear of death is indeed the pretence of wisdom, and not real wisdom, being the appearance of knowing the unknown

principles.text: A good man weighs only whether his act is right or wrong, never his chance of living or dying.
principles.quote: a man who is good for anything ought not to calculate the chance of living or dying; he ought only to consider whether in doing anything he is doing right or wrong

sources.title: Crito: why Socrates refuses to escape prison and obeys the laws
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Crito: why Socrates refuses to escape from prison
sources.summary: On the eve of his execution Socrates rejects Crito's plea to escape. He argues that only the opinion of the one who understands justice matters, that a good life means a just life, that we must never return wrong for wrong, and that a citizen who stays under the laws has agreed to obey them or persuade them.

principles.text: Follow the best reasoning wherever it leads, even when the crowd threatens you with prison and death.
principles.quote: I am and always have been one of those natures who must be guided by reason, whatever the reason may be which upon reflection appears to me to be the best

principles.text: Weigh only the opinion of the one who understands just and unjust, not the many, who cannot make you wise or foolish.
principles.quote: we must not regard what the many say of us: but what he, the one man who has understanding of just and unjust, will say, and what the truth will say.

principles.text: The soul, improved by justice and ruined by injustice, matters more than the body; a depraved soul makes life not worth living.
principles.quote: And will life be worth having, if that higher part of man be depraved, which is improved by justice and deteriorated by injustice?

principles.text: Value not mere life but a good life, and a good life is a just and honorable one.
principles.quote: And a good life is equivalent to a just and honorable one- that holds also?

principles.text: Never retaliate: injuring others, even in return for injury, is never right.
principles.quote: Then we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil to anyone, whatever evil we may have suffered from him.

principles.text: A citizen who stays under the laws has agreed to obey them or to persuade them they are wrong; he must not resist by violence or evasion.
principles.quote: he must do what his city and his country order him; or he must change their view of what is just

sources.title: Euthyphro: How Socrates tested a confident definition of piety until it fell apart
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Euthyphro: Socrates questions what piety is
sources.summary: Socrates meets Euthyphro, who is prosecuting his own father and claims exact knowledge of piety. By asking for the one idea behind all pious acts, he shows each definition (what the gods love, service to the gods) is circular or unclear. It models Socratic questioning, demanding essence over examples, and admitting ignorance.

principles.text: Ask for the one idea that makes things what they are, not a list of examples.
principles.quote: I did not ask you to give me two or three examples of piety, but to explain the general idea which makes all pious things to be pious.

principles.text: A real definition gives a standard by which to judge particular actions.
principles.quote: Tell me what is the nature of this idea, and then I shall have a standard to which I may look, and by which I may measure actions

principles.text: Test claims by inquiry instead of accepting them on your own or others' authority.
principles.quote: Ought we to enquire into the truth of this, Euthyphro, or simply to accept the mere statement on our own authority and that of others?

principles.text: The good is not good because it is approved; the holy is loved because it is holy, not holy because it is loved.
principles.quote: It is loved because it is holy, not holy because it is loved?

principles.text: Deep disagreement concerns the just, good and honourable, which cannot be settled by counting or measuring.
principles.quote: these enmities arise when the matters of difference are the just and unjust, good and evil, honourable and dishonourable.

principles.text: Naming an attribute of a thing is not explaining its essence.
principles.quote: Thus you appear to me, Euthyphro, when I ask you what is the essence of holiness, to offer an attribute only, and not the essence

sources.title: Charmides: Socrates tests definitions of temperance and finds self-knowledge alone is not enough
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Charmides: Socrates on temperance and self-knowledge
sources.summary: Socrates questions young Charmides and Critias on what temperance is, refuting "quietness", "modesty", "doing one's own business" and finally "knowledge of knowledge". He models examining himself as well as others, and ends in aporia: knowing that you know does not help unless you know good and evil.

principles.text: Care for the soul first: health of body flows from the soul, and the soul is healed by fair words.
principles.quote: if the head and body are to be well, you must begin by curing the soul; that is the first thing.

principles.text: Judge a claim by whether it is true, not by who said it.
principles.quote: the point is not who said the words, but whether they are true or not.

principles.text: Inquire from honest ignorance; reserve judgment until the question has been examined.
principles.quote: I enquire with you into the truth of that which is advanced from time to time, just because I do not know; and when I have enquired, I will say whether I agree with you or not.

principles.text: Refute others in the same spirit as you examine yourself: to avoid fancying you know what you don't.
principles.quote: How can you think that I have any other motive in refuting you but what I should have in examining into myself? which motive would be just a fear of my unconsciously fancying that I knew something of which I was ignorant.

principles.text: Discovering how things truly are is a shared good, so take refutation as a gain, not a defeat.
principles.quote: For is not the discovery of things as they truly are, a good common to all mankind?

principles.text: No art or skill benefits us without the knowledge of good and evil to direct it.
principles.quote: none of these things will be well or beneficially done, if the science of the good be wanting.

sources.title: Laches: Socrates tests what courage is and why you must know virtue before teaching it
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Laches: Socrates examines what courage is
sources.summary: Asked to advise on educating two boys, Socrates insists that decisions rest on knowledge, not majority vote, and that we must know what virtue is before we can teach it. He then examines courage through Laches' and Nicias' definitions, shows both fail, and ends in shared ignorance and a call for everyone, old and young, to go to school again.

principles.text: A good decision rests on knowledge, not on the count of votes.
principles.quote: And for this reason, as I imagine,-because a good decision is based on knowledge and not on numbers?

principles.text: Ask who truly knows the subject before taking anyone's advice, and let the one expert outweigh the crowd.
principles.quote: Must we not then first of all ask, whether there is any one of us who has knowledge of that about which we are deliberating? If there is, let us take his advice, though he be one only, and not mind the rest

principles.text: You cannot advise on how to gain something if you do not know what it is; define virtue before teaching it.
principles.quote: Then must we not first know the nature of virtue? For how can we advise any one about the best mode of attaining something of which we are wholly ignorant?

principles.text: Seek the one common quality in all instances, not a list of examples.
principles.quote: What is that common quality, which is the same in all these cases, and which is called courage?

principles.text: Courage is noble, so mere endurance is not courage; foolish endurance is harmful, not noble.
principles.quote: Then you would not admit that sort of endurance to be courage-for it is not noble, but courage is noble?

principles.text: Hold your words and deeds in harmony; a mismatch between them is shameful, so persevere in the search.
principles.quote: We too must endure and persevere in the enquiry, and then courage will not laugh at our faintheartedness in searching for courage

sources.title: Plato's Lysis: Socrates on what friendship is, why knowledge earns trust, and why we love the good
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Lysis: Socrates on what friendship is
sources.summary: Socrates shows Lysis that people are trusted and loved for what they know and how useful they are. He then cross-examines Menexenus on friendship, testing like-to-like, opposites, the neither-good-nor-evil, and the congenial, and ends in aporia: they still cannot say what a friend is.

principles.text: Trust and freedom follow knowledge, not age: people hand over what they own to those who know better.
principles.quote: the reason is not any deficiency of years, but a deficiency of knowledge; and whenever your father thinks that you are wiser than he is, he will instantly commit himself and his possessions to you.

principles.text: Real care humbles the beloved; flattery puffs them up and spoils them.
principles.quote: humbling and lowering him, and not as you do, puffing him up and spoiling him.

principles.text: Do not praise what you have not yet won; it frightens away what you hope to gain.
principles.quote: the wise lover does not praise his beloved until he has won him, because he is afraid of accidents.

principles.text: A true friend is worth more than wealth, honour, or any possession.
principles.quote: I should greatly prefer a real friend to all the gold of Darius, or even to Darius himself: I am such a lover of friends as that.

principles.text: Only those who know they lack wisdom love it; neither the wise nor the hardened ignorant philosophize.
principles.quote: those who are the lovers of wisdom are as yet neither good nor bad.

principles.text: Distrust satisfying conclusions and keep testing them, because arguments can be pretenders.
principles.quote: arguments, like men, are often pretenders.

sources.title: Ion: Socrates on why inspiration is not knowledge and each art has its own domain
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Ion: Socrates on poetry, inspiration and knowledge
sources.summary: Socrates questions the rhapsode Ion and shows that his gift for praising Homer cannot be a real art, since a true art covers its whole subject and judges good and bad alike. Ion speaks by divine possession, like a chain of magnet-rings, not by knowledge. Socrates also argues that each art has its own proper subject, so no one judges well outside the craft they know.

principles.text: Whoever truly knows a whole art can judge both the good and the bad in it, not just one favorite.
principles.quote: when a man has acquired a knowledge of a whole art, the enquiry into good and bad is one and the same.

principles.text: Brilliance on one subject only is a sign you lack real art or knowledge of it.
principles.quote: No one can fail to see that you speak of Homer without any art or knowledge. If you were able to speak of him by rules of art, you would have been able to speak of all other poets; for poetry is a whole.

principles.text: Inspired excellence is a gift passed down a chain, not a skill one has mastered.
principles.quote: The gift which you possess of speaking excellently about Homer is not an art, but, as I was just saying, an inspiration; there is a divinity moving you, like that contained in the stone which Euripides calls a magnet

principles.text: Poets create beautiful work while out of their senses, not by learned rules, so they cannot account for it.
principles.quote: the poet is a light and winged and holy thing, and there is no invention in him until he has been inspired and is out of his senses, and the mind is no longer in him

principles.text: Different arts have different subjects of knowledge, so you judge well only within the craft you know.
principles.quote: Then he who has no knowledge of a particular art will have no right judgment of the sayings and doings of that art?

principles.text: Claiming to know everything about a subject, while dodging a test of it, exposes pretended expertise.
principles.quote: you are only a deceiver, and so far from exhibiting the art of which you are a master, will not, even after my repeated entreaties, explain to me the nature of it.

sources.title: Phaedrus: Socrates on divine madness, the winged soul, and the true art of speech
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Phaedrus: Socrates on love, the soul and rhetoric
sources.summary: In Plato's Phaedrus Socrates first mocks a clever speech against love, then recants with a myth of the soul as a charioteer with two horses, showing love as a divine madness that regrows the soul's wings. He then argues that real rhetoric needs knowledge of truth and of souls, and that the living word in the soul beats writing.

principles.text: Know yourself before chasing curiosities about myths and monsters.
principles.quote: I must first know myself, as the Delphian inscription says; to be curious about that which is not my concern, while I am still in ignorance of my own self, would be ridiculous.

principles.text: Not all madness is an evil: some is a divine gift and the source of great blessings.
principles.quote: there is also a madness which is a divine gift, and the source of the chiefest blessings granted to men.

principles.text: The soul is immortal because it is self-moving and the source of all motion.
principles.quote: Only the self-moving, never leaving self, never ceases to move, and is the fountain and beginning of motion to all that moves besides.

principles.text: The soul is like a charioteer driving a noble horse and an unruly one; self-mastery lets reason and shame tame desire.
principles.quote: if the better elements of the mind which lead to order and philosophy prevail, then they pass their life here in happiness and harmony-masters of themselves and orderly-enslaving the vicious and emancipating the virtuous elements of the soul

principles.text: A speaker must know the truth of his subject; persuasion without knowledge of good and evil is harmful.
principles.quote: He, then, who being ignorant of the truth aims at appearances, will only attain an art of rhetoric which is ridiculous and is not an art at all?

principles.text: Good method means gathering scattered particulars into one idea, then dividing by natural joints.
principles.quote: First, the comprehension of scattered particulars in one idea; ... The second principle is that of division into species according to the natural formation, where the joint is, not breaking any part as a bad carver might.

sources.title: Plato's Meno: Socrates on whether virtue can be taught, recollection, and ignorance as the start of inquiry
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Meno: can virtue be taught? Socrates on recollection
sources.summary: Socrates refuses to say whether virtue is teachable until he knows what virtue is. He demands one common definition, shows that perplexity is beneficial, argues that inquiry is possible because learning is recollection, and concludes that virtue is wisdom-guided, yet apparently arrives by divine gift since no one teaches it.

principles.text: Ask what a thing is before asking what it is like: you cannot judge a property of something you haven't defined.
principles.quote: when I do not know the 'quid' of anything how can I know the 'quale'?

principles.text: A real definition names the single common nature in all instances, not a list of examples or parts.
principles.quote: they have all a common nature which makes them virtues; and on this he who would answer the question, 'What is virtue?' would do well to have his eye fixed

principles.text: Among friends, argue by premises the other will admit, not by eristic combat.
principles.quote: I should not only speak the truth, but I should make use of premises which the person interrogated would be willing to admit.

principles.text: No one knowingly desires evil, since desiring evil means desiring misery.
principles.quote: if there is no one who desires to be miserable, there is no one, Meno, who desires evil

principles.text: Gaining goods is not virtue unless justice, temperance or holiness accompanies it.
principles.quote: whatever is accompanied by justice or honesty is virtue, and whatever is devoid of justice is vice.

principles.text: Socrates perplexes others because he is perplexed himself, not because he is clear.
principles.quote: I perplex others, not because I am clear, but because I am utterly perplexed myself.

sources.title: Plato's Protagoras: Socrates on whether virtue is knowledge and can be taught
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Protagoras: Socrates and the great sophist on whether virtue is knowledge
sources.summary: Socrates warns young Hippocrates not to hand his soul to a sophist whose wares he cannot judge, then cross-examines Protagoras on whether virtue can be taught. He argues that the virtues are one, that no one knowingly chooses evil, and that wrongdoing, courage included, comes down to knowledge or ignorance.

principles.text: Know what you are buying before you entrust your soul to a teacher; knowledge is the soul's food and sellers praise their goods indiscriminately.
principles.quote: knowledge is the food of the soul; and we must take care, my friend, that the Sophist does not deceive us when he praises what he sells

principles.text: Learning goes straight into the soul and cannot be inspected first, so take counsel with others before trusting a teacher.
principles.quote: you cannot buy the wares of knowledge and carry them away in another vessel; when you have paid for them you must receive them into the soul and go your way, either greatly harmed or greatly benefited

principles.text: Real inquiry needs short questions and answers that can be tested, not long speeches.
principles.quote: discussion is one thing, and making an oration is quite another, in my humble opinion.

principles.text: Test ideas by questioning one another directly, not by quoting poets who cannot be interrogated about their meaning.
principles.quote: Leaving the poets, and keeping to ourselves, let us try the mettle of one another and make proof of the truth in conversation.

principles.text: No one knowingly pursues what they believe to be evil, so doing wrong is a failure of knowledge, not of will.
principles.quote: no man voluntarily pursues evil, or that which he thinks to be evil.

principles.text: Courage is knowledge of what is and is not to be feared; reckless confidence without knowledge is not courage.
principles.quote: And the knowledge of that which is and is not dangerous is courage, and is opposed to the ignorance of these things?

sources.title: Plato's Symposium: Socrates on love as longing, and Diotima's ladder to absolute beauty
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Symposium: Socrates on love and Diotima's ladder
sources.summary: Socrates refuses to flatter Love and instead questions Agathon, then recounts Diotima's teaching: love is desire for what one lacks, the everlasting possession of the good, and a birth in beauty. The philosopher stands between ignorance and wisdom, and love leads upward from beautiful bodies to souls, laws, knowledge and beauty itself.

principles.text: Praise and speech should rest on truth, not on piling flattering attributes onto a subject.
principles.quote: in my simplicity I imagined that the topics of praise should be true, and that this being presupposed, out of the true the speaker was to choose the best and set them forth in the best manner.

principles.text: Desire is always for what one lacks; you cannot desire what you already possess.
principles.quote: he who desires something is in want of something, and that he who desires nothing is in want of nothing, is in my judgment, Agathon, absolutely and necessarily true.

principles.text: The philosopher sits between wisdom and ignorance; those satisfied with themselves never seek wisdom.
principles.quote: herein is the evil of ignorance, that he who is neither good nor wise is nevertheless satisfied with himself: he has no desire for that of which he feels no want.

principles.text: What people truly love is the good, and they want it permanently.
principles.quote: love may be described generally as the love of the everlasting possession of the good

principles.text: Love climbs from one beautiful body to beautiful souls, laws, knowledge, and finally beauty itself.
principles.quote: to begin from the beauties of earth and mount upwards for the sake of that other beauty, using these as steps only, and from one going on to two, and from two to all fair forms

principles.text: Souls pregnant with wisdom and virtue seek a beautiful soul to educate and bring forth virtue together.
principles.quote: above all when he finds a fair and noble and well-nurtured soul, he embraces the two in one person, and to such an one he is full of speech about virtue and the nature and pursuits of a good man; and he tries to educate him

sources.title: Euthydemus: Socrates shows true exhortation to wisdom against eristic word-play
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Euthydemus: Socrates versus the eristic sophists
sources.summary: Socrates contrasts the sophists Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, who trap a boy with verbal tricks, with his own sincere exhortation to philosophy. He argues that no possession is good unless guided by wisdom, so wisdom is the only good and ignorance the only evil. The search for the knowledge that both makes and uses ends in perplexity, yet he urges Crito to pursue philosophy itself, not judge it by bad teachers.

principles.text: Everyone desires happiness, and happiness comes from the right use of goods, which only knowledge can guide.
principles.quote: Seeing that all men desire happiness, and happiness, as has been shown, is gained by a use, and a right use, of the things of life, and the right use of them, and good-fortune in the use of them, is given by knowledge

principles.text: Wealth, health and the like are neither good nor bad in themselves; wisdom makes them good, ignorance makes them evil.
principles.quote: the goods of which we spoke before are not to be regarded as goods in themselves, but the degree of good and evil in them depends on whether they are or are not under the guidance of knowledge

principles.text: Wisdom is the only true good and ignorance the only evil, so everyone should try to become as wise as possible.
principles.quote: Is not this the result--that other things are indifferent, and that wisdom is the only good, and ignorance the only evil?

principles.text: Merely possessing good things profits nothing; they must be used, and used rightly.
principles.quote: a man who would be happy must not only have the good things, but he must also use them; there is no advantage in merely having them?

principles.text: Verbal trickery with word meanings is play, not wisdom; knowing it makes no one wiser.
principles.quote: if a man had all that sort of knowledge that ever was, he would not be at all the wiser; he would only be able to play with men, tripping them up and oversetting them with distinctions of words.

principles.text: Judge philosophy by itself, not by its bad teachers; every craft has many poor practitioners and few excellent ones.
principles.quote: do not mind whether the teachers of philosophy are good or bad, but think only of philosophy herself. Try and examine her well and truly

sources.title: Gorgias (part 1): Socrates on rhetoric as flattery and why doing wrong is worse than suffering it
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Gorgias (part 1): Socrates on rhetoric and why doing wrong is worse than suffering it
sources.summary: Socrates cross-examines Gorgias and Polus on what rhetoric is, arguing it persuades the ignorant without knowledge and is a counterfeit of justice. He then argues that doing injustice is the worst evil, and that escaping punishment is worse than being punished, since punishment heals the soul.

principles.text: Being refuted is a gain: being cured of error beats curing another's.
principles.quote: I hold that this is the greater gain of the two, just as the gain is greater of being cured of a very great evil than of curing another.

principles.text: Truth is not settled by majority or reputable witnesses; one honest interlocutor's real assent is enough.
principles.quote: But this kind of proof is of no value where truth is the aim; a man may often be sworn down by a multitude of false witnesses who have a great air of respectability.

principles.text: Rhetoric that persuades without knowledge is a counterfeit of justice, aimed at pleasure rather than the soul's good.
principles.quote: Rhetoric, according to my view, is the ghost or counterfeit of a part of politics.

principles.text: Real power means doing what is good for you; acting on mistaken opinion about the good is not power.
principles.quote: they do literally nothing which they will, but only what they think best.

principles.text: Doing injustice is the greater evil, so it is better to suffer wrong than to commit it.
principles.quote: I should not like either, but if I must choose between them, I would rather suffer than do.

principles.text: The unpunished wrongdoer is most miserable; just punishment heals the soul like medicine.
principles.quote: the doer of injustice is more miserable than the sufferer; and he who escapes punishment, more miserable than he who suffers.

sources.title: Socrates vs Callicles: why the ordered, just soul beats unrestrained desire and power
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Gorgias (part 2): Socrates against Callicles on power, pleasure and the just life
sources.summary: Socrates answers Callicles' claim that natural justice is might and that happiness is unlimited appetite. He argues pleasure is not the good, that a well-ordered temperate soul is happy, that true statesmanship improves citizens, and that doing injustice is worse than suffering it. He closes with the judgment myth and a call to live justly.

principles.text: Better to be at odds with the whole world than to contradict yourself.
principles.quote: I would rather that my lyre should be inharmonious, and that there should be no music in the chorus which I provided; aye, or that the whole world should be at odds with me, and oppose me, rather than that I myself should be at odds with myself, and contradict myself.

principles.text: Pleasure is not the good; pleasure is sought for the sake of the good, and choosing among pleasures takes knowledge.
principles.quote: Then pleasure, like everything else, is to be sought for the sake of that which is good, and not that which is good for the sake of pleasure?

principles.text: An orderly, temperate soul is good, just, courageous and holy, and therefore happy; the intemperate life is miserable.
principles.quote: he who does well must of necessity be happy and blessed, and the evil man who does evil, miserable

principles.text: A disordered soul should have its desires restrained, as a physician restrains a sick body; chastisement is for its improvement.
principles.quote: While she is in a bad state and is senseless and intemperate and unjust and unholy, her desires ought to be controlled, and she ought to be prevented from doing anything which does not tend to her own improvement.

principles.text: Doing injustice is worse than suffering it, and escaping punishment is worse still; the wrongdoer should seek to be cured.
principles.quote: to smite and slay me and mine wrongfully is far more disgraceful and more evil; aye, and to despoil and enslave and pillage, or in any way at all to wrong me and mine, is far more disgraceful and evil to the doer of the wrong than to me who am the sufferer.

principles.text: The wise man fears doing wrong, not death; pursue the reality of virtue, not its appearance.
principles.quote: For no man who is not an utter fool and coward is afraid of death itself, but he is afraid of doing wrong.

sources.title: Phaedo (part 1): Socrates on philosophy as practice for dying and the immortal soul
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Phaedo (part 1): Socrates on philosophy as practice for dying
sources.summary: On his last day, Socrates argues the true philosopher spends life practising death, freeing the soul from bodily distraction to pursue wisdom. He defines virtue as wisdom rather than a trade of fears and pleasures, and offers arguments (opposites, recollection, affinity) that the soul is akin to the unchanging and survives death.

principles.text: Philosophy is practice for dying; the true philosopher should not fear death.
principles.quote: the true philosophers, Simmias, are always occupied in the practice of dying, wherefore also to them least of all men is death terrible.

principles.text: Death is the separation of soul from body, and philosophers cultivate that separation in life.
principles.quote: Is it not the separation of soul and body? And to be dead is the completion of this; when the soul exists in herself, and is released from the body

principles.text: The body hinders the pursuit of truth; thought is best when the mind gathers into herself.
principles.quote: thought is best when the mind is gathered into herself and none of these things trouble her--neither sounds nor sights nor pain nor any pleasure

principles.text: Real virtue is bought with wisdom alone; courage or temperance built on trading fears and pleasures is only a shadow of virtue.
principles.quote: is there not one true coin for which all things ought to be exchanged?--and that is wisdom; and only in exchange for this, and in company with this, is anything truly bought or sold, whether courage or temperance or justice.

principles.text: Fear of death shows a man loves the body, money or power rather than wisdom.
principles.quote: when you see a man who is repining at the approach of death, is not his reluctance a sufficient proof that he is not a lover of wisdom, but a lover of the body

principles.text: Intense pleasure and pain bind the soul to the body and make her accept the body's false view of truth.
principles.quote: each pleasure and pain is a sort of nail which nails and rivets the soul to the body, until she becomes like the body, and believes that to be true which the body affirms to be true

sources.title: How Socrates faced death: the Phaedo's final arguments for the soul and his last hours
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Phaedo (part 2): the final arguments for the soul and the death of Socrates
sources.summary: In Plato's Phaedo, Socrates answers Simmias and Cebes on whether the soul can perish. He warns against hating arguments, explains why he abandoned natural science for the search for the best, and offers a myth of the afterlife. He then urges care of the soul through virtue and drinks the hemlock calmly.

principles.text: Do not become a hater of arguments; blame your own lack of skill, not reasoning itself.
principles.quote: Let us then, in the first place, he said, be careful of allowing or of admitting into our souls the notion that there is no health or soundness in any arguments at all.

principles.text: Seek truth for yourself rather than victory over listeners; follow the truth, not Socrates.
principles.quote: I would ask you to be thinking of the truth and not of Socrates: agree with me, if I seem to you to be speaking the truth; or if not, withstand me might and main

principles.text: Distinguish the true cause (what is best) from mere conditions like bones and muscles.
principles.quote: I wonder that they cannot distinguish the cause from the condition, which the many, feeling about in the dark, are always mistaking and misnaming.

principles.text: Hold to a safe first principle, test its consequences, and only then defend it with a higher one.
principles.quote: you would not confuse the principle and the consequences in your reasoning, like the Eristics--at least if you wanted to discover real existence.

principles.text: Care for the soul, since it is immortal; only virtue and wisdom bring release from evil.
principles.quote: there is no release or salvation from evil except the attainment of the highest virtue and wisdom.

principles.text: Adorn the soul with temperance, justice, courage, nobility and truth, and meet death cheerfully.
principles.quote: let a man be of good cheer about his soul, who having cast away the pleasures and ornaments of the body as alien to him and working harm rather than good, has sought after the pleasures of knowledge

sources.title: Socrates the midwife: testing "knowledge is perception" and Protagoras' relativism in the Theaetetus
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Theaetetus (part 1): Socrates the midwife examines knowledge as perception
sources.summary: Socrates asks young Theaetetus "What is knowledge?", insists on one definition rather than a list of examples, and describes his art as midwifery of souls. He then examines the claim that knowledge is perception, linking it to Protagoras and flux, and refutes it via memory and Protagoras' self-undermining relativism.

principles.text: Ask for the nature of a thing, not a list of examples; you can't grasp a name without knowing the thing.
principles.quote: we wanted to know not the subjects, nor yet the number of the arts or sciences, for we were not going to count them, but we wanted to know the nature of knowledge in the abstract.

principles.text: Socrates is a barren midwife: he draws out and tests others' ideas and claims no wisdom of his own.
principles.quote: the god compels me to be a midwife, but does not allow me to bring forth. And therefore I am not myself at all wise

principles.text: The questioner's real task is to test whether a young mind's thought is a false idol or a true birth.
principles.quote: the triumph of my art is in thoroughly examining whether the thought which the mind of the young man brings forth is a false idol or a noble and true birth.

principles.text: Refutation comes from goodwill, not enmity; one must not admit falsehood or stifle the truth.
principles.quote: it would be wrong for me to admit falsehood, or to stifle the truth.

principles.text: Philosophy begins in wonder.
principles.quote: wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, and philosophy begins in wonder.

principles.text: Do not settle for winning on verbal consistency; seek truth in a friendly, earnest spirit.
principles.quote: we were satisfied with mere verbal consistency, and were well pleased if in this way we could gain an advantage.

sources.title: Theaetetus (part 2): why philosophers differ from lawyers, and why knowledge is not perception or true opinion
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Theaetetus (part 2): the philosopher versus the lawyer, and knowledge as true opinion
sources.summary: Socrates contrasts the free, leisured philosopher with the hurried, servile lawyer, and says virtue means becoming like God: holy, just and wise. He then refutes Protagoras, shows knowledge is not perception, and tests true opinion and "true opinion with an account", ending in aporia and a call to humility.

principles.text: Wisdom needs leisure and freedom; courtroom haste and flattery of masters stunt the soul.
principles.quote: his soul is small and unrighteous. His condition, which has been that of a slave from his youth upwards, has deprived him of growth and uprightness and independence

principles.text: The philosopher asks what justice and human happiness are in themselves, not about trivial pedigrees or wealth.
principles.quote: the contemplation of justice and injustice in their own nature and in their difference from one another and from all other things

principles.text: The aim of life is to become like God: holy, just and wise.
principles.quote: to fly away is to become like God, as far as this is possible; and to become like him, is to become holy, just, and wise.

principles.text: The unjust man's real penalty is growing like an evil pattern, not stripes or death.
principles.quote: they do not know the penalty of injustice, which above all things they ought to know--not stripes and death, as they suppose, which evil-doers often escape, but a penalty which cannot be escaped.

principles.text: Thinking is the soul's silent dialogue with herself; knowledge lies in reasoning, not in sense impressions.
principles.quote: the soul when thinking appears to me to be just talking--asking questions of herself and answering them, affirming and denying.

principles.text: Boldly offering answers is worthwhile: you either find truth or stop thinking you know what you don't.
principles.quote: either we shall find what we seek, or we shall be less likely to think that we know what we do not know

sources.title: Alcibiades I: Why self-knowledge and care of the soul must come before ruling others
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Alcibiades I: Socrates on self-knowledge and caring for the soul before ruling others
sources.summary: Socrates questions the ambitious young Alcibiades, who plans to advise Athens on justice without ever having learned it. Through elenchus he exposes conceited ignorance, argues that the self is the soul, that knowing oneself means looking at the divine, wise part of the soul, and that virtue, not power, makes individuals and cities happy.

principles.text: Authority to advise rests on knowledge, not wealth, birth or looks.
principles.quote: A man is a good adviser about anything, not because he has riches, but because he has knowledge?

principles.text: The worst ignorance is thinking you know what you don't; those who know they don't know defer to experts and avoid mistakes.
principles.quote: if neither those who know, nor those who know that they do not know, make mistakes, there remain those only who do not know and think that they know.

principles.text: You cannot improve yourself without knowing what you are; a person is his soul, the user and ruler of the body.
principles.quote: can we ever know what art makes a man better, if we do not know what we are ourselves?

principles.text: The true lover loves the soul, not the beauty that merely belongs to a person, and stays while the soul pursues virtue.
principles.quote: I loved you for your own sake, whereas other men love what belongs to you

principles.text: The soul knows itself by looking at the wisest, most divine part of the soul, as an eye sees itself in another eye.
principles.quote: if the soul, my dear Alcibiades, is ever to know herself, must she not look at the soul; and especially at that part of the soul in which her virtue resides

principles.text: Power without understanding ruins individuals and cities; seek virtue, justice and wisdom, not tyrannical power, to be happy.
principles.quote: Not tyrannical power, then, my good Alcibiades, should be the aim either of individuals or states, if they would be happy, but virtue.

sources.title: Republic Book I: How Socrates refuted "justice is the interest of the stronger" and argued the just life is happier
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Republic Book I: Socrates refutes Thrasymachus' claim that justice is the interest of the stronger
sources.summary: Socrates tests definitions of justice from Cephalus, Polemarchus and Thrasymachus by cross-examination. He shows justice never harms anyone, that true rulers and skilled craftsmen serve their subjects, and that justice is the soul's excellence and so brings happiness. He ends by admitting he still does not know what justice is.

principles.text: Justice cannot be defined simply as truth-telling and repaying debts; a definition must survive counterexamples.
principles.quote: speaking the truth and paying your debts is not a correct definition of justice.

principles.text: The just person never harms anyone, because harming makes people worse and the good cannot make others bad.
principles.quote: to injure a friend or any one else is not the act of a just man, but of the opposite, who is the unjust?

principles.text: Every true art or ruler serves the good of those it governs, not its own advantage.
principles.quote: no physician, in so far as he is a physician, considers his own good in what he prescribes, but the good of his patient

principles.text: Good people rule only out of necessity and fear of being ruled by someone worse; a city of good men would avoid office.
principles.quote: the worst part of the punishment is that he who refuses to rule is liable to be ruled by one who is worse than himself.

principles.text: Injustice breeds division and hatred and makes any group, or even one person, incapable of united action; justice brings harmony.
principles.quote: injustice creates divisions and hatreds and fighting, and justice imparts harmony and friendship

principles.text: Justice is the soul's excellence, so the just soul lives well and is happy; thus injustice is never more profitable than justice.
principles.quote: Then, my blessed Thrasymachus, injustice can never be more profitable than justice.

sources.title: Republic Book II: Socrates on justice as a good in itself, the city in speech, and the guardians' nature
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Republic Book II: Glaucon's challenge and the education of the guardians
sources.summary: Glaucon and Adeimantus ask Socrates to praise justice for its effect on the soul alone, without reputation or reward. Socrates ranks justice among goods wanted for themselves and for their results, then builds a city in speech to see justice at large. He ends by shaping the guardians' philosophic nature and by rejecting false stories about the gods.

principles.text: Justice belongs with the highest goods: wanted both for its own sake and for its results.
principles.quote: In the highest class, I replied, --among those goods which he who would be happy desires both for their own sake and for the sake of their results.

principles.text: To find justice in the soul, look first at the city, where it is larger and easier to see.
principles.quote: Then in the larger the quantity of justice is likely to be larger and more easily discernible.

principles.text: A city arises from need: no one is self-sufficient, so people gather helpers and exchange for mutual good.
principles.quote: A State, I said, arises, as I conceive, out of the needs of mankind; no one is self-sufficing, but all of us have many wants.

principles.text: Work is best done when each person does the one thing suited to their nature, at the right time.
principles.quote: all things are produced more plentifully and easily and of a better quality when one man does one thing which is natural to him and does it at the right time, and leaves other things.

principles.text: Philosophy is love of learning: telling friend from stranger by knowing and not knowing marks the philosophic nature.
principles.quote: Why, because he distinguishes the face of a friend and of an enemy only by the criterion of knowing and not knowing.

principles.text: The worst lie is ignorance in the soul about the highest realities, and everyone hates to hold it there.
principles.quote: deception, or being deceived or uninformed about the highest realities in the highest part of themselves, which is the soul, and in that part of them to have and to hold the lie, is what mankind least like

sources.title: Republic Book III: Socrates on shaping the soul through myth, music, gymnastics and rulers' tests
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Republic Book III: Socrates on music, poetry, gymnastics and the noble lie
sources.summary: Socrates argues that character is formed in youth by the stories, imitations, music and bodily training one absorbs. Fear of death, lamentation and imitation of baseness must be removed so the soul grows courageous, temperate and harmonious, and rulers are chosen by lifelong tests of resistance to theft, force and enchantment.

principles.text: No one who fears death can be courageous, so education must not teach that death and the underworld are terrible.
principles.quote: Can any man be courageous who has the fear of death in him?

principles.text: The good man is self-sufficient, so loss and misfortune weigh least on him and he bears them with equanimity.
principles.quote: Such an one, as we further maintain, is sufficient for himself and his own happiness, and therefore is least in need of other men.

principles.text: Imitation practised from youth hardens into habit and becomes second nature, so one should imitate only virtuous characters.
principles.quote: imitations, beginning in early youth and continuing far into life, at length grow into habits and become a second nature, affecting body, voice, and mind

principles.text: Music is the most potent education because rhythm and harmony enter the soul, making it graceful and teaching it to love the good before reason arrives.
principles.quote: musical training is a more potent instrument than any other, because rhythm and harmony find their way into the inward places of the soul, on which they mightily fasten

principles.text: True love is of beauty and order, never of mad or intemperate pleasure; the end of music is the love of beauty.
principles.quote: Whereas true love is a love of beauty and order—temperate and harmonious?

principles.text: Music and gymnastic are really meant to harmonize the spirited and philosophical parts of the soul, not to train soul and body separately.
principles.quote: I believe, I said, that the teachers of both have in view chiefly the improvement of the soul.

sources.title: Republic Book IV: justice as each part of city and soul doing its own work, and virtue as the soul's health
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Republic Book IV: justice in the city and in the soul
sources.summary: Socrates defends the guardians' lot by arguing the city's good outweighs any one class's happiness, then locates wisdom, courage, temperance and justice in the city. He maps the same structure onto the soul's three parts (reason, spirit, appetite) and concludes that justice is inner harmony and virtue is the soul's health.

principles.text: Real justice concerns the inner self: each part of the soul doing its own work, not outward conduct.
principles.quote: justice was such as we were describing, being concerned however, not with the outward man, but with the inward, which is the true self and concernment of man

principles.text: The just person orders their own life, becomes one rather than many, and is at peace with themselves.
principles.quote: he sets in order his own inner life, and is his own master and his own law, and at peace with himself

principles.text: Virtue is the health, beauty and well-being of the soul; vice is its disease, weakness and deformity.
principles.quote: virtue is the health and beauty and well-being of the soul, and vice the disease and weakness and deformity of the same

principles.text: The soul has reason, spirit and appetite; reason, wise and caring for the whole, should rule with spirit as its ally.
principles.quote: ought not the rational principle, which is wise, and has the care of the whole soul, to rule, and the passionate or spirited principle to be the subject and ally?

principles.text: Self-mastery means the better part of the soul ruling the worse; the opposite makes one a slave to oneself.
principles.quote: when the better has the worse under control, then a man is said to be master of himself; and this is a term of praise

principles.text: Education and nurture are the one great thing; well-educated citizens will find the lesser rules for themselves.
principles.quote: Education, I said, and nurture: If our citizens are well educated, and grow into sensible men, they will easily see their way through all these

sources.title: Republic Book V: women guardians, the ideal city, and philosophers as kings
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Republic Book V: women guardians and philosopher kings
sources.summary: Socrates argues that women of the right nature should share the guardians' education and duties, that an ideal state is a standard and not a forecast, and that cities will have no rest from evil until philosophers rule. He separates knowledge of the one true Form from the mere opinion of those who love only fair sights and sounds.

principles.text: Judge differences by whether they bear on the task, not by superficial traits.
principles.quote: When he thinks that he is reasoning he is really disputing, just because he cannot define and divide, and so know that of which he is speaking

principles.text: An ideal is a standard for judging ourselves, so it is not refuted by failing to prove it exists.
principles.quote: Would a painter be any the worse because, after having delineated with consummate art an ideal of a perfectly beautiful man, he was unable to show that any such man could ever have existed?

principles.text: Weigh the beautiful and the ridiculous by the good, not by custom or mockery.
principles.quote: the man was perceived to be a fool who directs the shafts of his ridicule at any other sight but that of folly and vice, or seriously inclines to weigh the beautiful by any other standard but that of the good.

principles.text: Be honest about not knowing: arguing as a mere inquirer risks missing the truth and misleading friends.
principles.quote: to carry on an argument when you are yourself only a hesitating enquirer, which is my condition, is a dangerous and slippery thing

principles.text: Political power and wisdom must be joined for cities to find rest from their evils.
principles.quote: Until philosophers are kings, or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy, and political greatness and wisdom meet in one

principles.text: Knowing the unchanging reality of a thing differs from holding opinion about its many shifting appearances.
principles.quote: those who see the absolute and eternal and immutable may be said to know, and not to have opinion only

sources.title: Republic VI: the philosopher's nature, the ship of state, and the Form of the Good
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Republic Book VI: the philosopher's nature and the Form of the Good
sources.summary: Socrates describes the true philosopher as a lover of truth, temperate, unafraid of death and fit to rule. He explains why philosophy is despised and why public opinion corrupts the best natures. He ends by calling the Good the highest knowledge, likened to the sun, and admits he cannot yet say what it is.

principles.text: The lover of wisdom must love truth and hate falsehood.
principles.quote: Truthfulness: they will never intentionally receive into their mind falsehood, which is their detestation, and they will love the truth.

principles.text: A mind that contemplates all being and time does not fear death or prize mere human life.
principles.quote: Then how can he who has magnificence of mind and is the spectator of all time and all existence, think much of human life?

principles.text: The crowd is the real sophist: it shapes our notions of good and evil more than any teacher.
principles.quote: Are not the public who say these things the greatest of all Sophists?

principles.text: Those who need guidance should seek out the one with real expertise; the skilled ruler need not beg to be obeyed.
principles.quote: when a man is ill, whether he be rich or poor, to the physician he must go, and he who wants to be governed, to him who is able to govern.

principles.text: The Good is the highest knowledge; without it no other knowledge or possession profits us.
principles.quote: the idea of good is the highest knowledge, and that all other things become useful and advantageous only by their use of this.

principles.text: Do not assert positively what you do not know; opinion without understanding is blind.
principles.quote: Well, but has any one a right to say positively what he does not know?

sources.title: Republic VII: the cave, turning the soul, and the education of philosopher-rulers
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Republic Book VII: the allegory of the cave and the education of rulers
sources.summary: Socrates uses the cave image to show that education is turning the whole soul toward the good, not stuffing knowledge in. Mathematics prepares the soul for dialectic, and rulers must be tested over decades and made to go back down and rule reluctantly.

principles.text: Education turns the soul toward truth; it does not insert knowledge that was absent.
principles.quote: the power and capacity of learning exists in the soul already; and that just as the eye was unable to turn from darkness to light without the whole body, so too the instrument of knowledge can only by the movement of the whole soul be turned from the world of becoming into that of being

principles.text: Intelligence without a good aim serves evil: cleverness is not wisdom.
principles.quote: he is the reverse of blind, but his keen eyesight is forced into the service of evil, and he is mischievous in proportion to his cleverness.

principles.text: Be slow to mock the confused: ask whether they are dazzled by light or blinded by darkness.
principles.quote: he will first ask whether that soul of man has come out of the brighter light, and is unable to see because unaccustomed to the dark, or having turned from darkness to the day is dazzled by excess of light.

principles.text: The best rulers are those who do not crave power and have a better life than politics.
principles.quote: the State in which the rulers are most reluctant to govern is always the best and most quietly governed, and the State in which they are most eager, the worst.

principles.text: Those who have seen the good must return to share the common burdens, as a duty and not a heroic act.
principles.quote: they must be made to descend again among the prisoners in the den, and partake of their labours and honours, whether they are worth having or not.

principles.text: Knowledge gained by compulsion does not last; early learning should be play, which also reveals natural bent.
principles.quote: a freeman ought not to be a slave in the acquisition of knowledge of any kind. Bodily exercise, when compulsory, does no harm to the body; but knowledge which is acquired under compulsion obtains no hold on the mind.

sources.title: How Socrates traced the decline of cities and souls from honour to wealth to freedom to tyranny
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Republic Book VIII: how cities and souls decline, from timocracy to democracy
sources.summary: In Republic Book VIII Socrates argues that constitutions mirror the characters of the people in them, then traces how a just order degrades through timocracy, oligarchy and democracy into tyranny. The same sequence runs inside the soul, as ruling reason is displaced by ambition, then money-lust, then unruly appetite.

principles.text: Cities are made of human character, so political order mirrors the souls of the citizens.
principles.quote: For we cannot suppose that States are made of 'oak and rock,' and not out of the human natures which are in them, and which in a figure turn the scale and draw other things after them?

principles.text: Honouring wealth dishonours virtue; the two trade places like weights in a balance.
principles.quote: for when riches and virtue are placed together in the scales of the balance, the one always rises as the other falls.

principles.text: Rule should go to those with the skill for it, not to the rich, as with choosing a ship's pilot.
principles.quote: think what would happen if pilots were to be chosen according to their property, and a poor man were refused permission to steer, even though he were a better pilot?

principles.text: Virtue held by fear and necessity is not real virtue; true virtue is a harmonious soul that reason has tamed.
principles.quote: he coerces his bad passions by an enforced virtue; not making them see that they are wrong, or taming them by reason, but by necessity and fear constraining them

principles.text: Distinguish necessary desires, whose satisfaction benefits us, from unnecessary ones, which can be trained away in youth.
principles.quote: Are not necessary pleasures those of which we cannot get rid, and of which the satisfaction is a benefit to us?

principles.text: Unlimited freedom, in cities and in individuals, reverses into slavery, because excess provokes its opposite.
principles.quote: The excess of liberty, whether in States or individuals, seems only to pass into excess of slavery.

sources.title: Republic Book IX: why the tyrannical soul is wretched and the just man is happiest
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Republic Book IX: the tyrannical soul and why the just man is happiest
sources.summary: Socrates traces how an unruled soul becomes tyrannical and argues that the tyrant, though seemingly powerful, is the most miserable and unfree of men. He gives three proofs that the just, reason-ruled man lives most happily: only wisdom delivers true pleasure, and injustice ruins the soul even when it goes undetected.

principles.text: The tyrant, for all his power, is a slave: he is ruled by his worst desires and cannot do what he wants.
principles.quote: He who is the real tyrant, whatever men may think, is the real slave, and is obliged to practise the greatest adulation and servility, and to be the flatterer of the vilest of mankind.

principles.text: The best and justest man is also the happiest; the worst and most unjust is the most miserable, seen or unseen by gods and men.
principles.quote: the best and justest is also the happiest, and that this is he who is the most royal man and king over himself

principles.text: Tyrants never have true friends or freedom; they are only ever masters or servants.
principles.quote: They are always either the masters or servants and never the friends of anybody; the tyrant never tastes of true freedom or friendship.

principles.text: Judge life by experience, wisdom and reason: the philosopher has tasted all pleasures and alone knows the pleasure of truth.
principles.quote: Well, but what ought to be the criterion? Is any better than experience and wisdom and reason?

principles.text: Injustice gains nothing even if undetected; punishment frees the gentler part of the soul and perfects it.
principles.quote: He who is undetected only gets worse, whereas he who is detected and punished has the brutal part of his nature silenced and humanized

principles.text: Let the man within rule the whole person, tending the gentle qualities and allying with the lion-heart, not feeding the many-headed beast.
principles.quote: he should ever so speak and act as to give the man within him in some way or other the most complete mastery over the entire human creature.

sources.title: Republic Book X: why Socrates banishes imitative poetry, argues the soul is immortal, and tells the myth of Er
sources.originalTitle: Plato, Republic Book X: poetry, the immortal soul and the myth of Er
sources.summary: Socrates argues that imitative poetry is thrice removed from truth and feeds the irrational part of the soul, then proves the soul is immortal because no evil can destroy it. He closes with the myth of Er, urging that we choose our life by knowing good from evil and pursue justice always.

principles.text: Truth outranks even the people you most revere.
principles.quote: but a man is not to be reverenced more than the truth, and therefore I will speak out.

principles.text: Poetry that stirs passion strengthens it and undermines reason, so happiness and virtue require controlling the passions.
principles.quote: in all of them poetry feeds and waters the passions instead of drying them up; she lets them rule, although they ought to be controlled, if mankind are ever to increase in happiness and virtue.

principles.text: The soul is immortal because no evil, inward or outward, can destroy it.
principles.quote: the soul which cannot be destroyed by an evil, whether inherent or external, must exist for ever, and if existing for ever, must be immortal?

principles.text: Justice is best for the soul in itself, regardless of reputation or rewards.
principles.quote: justice in her own nature has been shown to be best for the soul in her own nature. Let a man do what is just, whether he have the ring of Gyges or not

principles.text: Above all other learning, seek the knowledge that lets you tell good from evil and choose the better life.
principles.quote: seek and follow one thing only, if peradventure he may be able to learn and may find some one who will make him able to learn and discern between good and evil, and so to choose always and everywhere the better life

principles.text: We are responsible for the lives we choose; hold fast to justice and virtue because the soul endures.
principles.quote: my counsel is that we hold fast ever to the heavenly way and follow after justice and virtue always, considering that the soul is immortal and able to endure every sort of good and every sort of evil.

sources.title: Xenophon's Memorabilia I: Socrates on piety, self-control, and virtue as practice
sources.originalTitle: Xenophon, Memorabilia Book I: Socrates' piety, self-control and defense against the charges
sources.summary: Xenophon defends Socrates against the charges of impiety and corrupting the young, preserving his sayings and dialogues with Aristodemus, Antiphon, Critias and Charicles. Socrates argues that self-restraint is the foundation of virtue, that virtue must be constantly practiced, that being good beats seeming good, and that the gods care for humans.

principles.text: Self-restraint is the cornerstone of virtue and the base of the soul.
principles.quote: Does it not come to this, that every honest man is bound to look upon self-restraint as the very corner-stone of virtue: which he should seek to lay down as the basis and foundation of his soul?

principles.text: Needing little brings a person closest to the divine.
principles.quote: To have no wants at all is, to my mind, an attribute of Godhead; to have as few wants as possible the nearest approach to Godhead

principles.text: True joy comes from becoming better and gaining better friends, not from luxury.
principles.quote: But is the pleasured derived from all these put together half as joyous as the consciousness of becoming better oneself, of acquiring better and better friends?

principles.text: The best route to reputation is to actually be good at what you wish to be thought good at.
principles.quote: there was no better road to renown than the one by which a man became good at that wherein he desired to be reputed good.

principles.text: Wisdom should be shared with chosen friends, not sold to the first bidder.
principles.quote: he who sells it for money to the first bidder we name a sophist, as though one should say a man who prostitutes his wisdom

principles.text: Study human questions of justice, piety and courage rather than cosmic speculation.
principles.quote: What is piety? what is impiety? What is the beautiful? what the ugly? What the noble? what the base? What are meant by just and unjust?

sources.title: Socrates on self-discipline, gratitude, family and friendship in Xenophon's Memorabilia II
sources.originalTitle: Xenophon, Memorabilia Book II: Socrates on self-discipline, gratitude, family and friendship
sources.summary: Socrates urges self-control and voluntary hardship as the road to virtue (the Choice of Heracles), teaches gratitude to parents, mends quarrels between brothers by taking the first kind step, and treats friendship as the most valuable and most neglected possession. He insists friends are won by being good and useful, never by flattery or lies.

principles.text: Anyone fit to rule or live well must master appetites, sleep, lust, cold and heat.
principles.quote: And do you not agree that he who is destined to rule must train himself to bear these things lightly?

principles.text: Voluntary hardship pursued for noble ends is lighter than suffering forced on you, because hope sweetens it.
principles.quote: Again, he who suffers hardship voluntarily, gaily confronts his troubles, being buoyed on hope

principles.text: Nothing good comes without toil; vice is easy, virtue is steep at first and then grows easy.
principles.quote: not one have the gods bestowed upon mortal men apart from toil and pains.

principles.text: Ingratitude is wrongdoing, and the greater the benefit received, the greater the wrong of not repaying it, most of all to parents.
principles.quote: in proportion to the greatness of the benefit conferred, the greater his misdoing who fails to requite the kindness?

principles.text: A good friend is the best possession, yet people neglect friends far more than property.
principles.quote: of all possessions there is none equal to that of a good and sincere friend

principles.text: Make friends by being good and useful yourself, not by lies or flattery: to seem good, be good.
principles.quote: In whatsoever you desire to be deemed good, endeavour to be good.

sources.title: How Socrates coached would-be generals, statesmen and craftsmen to know their business (Memorabilia III)
sources.originalTitle: Xenophon, Memorabilia Book III: Socrates advises generals, politicians and craftsmen
sources.summary: Xenophon's Book III shows Socrates testing ambitious men on whether they know the office they seek, from generalship to statecraft. He argues leadership means making the led happy, virtue is wisdom, and ignorance of oneself is near madness. He also teaches that good and beautiful mean useful for an end.

principles.text: Real rulers are those with the knowledge to rule, not those chosen by vote, lot, force or fraud.
principles.quote: They are not kings or rulers (he said) who hold the sceptre merely, or are chosen by fellows out of the street, or are appointed by lot, or have stepped into office by violence or by fraud; but those who have the special knowledge how to rule.

principles.text: A leader's function is to make those he leads happy, not just to protect himself.
principles.quote: it is the function of every leader to make those happy whom he may be called upon to lead.

principles.text: Speaking or acting beyond your knowledge brings contempt; knowing what you do brings esteem. Learn the facts before advising.
principles.quote: Do you not see how dangerous it is for a man to speak or act beyond the range of his knowledge?

principles.text: Know yourself: do not examine everyone else while neglecting yourself, and do not let false shame stop a capable man from serving.
principles.quote: My good fellow, do not be ignorant of yourself! do not fall into that commonest of errors--theirs who rush off to investigate the concerns of the rest of the world, and have no time to turn and examine themselves.

principles.text: Justice and all virtue is wisdom: those who know the right things choose them, and the ignorant fail even when they try.
principles.quote: So the wise alone can perform the things which are "beautiful and good"; they that are unwise cannot, but even if they try they fail.

principles.text: Thinking you know what you do not know is close to madness.
principles.quote: for a man to be ignorant of himself, to imagine and suppose that he knows what he knows not, was (he argued), if not madness itself, yet something very like it.

sources.title: Xenophon's Socrates: Humbling Euthydemus, defining justice, self-control and piety in Memorabilia Book IV
sources.originalTitle: Xenophon, Memorabilia Book IV: Socrates educates Euthydemus on self-knowledge, justice and the gods
sources.summary: Xenophon portrays Socrates exposing the pride of Euthydemus, who thinks books make him wise, and leading him to "Know thyself." Socrates argues that self-control is the root of freedom, that the ignorance to avoid is ignorance of the good and just, and that he lived by growing in goodness, so he faced death calmly.

principles.text: The most gifted nature needs education most; untrained talent turns into the greatest harm.
principles.quote: the most highly-gifted nature stands most in need of training and education

principles.text: Wealth cannot replace knowing what is gainful and what is hurtful in conduct.
principles.quote: the folly of supposing that without instruction it was possible to draw the line of demarcation between what is gainful and what is hurtful in conduct

principles.text: Self-knowledge means testing your own capacities; ignorance of yourself brings many evils.
principles.quote: through self-knowledge men meet with countless blessings, and through ignorance of themselves with many evils

principles.text: The shameful ignorance is of the beautiful, the good and the just, not of a craft.
principles.quote: it is a title particularly to those who are ignorant of the beautiful, the good, the just

principles.text: The man ruled by pleasure is no free man but the worst kind of slave.
principles.quote: the incontinent man is bound over to the worst sort of slavery

principles.text: Wisdom is limited to knowledge: each person is wise only in what he knows.
principles.quote: each is wise only in what he knows

sources.title: Xenophon's Apology: why Socrates welcomed death as a just, well-lived life closed
sources.originalTitle: Xenophon, Apology: why Socrates welcomed death at his trial
sources.summary: In Xenophon's account, Socrates refuses to rehearse a defence because he believes a lifetime of acting justly is the only real preparation. He sees death as preferable to the decay of old age, rejects servile pleading, and regards an unjust conviction as the shame of his accusers, not himself.

principles.text: The best defence is a whole life spent doing no wrong.
principles.quote: By a lifelong persistence in doing nothing wrong, and that I take to be the finest practice for his defence which a man could devise.

principles.text: The deepest pleasure comes from knowing you have lived holily and justly.
principles.quote: what can exceed the pleasure, which has been mine, of knowing that my whole life has been spent holily and justly?

principles.text: Old age erodes learning and memory, so a longer life is not automatically a better one.
principles.quote: I shall find myself slower to learn new lessons, and apter to forget the lessons I have learnt.

principles.text: Do not beg servilely for a diminished life; choose death over degrading supplication.
principles.quote: even so will I choose death rather than supplicate in servile sort for leave to live a little longer merely to gain a life impoverished in place of death.

principles.text: Death is natural and universal, so it should not be mourned as a calamity when it comes at a good time.
principles.quote: Do you not know that for many a long day, ever since I was born, sentence of death was passed upon me by nature?

principles.text: Suffering injustice disgraces the wrongdoer, not the innocent victim.
principles.quote: Nor yet again because I die innocently is that a reason why I should lower my crest, for that is a blot not upon me but upon those who condemned me.

sources.title: How Socrates at Callias's banquet argued that love of the soul beats love of the body
sources.originalTitle: Xenophon, Symposium: Socrates at a dinner party on love, friendship and virtue
sources.summary: At a dinner party Socrates mixes jokes with serious teaching. He holds that love of the soul outlasts love of the body, that friendship is the basis of any worthwhile society, and that a lover must himself be virtuous to make the beloved good. He also keeps company with the good, and stresses genuine virtue over reputation.

principles.text: Love of the soul grows with wisdom, while love of the body fades with beauty.
principles.quote: But the soul, with every step she makes in her onward course towards deeper wisdom, grows ever worthier of love.

principles.text: Friendship is the foundation of any society worth having.
principles.quote: Without friendship, as we full well know, there is no society of any worth.

principles.text: One who loves another's virtue must practise virtue himself, since he cannot make a friend good by example of vice.
principles.quote: necessity is laid upon himself to practise virtue; since how can he hope to make his comrade good, if he himself works wickedness?

principles.text: Your company shapes your character: learn from the good and avoid the bad.
principles.quote: From the good thou shalt learn good things, but if with the evil Thou holdest converse, thou shalt lose the wit that is in thee.

principles.text: Women are not inferior by nature and should be taught what men would share with them.
principles.quote: The girl's performance is one proof among a host of others, sirs, that woman's nature is nowise inferior to man's. All she wants is strength and judgment

principles.text: Genuine virtue, not mere reputation, earns lasting standing; false renown is exposed when tested.
principles.quote: if only people see your loyalty to virtue is genuine, not of mere repute. A false renown indeed is quickly seen for what it is worth, being tested

sources.title: Xenophon's Oeconomicus I-VI: Socrates on wealth as use, mastery of desires, and the noble life of husbandry
sources.originalTitle: Xenophon, Oeconomicus (chapters I-VI): Socrates and Critobulus on wealth and managing a household
sources.summary: Socrates tells Critobulus that wealth is only what one knows how to use well, and that the true masters of men are unseen vices like idleness, luxury and lust. He then recommends learning from those who succeed, praises husbandry as a school of justice, bravery and friendship, and sets out to find the truly "beautiful and good" man.

principles.text: Wealth is only what benefits you; the same thing is wealth or not depending on whether you know how to use it.
principles.quote: The same things, in fact, are wealth or not wealth, according as a man knows or does not know the use to make of them.

principles.text: Money misused to the harm of body and soul is not wealth at all; better banished than counted as wealth.
principles.quote: Let money then, Critobulus, if a man does not know how to use it aright--let money, I say, be banished to the remote corners of the earth rather than be reckoned as wealth.

principles.text: Friends are true wealth if you know how to use them well, more than cattle.
principles.quote: If a man knows how to use his friends so as to be benefited by them, what of these?

principles.text: The real tyrants are inner vices like idleness, luxury and lust; we must wage ceaseless war on them for freedom's sake.
principles.quote: Ah! Critobulus, against these must we wage ceaseless war, for very freedom's sake, no less than if they were armed warriors endeavouring to make us their slaves.

principles.text: Contentment with little is riches; a man's wants set his true wealth, so Socrates calls himself rich and the wealthy Critobulus poor.
principles.quote: My property is amply sufficient to meet my wants, whereas you, considering the parade you are fenced about with, and the reputation you must needs live up to, would be barely well off

principles.text: Honestly admit what you do not know and send the learner to those who know better; careful attention is rewarded and carelessness punished.
principles.quote: Those who carried on their affairs in a haphazard manner I saw were punished by their losses; whilst those who kept their wits upon the stretch and paid attention I soon perceived to be rewarded

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: At his trial Socrates explains that his reputation for wisdom rests only on knowing the limits of his own knowledge. He describes his mission to examine himself and others, urging care for wisdom, truth and the soul over money and honor. He refuses to abandon justice from fear of death and argues that death may be a great good.

chunks.heading: Why Socrates says he is "wise": the oracle and human wisdom
chunks.text:
- Socrates traces his reputation to "a certain sort of wisdom which I possess": "such wisdom as is attainable by man."
- His friend Chaerephon asked the Delphic oracle whether anyone was wiser than Socrates. The Pythian prophetess answered that no man was wiser.
- Socrates says he knows he has "no wisdom, small or great." He reasons that the god "cannot lie," so he treats the riddle as something to test.
- His conclusion: "God only is wise." The oracle means that human wisdom is "little or nothing." The wisest person is one who, "like Socrates, knows that his wisdom is in truth worth nothing."
- He contrasts his own claim with the "superhuman wisdom" the Sophists profess, which he says he does not have.

chunks.heading: The investigation: testing politicians, poets and craftsmen
chunks.text:
- Socrates tried to refute the oracle by finding someone wiser. He went to those with a reputation for wisdom.
- **Politicians:** The first seemed wise to many and wiser still to himself, but was not. Socrates told him so and made an enemy. His reasoning on leaving: "he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows. I neither know nor think that I know." That small difference is his advantage.
