- **Poets:** He asked them to explain their own most elaborate passages. Nearly any bystander could have explained them better. He concluded poets write "not by wisdom" but "by a sort of genius and inspiration," like diviners who say fine things without understanding them. They also thought themselves wise in other matters.
- **Artisans:** They really did know many fine things he did not. But because they were good at their craft, they believed they also knew "high matters," and that error overshadowed their wisdom.
- Result: those most in repute were "all but the most foolish," and some lesser men were wiser. He calls the labor "Herculean" and says it left the oracle "irrefutable."
- Cost: many dangerous enemies, and a reputation for wisdom, because listeners assume he possesses the wisdom he finds missing in others.

chunks.heading: Why the accusations exist, and how he answers them
chunks.text:
- He separates old slanderers (Aristophanes' comedy, rumors spread since the jurors' childhood) from the formal accusers Meletus (for the poets), Anytus (for the craftsmen) and Lycon (for the rhetoricians).
- The old charge: he studies the heavens and earth and "makes the worse appear the better cause." He denies any interest in natural philosophy and asks the audience to say whether they ever heard him discuss it.
- He denies teaching for pay. His proof is his poverty ("my poverty is a sufficient witness"). He notes Evenus of Paros charges five minae and says that if he had such knowledge he would be proud.
- Young men of leisure follow him and imitate his questioning. Those they refute blame Socrates. When asked what he teaches that corrupts, they repeat stock charges about "things up in the clouds and under the earth," since they do not want to admit their pretended knowledge was exposed.
- He says he has no disciples. Anyone, rich or poor, may listen, and he never taught anyone anything in private that the public did not hear.
- He argues that the hatred he provokes is itself evidence he is telling the truth.

chunks.heading: Cross-examining Meletus: logic against the indictment
chunks.text:
- **Who improves youth?** Meletus says everyone improves the young except Socrates. Socrates compares this to horses, where one trainer improves and most others harm. Experts are few. Meletus has shown he has never thought about the young.
- **Intentional corruption is absurd.** The good do their neighbors good and the bad do them harm, and no one wants to be harmed. So Socrates would not knowingly corrupt those he lives among. If the harm was unintentional, the law does not punish it. Meletus should have privately taught and warned him, since a court is "a place not of instruction, but of punishment."
- **Atheism versus "new divinities."** Meletus calls him a complete atheist, which contradicts the indictment's claim that he introduces new gods. Socrates points out that the claim that the sun is stone is from Anaxagoras, whose books were sold cheaply (one drachma at most).
- **Spirits imply gods.** No one believes in horsemanship without horses. Believing in spiritual agencies means believing in spirits, who are children of gods. Denying gods while affirming demigods is like affirming mules while denying horses and asses.
- He says the real danger is not Meletus or Anytus but "the envy and detraction of the world, which has been the death of many good men."

chunks.heading: Duty over safety: the philosopher's mission
chunks.text:
- A good man "ought not to calculate the chance of living or dying" but only whether he is acting rightly or wrongly. He cites Achilles, who feared "to live in dishonor" more than death.
- He kept his post as a soldier at Potidaea, Amphipolis and Delium. He says he would be a deserter if he abandoned the god's command to philosophize out of fear.
- If acquitted on condition that he stop philosophizing, he would refuse: "I shall obey God rather than you, and while I have life and strength I shall never cease from the practice and teaching of philosophy."
- His standing exhortation: why care so much for "money and honor and reputation," and so little for "wisdom and truth and the greatest improvement of the soul"? He examines and cross-examines anyone who claims to care, and reproaches those who overvalue the less and undervalue the greater.
- Core claim: "virtue is not given by money, but ... from virtue come money and every other good of man, public as well as private."
- He calls himself a gadfly given to the state by the god, which is "like a great and noble steed" made sluggish by its size. Killing him means the city will "sleep on" unless the god sends another.
- His neglect of his own affairs and his poverty over many years show he acts from duty. He compares himself to a father or elder brother urging people toward virtue.

chunks.heading: Why he avoided politics, and two acts of courage
chunks.text:
- His divine sign (a voice since childhood) only ever forbids him and never commands. It stopped him entering politics.
- He believes a man who honestly fights injustice against a multitude cannot survive long. To fight for the right even briefly, "he must have a private station and not a public one."
- **Arginusae:** As a senator, he alone among the presiding Prytanes opposed the illegal collective trial of the generals. He took the risk of imprisonment and death rather than join an injustice, "having law and justice with me."
- **The Thirty:** The oligarchs ordered him and four others to arrest Leon of Salamis. The other four went; Socrates "went quietly home." He says his only fear was "the fear of doing an unrighteous or unholy thing." He might have died had the Thirty not fallen soon after.
- He cites many witnesses: Crito and Critobulus, Plato, Apollodorus and others, including relatives of the supposedly corrupted, who support him "for the sake of truth and justice."

chunks.heading: Refusing to beg, and his reasoning about the sentence
chunks.text:
- He will not bring his three sons or weep before the jury. He says it is dishonorable for a man of reputation, shames the city, and is wrong in principle, because a judge's duty "is, not to make a present of justice, but to give judgment" under oath. Begging would teach jurors to break their oaths, which would undermine the very piety he is accused of lacking.
- After conviction (he says a shift of thirty votes would have acquitted him), he proposes as his "due" free meals in the Prytaneum. He argues an Olympic victor gives "the appearance of happiness" while he gives "the reality."
- He refuses to propose imprisonment, exile or death. He does not know whether death is good or evil, so he will not propose something that is certainly an evil. He does not wrong himself, because he believes he never wronged anyone.
- Exile would not help: wherever he went, young men would follow and their elders would expel him.
- He cannot "hold my tongue" because it would disobey the god. He states: "the greatest good of man is daily to converse about virtue ... and the life which is unexamined is not worth living."
- He finally offers a fine of one mina, then thirty minae with Plato, Crito, Critobulus and Apollodorus as sureties.

chunks.heading: Death, injustice and his parting words
chunks.text:
- Fear of death is "the pretence of wisdom," because it is "the appearance of knowing the unknown." No one knows whether death "may not be the greatest good." He calls this conceit of knowledge "a disgraceful sort of ignorance."
- What he does know: "injustice and disobedience to a better, whether God or man, is evil and dishonorable." He will not fear a possible good rather than a certain evil.
- He says he was convicted not for lack of words but because he refused to speak as juries expect, with weeping and wailing. He would "rather die having spoken after my manner, than speak in your manner and live."
- "The difficulty, my friends, is not in avoiding death, but in avoiding unrighteousness; for that runs faster than death." Age let death overtake him, while unrighteousness overtook his accusers.
- Prophecy to his judges: they killed him to escape having to account for their lives, but more and harsher accusers will follow. "The easiest and noblest way is not to be crushing others, but to be improving yourselves."
- His divine sign did not oppose him that day, not on leaving home, at court or in his speech. He takes this as evidence that what has happened is good.
- Two possibilities for death:
  - **Nothingness:** like a dreamless sleep, which even the Great King would rank above most of his days and nights. Then "eternity is then only a single night."
  - **Migration of the soul:** he would meet true judges (Minos, Rhadamanthus, Aeacus, Triptolemus), converse with Orpheus, Musaeus, Hesiod and Homer, and meet Palamedes and Ajax, who were also unjustly condemned. He would keep examining who is wise and who only pretends, and says they do not put a man to death for that there.
- Conclusion: "no evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death." The gods do not neglect him.
- He is not angry with his accusers and condemners; they did him no harm, though they did not intend good.
- Last request: when his sons grow up, his friends should trouble them as he troubled others if they care for riches or anything more than virtue, or pretend to be something when they are nothing.
- His final line: "I to die, and you to live. Which is better God only knows."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: On the eve of his execution Socrates rejects Crito's plea to escape. He argues that only the opinion of the one who understands justice matters, that a good life means a just life, that we must never return wrong for wrong, and that a citizen who stays under the laws has agreed to obey them or persuade them.

chunks.heading: Why Socrates Refuses to Escape: Reason Over Fear and Opinion
chunks.text:
- Socrates sleeps calmly the morning before his execution. He says "when a man has reached my age he ought not to be repining at the prospect of death."
- He is "one of those natures who must be guided by reason, whatever the reason may be which upon reflection appears to me to be the best."
- His rule for a crisis: principles honored in good times are not dropped because fortune turns. Unless "other and better principles" can be found "on the instant," he keeps the old ones.
- He will not be moved by threats, "not even if the power of the multitude could inflict many more imprisonments, confiscations, deaths, frightening us like children with hobgoblin terrors."
- He asks whether the earlier argument was "talk for the sake of talking; in fact an amusement only, and altogether vanity," and tests it again with Crito instead of assuming it holds.
- He asks Crito to refute him or stop pressing: "I am extremely desirous to be persuaded by you, but not against my own better judgment."

chunks.heading: Whose Opinion Counts: The One Who Understands
chunks.text:
- Crito warns that the many will think he cared more about money than his friend, and that the many can do great harm to those who lose their good opinion.
- Socrates replies that only good men are worth considering, and they will see the truth of events.
- The many "can do neither good nor evil: they cannot make a man wise or make him foolish; and whatever they do is the result of chance."
- Analogy from gymnastics: an athlete heeds the praise and blame of his one trainer or physician, not everyone. Ignoring that one man ruins the body.
- The same holds for just and unjust, fair and foul, good and evil. He follows "the one man who has understanding of just and unjust," and "what the truth will say," not the crowd.
- Crito concedes that the part of a person improved by justice and ruined by injustice is far more honored than the body. Life is not worth living with that part corrupted.
- To "the many can kill us," he answers that the old principle stands: "not life, but a good life, is to be chiefly valued," and a good life is "a just and honorable one."

chunks.heading: Practical Worries Are the Crowd's Doctrines
chunks.text:
- Crito offers many reasons to escape:
  - Simmias the Theban has brought money.
  - Cebes and others will pay.
  - Friends in Thessaly will protect him.
  - He would be betraying his children.
  - Staying is the "easier part," not the "manlier."
  - His friends will look cowardly.
- Socrates files money, reputation and the education of children under "the doctrines of the multitude, who would be as ready to call people to life, if they were able, as they are to put them to death - and with as little reason."
- The only question is whether escaping would be right. If it is wrong, "death or any other calamity which may ensue on my remaining here must not be allowed to enter into the calculation."

chunks.heading: Never Do Wrong, Never Retaliate
chunks.text:
- Socrates restates the premise of the whole inquiry: injustice is always an evil and a dishonor to the one who commits it, whatever the consequences.
- He draws a chain of conclusions:
  - We must do no wrong.
  - We must not return injury for injury, "as the many imagine."
  - Doing evil to someone is the same as injuring him.
  - So no evil is to be rendered for evil, whatever we have suffered.
- He admits that few hold this view and that those who accept it and those who reject it "have no common ground, and can only despise one another."
- He checks that Crito truly agrees: "neither injury nor retaliation nor warding off evil by evil is ever right." Crito says he has not changed his mind.
- The next premise: a man ought to do what he admits to be right, not betray it.
- Escaping would wrong those he ought "least to wrong" and abandon principles they had both agreed were just.

chunks.heading: The Laws Speak: Obligation to the City
chunks.text:
Socrates imagines the laws and the State confronting him, using the question-and-answer style he practices himself.

- **Overturning the State.** A State cannot survive if court decisions "have no power, but are set aside and overthrown by individuals." Replying "the State has injured us and given an unjust sentence" does not answer the point.
- **Parent and nurse.** The laws regulated his parents' marriage and his upbringing and education, so he is their "child and slave." He is not on equal terms and cannot return harm for harm to them, just as he could not strike a father who struck him.
- **Country above family.** The country is "more to be valued and higher and holier far than mother or father." Its punishments are endured in silence.
- **Persuade or obey.** A citizen must do what the city orders "or he must change their view of what is just." The laws "do not rudely impose" commands but offer the alternative of obeying or convincing them. He does neither.
- **Leave if dissatisfied.** Every Athenian may, once grown and acquainted with the laws, take his goods and go elsewhere. Staying means "an implied contract that he will do as we command him."
- **Disobedience is a triple wrong.** It disobeys parents, defies the authors of his education, and breaks an agreement.

chunks.heading: Evidence That Socrates Consented
chunks.text:
- He was the most constant resident of Athens, left only once for the Isthmus games, and otherwise only on military service. He showed no curiosity about other States and their laws.
- He begat his children there.
- At his trial he could have proposed banishment as his penalty but "pretended that you preferred death to exile."
- He had seventy years to leave. Sparta (Lacedaemon) and Crete, which he often praised, were open to him.
- The agreement was made "in deed, and not in word only," not in haste, compulsion or deception.

chunks.heading: What Escape Would Cost
chunks.text:
- His friends would face exile, loss of citizenship or property.
- In a well-governed city like Thebes or Megara he would arrive as an enemy of the laws, and would confirm the judges' verdict: "he who is a corrupter of the laws is more than likely to be corrupter of the young."
- He could not talk about virtue, justice and law there without shame.
- In lawless Thessaly he would be the flatterer and servant of all, "eating and drinking in Thessaly, having gone abroad in order that you may get a dinner," mocked for fleeing in a goatskin disguise "from a miserable desire of a little more life."
- Taking his children to Thessaly would deprive them of Athenian citizenship. If their guardians are true friends, they will care for them whether he is in Thessaly or in the other world.
- The laws' counsel: "Think not of life and children first, and of justice afterwards, but of justice first, that you may be justified before the princes of the world below."
- He departs "in innocence, a sufferer and not a doer of evil; a victim, not of the laws, but of men."

chunks.heading: Conclusion
chunks.text:
- He hears the laws' voice "like the sound of the flute in the ears of the mystic," humming so loudly he cannot hear anything else.
- Crito has nothing left to say.
- Socrates ends: "Then let me follow the intimations of the will of God."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Socrates meets Euthyphro, who is prosecuting his own father and claims exact knowledge of piety. By asking for the one idea behind all pious acts, he shows each definition (what the gods love, service to the gods) is circular or unclear. It models Socratic questioning, demanding essence over examples, and admitting ignorance.

chunks.heading: The pious must be defined by one form, not by examples
chunks.text:
- Socrates asks Euthyphro, who is prosecuting his own father for murder and claims exact knowledge of piety, "what is piety, and what is impiety?"
- Euthyphro answers that piety is "doing as I am doing," meaning prosecuting wrongdoers, even a father.
- Socrates rejects this: "I did not ask you to give me two or three examples of piety, but to explain the general idea which makes all pious things to be pious."
- He wants one idea that makes the pious pious and the impious impious, in every action.
- Reason: with that standard "I may look, and by which I may measure actions, whether yours or those of any one else."
- Rule drawn from this: a single example, even a admired one, does not define a virtue.

chunks.heading: Gods who disagree make "dear to the gods" an unusable definition
chunks.text:
- Euthyphro's second answer: piety is "that which is dear to the gods," impiety is what is not.
- Socrates tests it against Euthyphro's own admission that the gods quarrel.
- He argues that disputes over number, size or weight are settled by counting, measuring or weighing, so they do not breed enmity.
- Quarrels arise over "the just and unjust, good and evil, honourable and dishonourable." Gods quarrel about the same things, so each loves what it deems just and hates the opposite.
- Result: the same act is loved by some gods and hated by others, so it would be both pious and impious. Chastising the father may please Zeus but displease Cronos or Uranus.
- Socrates notes that people and gods alike do not argue that the guilty should go unpunished. They dispute the particulars: who did it, what, and when.
- He does not ask for proof that all the gods approve Euthyphro's act, saying it would not settle what piety is.
- He then amends the definition to "what all the gods love is pious, and what all hate, impious," and tests that too.

chunks.heading: The Euthyphro question: loved because holy, or holy because loved?
chunks.text:
- Socrates asks: "whether the pious or holy is beloved by the gods because it is holy, or holy because it is beloved of the gods."
- His method: a thing is carried because someone carries it, led because someone leads it, seen because someone sees it. The state follows the act, never the reverse.
- Applied to love, the state of being loved follows the act of loving.
- Euthyphro agrees the holy is loved because it is holy, not holy because it is loved.
- But what is "dear to the gods" is dear because it is loved by them.
- So the two differ. One kind of thing is loved because of what it is; the other is loved only because it is loved.
- Conclusion: Euthyphro has offered "an attribute only, and not the essence," namely being loved by all the gods. He still has not said what holiness is.
- Socrates says to leave aside whether it is dear to the gods ("a matter about which we will not quarrel") and say what holiness really is.

chunks.heading: Piety as a part of justice: genus and species
chunks.text:
- Euthyphro admits his arguments "turn round and walk away." Socrates jokes that he is more than Daedalus: "I move those of other people as well," and he would rather not.
- Socrates asks whether all that is just is pious, or all that is pious is just.
- He illustrates with the poet Stasinus ("where there is fear there is also reverence"), which he disputes. Many fear poverty and disease without reverencing them.
- Where reverence exists, fear exists, so reverence is a part of fear, "just as the odd is a part of number."
- Likewise justice is the wider notion and piety only a part. The next question is what part, as one could say an even number is "a number which represents a figure having two equal sides."
- Euthyphro answers that piety is the part of justice that attends to the gods, while the other part attends to men.

chunks.heading: Testing "attention to the gods" by analogy with the crafts
chunks.text:
- Socrates asks what "attention" means. Horsemanship attends to horses, the huntsman's art to dogs, the herdsman's to oxen.
- In each craft, attention aims at the good or benefit of what is tended, and never at its hurt.
- Does piety then improve the gods? Euthyphro says no.
- He retreats to "such as servants show to their masters," a ministration. Socrates asks what end it serves, as medicine serves health, shipbuilding a ship, housebuilding a house.
- What is the "fair work" the gods accomplish with human help? Euthyphro dodges, saying it would be tiresome to learn.
- Socrates notes the evasion, observing "the asker of a question is necessarily dependent on the answerer, whither he leads I must follow."

chunks.heading: Piety as trade with the gods circles back to the start
chunks.text:
- Euthyphro says piety is knowing how to please the gods by prayers and sacrifices, the "salvation of families and states."
- Socrates restates it as a science of asking and giving: sacrificing is giving, prayer is asking.
- The right way to ask is to ask what we want, and the right way to give is to give what the gods want. Piety becomes "an art which gods and men have of doing business with one another."
- Socrates objects: "I have no particular liking for anything but the truth."
- The gods give every good thing, so humans seem to get the better of the deal. What benefit do the gods receive?
- Euthyphro says gifts are "tributes of honour" and what pleases them. Socrates points out that this returns to piety as "dear to the gods," the definition already refuted.
- He says the argument comes "round to the same point" and that Euthyphro is the greater artist than Daedalus.

chunks.heading: Method and attitude: feigned ignorance and persistence in inquiry
chunks.text:
- Socrates states he is charged with impiety by Meletus. He ironically calls Meletus a good "husbandman" who starts by clearing the young shoots.
- He says he wants to learn piety from Euthyphro so he can clear himself, and offers to become his disciple.
- He doubts the myths: that Zeus bound Cronos, and that gods fight. "What else can I say, confessing as I do, that I know nothing about them?"
- He says he is "a benevolent" talker who would "even pay for a listener," and that Athenians resent a man only once he imparts his wisdom.
- He insists inquiry should test claims: "Ought we to enquire into the truth of this... or simply to accept the mere statement on our own authority and that of others?"
- He argues that someone who truly knew piety would not risk prosecuting his father, so Euthyphro must know it. He urges him to speak, "like Proteus," saying he will detain him until he tells.
- The dialogue ends without a definition. Euthyphro leaves in a hurry, and Socrates laments that he was left "in despair."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Socrates questions young Charmides and Critias on what temperance is, refuting "quietness", "modesty", "doing one's own business" and finally "knowledge of knowledge". He models examining himself as well as others, and ends in aporia: knowing that you know does not help unless you know good and evil.

chunks.heading: Temperance cannot be reduced to quietness
chunks.text:
- Socrates asks Charmides to say what temperance is, reasoning that if it is present in him it must give him some notion of its nature.
- Charmides first answers that temperance is "quietness", doing things orderly and quietly.
- Socrates first gets agreement that temperance is noble and good. He then shows that in writing, reading, playing the lyre, wrestling, boxing, running, learning, teaching and remembering, the quick and agile is better than the slow and quiet.
- The same goes for the soul: shrewdness is "a quickness or cleverness of the soul". He who deliberates and discovers most easily and quickly is the one worthy of praise.
- Conclusion: quick actions are at least as good as quiet ones, so temperance cannot be quietness, and the quiet life is not more temperate than the unquiet.

chunks.heading: Temperance as modesty fails because modesty is not always good
chunks.text:
- Charmides next defines temperance as modesty, being ashamed.
- Socrates secures two admissions: temperance is noble and good, and whatever is good makes men good.
- He quotes Homer, "Modesty is not good for a needy man", to show that modesty is sometimes bad.
- Temperance makes men only good and is always good, while modesty is "as much an evil as a good". So the two cannot be the same.
- The method is to test a proposed definition against things already agreed, and drop it when it contradicts them.

chunks.heading: "Doing one's own business" is a riddle, and truth matters more than the speaker
chunks.text:
- Charmides offers a third definition he heard from someone else: temperance is "doing our own business".
- Socrates says it does not matter who said it: "the point is not who said the words, but whether they are true or not."
- He tests it literally. A scribe, a physician, a builder or a weaver does things for others as well as for himself. A state that made everyone weave his own coat and make his own shoes would not be well ordered. Yet a temperate state is a well-ordered state.
- He concludes that the author must have meant something hidden, since he could not have been a fool.
- Critias then rescues the definition by splitting "making" from "doing" (citing Hesiod) and equating temperance with doing good actions.
- Socrates answers by asking whether a physician who cures well but does not know whether his treatment will help is acting temperately. He may do good and not know it. Critias will not accept a man being temperate or wise without knowing himself, and so he drops the definition.

chunks.heading: Why Socrates argues: examining himself, not winning
chunks.text:
- Critias complains that Socrates is only trying to refute him. Socrates replies that his motive is the same as when he examines himself: "a fear of my unconsciously fancying that I knew something of which I was ignorant."
- He says he pursues the argument "chiefly for my own sake, and perhaps in some degree also for the sake of my other friends."
- His reason: "the discovery of things as they truly are, a good common to all mankind."
- He tells Critias to ignore "whether Critias or Socrates is the person refuted" and attend only to the argument.
- He disclaims knowledge: "I enquire with you into the truth of that which is advanced from time to time, just because I do not know," and says he will decide whether he agrees only after reflecting.
- He counts it a duty to examine a thought that comes to mind: "if a man has any feeling of what is due to himself, he cannot let the thought ... pass away unheeded and unexamined."

chunks.heading: Temperance as self-knowledge, and the "science of science"
chunks.text:
- Critias proposes that temperance is "Know thyself". He reads the Delphic inscription as the god's greeting to worshippers, equivalent to "Be temperate!".
- Critias then says temperance is a science of itself and of other sciences, which also knows the absence of science. The wise man would know what he knows and does not know, and could test what others know or only think they know.
- Socrates notes that every other science has a subject distinct from itself and a product, such as health from medicine and houses from building. He asks what the subject or product of this science would be.
- He argues that a self-directed science with no object is monstrous. There is no vision that sees no colour but only itself, no hearing that hears no sound, and no desire, wish, love, fear or opinion that is only about itself.
- For relative things, he reasons, a thing related to itself takes on the nature of its object. Something greater than itself would also be less than itself, and sight that sees itself would have to see a colour.
- He says he is not sure such a science exists, and that someone wiser is needed to decide whether anything can be related to itself. Even if it exists, he will not call it wisdom until he sees whether it does any good.

chunks.heading: Even granted, knowing that you know is not knowing what you know
chunks.text:
- Granting for argument's sake that the science of science exists, Socrates asks how it would show a man what he knows.
- It would only tell him that something is or is not knowledge. It would not teach health, building or justice. Those come from medicine, building and politics.
- So the wise man would know that he has knowledge, not what the knowledge is about.
- Such a man could not tell a true physician from a pretender. To test a doctor he would have to ask about health and disease, and for that he would have to be a physician himself. He could at most recognize someone with some knowledge, as a fellow expert.
- Socrates describes the real benefit that was hoped for. If the wise man could discern what he and others know, we would never err. We would hand each task to the one who knows it, and houses and states would be well ordered, and men "would have done well, and would have been happy."
- He concludes that no such science has been found, and that the knowledge of knowledge brings only the minor gain of learning more easily.

chunks.heading: Knowledge of good and evil is what makes life go well
chunks.text:
- In his "dream", Socrates imagines wisdom ruling absolutely: no false pilot, physician, general or prophet could deceive us, and every craft would be done well.
- He still doubts that living by knowledge makes us act well and be happy.
- Pressed by Critias on which knowledge makes a man happy, Socrates eliminates draughts, computation, health, shoemaking and metalwork. What remains is "the knowledge with which he discerns good and evil."
- His conclusion: without the science of good and evil, medicine would still give health, shoemaking shoes, piloting would save lives at sea and generalship would save them in war. Yet "none of these things will be well or beneficially done, if the science of the good be wanting."
- That science is "a science of human advantage" and "not a science of other sciences, or of ignorance, but of good and evil."
- Since wisdom as defined produces neither health nor advantage, it seems useless. Socrates holds that this must reflect a failure in the inquiry, not in wisdom: "wisdom or temperance I believe to be really a great good."
- The dialogue ends without a definition. Socrates calls himself "a bad enquirer" and tells Charmides to examine himself to see whether he has the gift and can do without the charm. He adds that "the more wise and temperate you are, the happier you will be."

chunks.heading: The charm: curing the soul before the body
chunks.text:
- Socrates tells Charmides, who complains of headaches, that doctors say the eyes cannot be cured without the head, nor the head without the whole body. He reports that a Thracian physician added that the body cannot be cured without the soul.
- On this view, "all good and evil, whether in the body or in human nature, originates ... in the soul, and overflows from thence." Hence "the part can never be well unless the whole is well."
- The cure for the soul is "fair words", and by these "temperance is implanted in the soul". Where temperance is, health follows for the whole body.
- He swears not to cure the head until the person has first "given you his soul to be cured by the charm."
- He asks Charmides to examine whether temperance is in him, instead of accepting praise from others. He will not press him: "I will not press you if you would rather not."
- Charmides ends by saying he does not know if he has temperance, and agrees to be "charmed" by Socrates daily until Socrates says he has had enough.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Asked to advise on educating two boys, Socrates insists that decisions rest on knowledge, not majority vote, and that we must know what virtue is before we can teach it. He then examines courage through Laches' and Nicias' definitions, shows both fail, and ends in shared ignorance and a call for everyone, old and young, to go to school again.

chunks.heading: Courage cannot be defined by listing what brave people do
chunks.text:
- Laches first says a courageous man "remains at his post and fights against the enemy." Socrates says this answers a different question from the one he asked.
- He counters with Scythian cavalry who fight while flying, and with the Spartans at Plataea, who fled the light Persian shields, then turned and won once the Persian ranks broke.
- He widens the target beyond hoplites to courage "in perils by sea," in disease, in poverty, in politics, and against desires and pleasures as well as against pain and fear.
- His method is to ask for the one quality common to all the cases, not for examples of it.

chunks.heading: Defining by the common quality: the "quickness" analogy
chunks.text:
- To show what he wants, Socrates asks what quickness is. It shows up in running, playing the lyre, speaking and learning.
- His answer is "the quality which accomplishes much in a little time."
- He asks Laches to give courage the same kind of answer, one that covers every use of the word, in pleasure and in pain.

chunks.heading: Testing "courage is endurance of the soul"
chunks.text:
- Laches proposes that courage is "a sort of endurance of the soul."
- Socrates objects that not all endurance is good. Courage is noble, foolish endurance is "evil and hurtful," and nothing evil and hurtful is noble. So only wise endurance can count as courage.
- He then asks "wise in what?" Wise spending of money, or a physician refusing a patient's request for food and drink, is not courage.
- He sets two soldiers side by side. One endures with good odds, support and position. The other endures with none of those advantages. Laches says the second is braver.
- Socrates follows this through cavalry, slingers, archers and divers. Laches ends up saying that people who endure without skill are braver than people who endure with it.
- This contradicts the earlier agreement that foolish endurance is base. Laches admits "we are not right."
- Socrates notes that their deeds look courageous but their words about courage do not. They are "not attuned to the Dorian mode, which is a harmony of words and deeds."
- His remedy is to persevere in the inquiry itself: "we too must endure and persevere in the enquiry." He compares this to a good sportsman who follows the track and does not give up.

chunks.heading: Testing "courage is knowledge of what is fearful and hopeful"
chunks.text:
- Nicias recalls a saying he heard from Socrates: "Every man is good in that in which he is wise, and bad in that in which he is unwise." He concludes that courage is a kind of wisdom.
- Nicias defines courage as "the knowledge of that which inspires fear or confidence in war, or in anything."
- Laches objects that physicians and farmers know the dangers of their own crafts and are not courageous for it. Nicias replies that a physician knows health and disease but not whether living is better than dying for a given person.
- Socrates raises the problem that animals would then lack courage. A lion, stag, bull or monkey would be no braver than a pig unless it had rare wisdom.
- Nicias bites the bullet. Fearlessness without forethought is "rashness," found in "many men, many women, many children, many animals." Courage is thoughtful and rare, and courageous actions are wise actions.

chunks.heading: Why the knowledge definition collapses
chunks.text:
- Socrates says the terrible things are "the evils which are future," and the hopeful are the good or not-evil things which are future.
- He holds that one science covers past, present and future of the same subject. Medicine looks at health at all times, farming at the earth's produce at all times, and the general knows the future of war better than the soothsayer, which is why law puts the soothsayer under the general.
- So the knowledge of future goods and evils is only one-third of a larger knowledge of good and evil at every time.
- A person who knew all good and evil, and how they are, were and will be produced, would be perfect, with justice, temperance and holiness as well. Courage would then be "all virtue," not a part of it.
- That contradicts the starting premise that courage is one part of virtue alongside justice and temperance. The dialogue ends with "we have not discovered what courage is."

chunks.heading: Settle questions by knowledge, not by vote
chunks.text:
- When Lysimachus wants a majority ruling between Nicias and Laches, Socrates asks whether he would take the majority's advice on his son's gymnastic training. Melesias says no; he would follow the one trained under a skilful master.
- Socrates's reason is that "a good decision is based on knowledge and not on numbers."
- So the first question is whether anyone present has knowledge of the matter under discussion.
- The stakes are high. Children are "your riches," and how they turn out decides the whole order of a father's house.

chunks.heading: Ask about the end before the means
chunks.text:
- Socrates distinguishes the means from the end being served. Someone applying medicine to the eyes is thinking about the eyes. Someone bridling a horse is thinking about the horse.
- The question about fighting in armour is therefore really about the soul of the youth, and a good adviser must be skilled in treating that.
- Advisers should show proof, either teachers who were themselves proven or works of their own. He asks whom they have improved, whether Athenians or strangers, bond or free.
- Otherwise they risk experimenting on friends' children, and he quotes the proverb about "break the large vessel in learning to make pots."
- Socrates also says that to advise how a thing is attained, one must first know what it is. We cannot advise on giving sight without knowing what sight is, or on imparting virtue without knowing the nature of virtue.
- He proposes starting with one part of virtue, courage, since the whole may be more than they can manage.

chunks.heading: Admitting ignorance and learning together
chunks.text:
- Socrates says he has never had a teacher of the art of virtue, though he wished for one from youth, and he was too poor to pay the Sophists.
- He admits he has not discovered it himself either, and says he cannot decide which of the two speaks truly.
- Nicias warns that anyone who talks with Socrates "is liable to be drawn into an argument" until he has to give an account of his present and past life. Nicias welcomes this, quoting Solon: a man should wish to be learning as long as he lives, and old age does not itself bring wisdom.
- Laches says he admires the man whose life is "a harmony of words and deeds" and dislikes the man whose actions contradict his words. He adds that Solon's learning should be "of the good only."
- Socrates declines to take the boys as pupils, since all three men are equally perplexed and none should be preferred.
- His advice is to seek out the best teacher available, "regardless of expense," first for themselves and then for the youth. If others laugh at them for going to school at their age, he cites Homer: "Modesty is not good for a needy man."
- He concludes that "the education of the youths" should become "our own education."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Socrates shows Lysis that people are trusted and loved for what they know and how useful they are. He then cross-examines Menexenus on friendship, testing like-to-like, opposites, the neither-good-nor-evil, and the congenial, and ends in aporia: they still cannot say what a friend is.

chunks.heading: Friendship cannot be bought with praise: how a lover should speak to his beloved
chunks.text:
- Socrates notes that Hippothales, who is in love with the boy Lysis, only sings of Lysis's wealth, ancestors, horses and Olympic-style victories. He calls this "twaddle" a child could produce.
- He argues such songs are really hymns in honour of the lover himself. If the lover wins, he glories in them. If he loses the beloved, "the more you have praised him, the more ridiculous you will look".
- The wise lover "does not praise his beloved until he has won him, because he is afraid of accidents."
- Praise also fills the beloved with pride and vainglory, which makes him harder to win. Socrates compares this to a hunter who frightens off his prey, which is the mark of a bad hunter.
- His counter-method is to talk with the youth and humble him, not puff him up. He offers to demonstrate this by conversing with Lysis, and he almost tells Hippothales so directly.

chunks.heading: Freedom and trust follow knowledge, not age
chunks.text:
- Socrates asks Lysis whether his parents, who love him and want him happy, let him do what he likes. Lysis admits they do not. A hired charioteer drives the family chariot, a slave muleteer holds the whip, and a slave tutor governs Lysis himself.
- Lysis blames his age. Socrates doubts this. Lysis is already trusted to read, write and play the lyre as he pleases. The difference is not "a deficiency of years, but a deficiency of knowledge".
- He generalises: "whenever your father thinks that you are wiser than he is, he will instantly commit himself and his possessions to you." The same holds for neighbours and the Athenian people.
- His example is the Great King, who would let two better cooks season the soup, or two better physicians treat his own son's eyes, before his son.
- Where we have knowledge, everyone trusts us and we are "free, and masters of others". Where we lack it, even parents and dearest friends will hinder us, and those things are not truly ours because we do not benefit from them.

chunks.heading: Usefulness is the root of being loved, and conceit has no ground without knowledge
chunks.text:
- Socrates concludes that nobody loves anybody "in so far as they are useless to them." If Lysis is wise, "all men will be your friends and kindred, for you will be useful and good". If he is not, not even his father or mother will be his friend.
- A person who still needs a teacher has not attained wisdom, so he has nothing to be conceited about. Lysis agrees.
- This is Socrates's practice of humbling the beloved, in contrast to Hippothales's flattery.

chunks.heading: A passion for friends, and the first failed definitions
chunks.text:
- Socrates says that from childhood his passion has been for friends. He would rather have "a good friend than the best cock or quail in the world", or the best horse or dog, or "all the gold of Darius". He admits he does not know how a friend is acquired.
- **Either party in a one-sided love?** If only one loves, are both friends? Menexenus first says either may be the friend. Socrates presses: if the lover is not loved back, or is hated, who is the friend? Without return love there seems to be no friendship, which contradicts the first answer.
- **The beloved as the friend?** Using the poet's line about dear children, horses and dogs, and children who are dearest to parents even while hating them for punishing, Socrates tries making the beloved the friend. That makes many men "friends of their enemies, and enemies of their friends", which he calls absurd, even impossible.
- With the lover not a friend, the beloved not a friend, and both together not friends, Menexenus cannot find any friends left.

chunks.heading: Like loves like? Opposites attract? Both fail
chunks.text:
- **Like to like.** Poets and natural philosophers say god draws like to like. Socrates argues bad men grow to hate each other the more they deal with each other, since an injurer and the injured cannot be friends. Bad men are also restless and at odds with themselves, so they cannot be at unity with anything. So only the good could be friends of the good.
- He then undermines this. Like can do nothing for like that it cannot do for itself. The good, in so far as good, is self-sufficient, wants nothing, desires nothing and therefore loves nothing. "How can such persons ever be induced to value one another?"
- **Opposites.** He recalls a claim attributed to Hesiod that likes are full of envy and strife ("Potter quarrels with potter, hard with bard, beggar with beggar"). On this view the poor need the rich, the sick the physician, the ignorant the knower, and opposites feed opposites (dry and moist, hot and cold, empty and full).
- He rejects this too: it would make the just friends of the unjust, the temperate of the intemperate, the good of the bad, and love the friend of hate. "Neither like and like nor unlike and unlike are friends."

chunks.heading: The neither-good-nor-evil loves the good because of evil
chunks.text:
- Socrates dizzily ventures a guess: "the beautiful is the friend", and the beautiful is the good. He assumes three kinds: good, bad, and what is neither.
- Since good cannot befriend good, bad or like, what is neither good nor evil must be the friend of the good.
- His illustration is medicine. A healthy body does not court the physician. A sick body does. The body is neither good nor evil in itself, but disease (evil) drives it to befriend medicine (a good).
- This only works while the thing is not yet corrupted: a presence of evil that has not yet made it evil. His analogy is white lead on hair, which makes it only appear white, unlike the real whiteness of old age.
- This explains who loves wisdom. Gods and the already wise do not, and the ignorant who are hardened and "fancy that they know what they do not know" do not either. Only those who are ignorant but aware of it, neither good nor bad, are lovers of wisdom.
- His first formula: friendship is "the love which by reason of the presence of evil the neither good nor evil has of the good".

chunks.heading: Doubting his own conclusion: friends for the sake of a first friend
chunks.text:
- Socrates immediately distrusts his result: "arguments, like men, are often pretenders." He says they may have been "grasping at a shadow only".
- He notes that the sick man loves the physician because of disease and for the sake of health. If health is dear, it is dear for the sake of something further, and so on. The chain of "dear for the sake of" must end in a first principle of friendship, "which is not capable of being referred to any other". Everything else called dear is only an illusion of friendship.
- His example is a father whose son has drunk hemlock. The father values the wine that might save him, and the cup holding it, only for the son's sake. Likewise we say we value gold and silver, but we really value the further end for which we acquire them.
- A deeper difficulty follows. If the good is loved only as a remedy for evil, then with evil gone the good would be useless and love would vanish. Yet bodily desires like hunger and thirst would remain and would be neither good nor evil, so some friendship would still exist. So evil cannot be the cause of friendship.

chunks.heading: Desire, the congenial, and the unresolved ending
chunks.text:
- Socrates's next proposal is that desire causes friendship. What desires is dear to what it desires, and it desires what it lacks. So love and friendship belong to "the natural or congenial".
- No one would love or desire another unless that person were somehow congenial to him, "either in his soul, or in his character, or in his manners, or in his form". So a true lover must be loved in return. Lysis gives only a faint assent.
- He cannot separate the congenial from the like. If they are the same, the old objection returns that like is useless to like. If the congenial means the good, only the good befriends the good, which was already refuted. If the congenial includes evil to evil, then the bad become friends of the bad.
- He sums up that if the beloved, lover, like, unlike, good and congenial are all ruled out, "I know not what remains to be said."
- The dialogue ends without a definition. The boys' tutors drag them home. Socrates says: "how ridiculous that you two boys, and I, an old boy... should imagine ourselves to be friends... and as yet we have not been able to discover what is a friend!"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Socrates questions the rhapsode Ion and shows that his gift for praising Homer cannot be a real art, since a true art covers its whole subject and judges good and bad alike. Ion speaks by divine possession, like a chain of magnet-rings, not by knowledge. Socrates also argues that each art has its own proper subject, so no one judges well outside the craft they know.

chunks.heading: Socrates's craft test: judging a work requires knowing the whole art
chunks.text:
- Socrates asks whether a person who can judge one speaker well on a subject can also judge the others. His examples:
  - In a discussion of arithmetic, the one who recognizes the best speaker is the arithmetician, and the same person recognizes the worst.
  - In a discussion of wholesome food, that person is the physician.
- His general rule: "he who knows the good" speaker on a topic "will know the bad speaker also." If you cannot judge the bad, you cannot truly judge the good.
- He applies it to Ion, who claims to speak brilliantly about Homer only. Socrates argues that poets such as Hesiod and Archilochus treat the same themes (war, human society, gods, the underworld). So real skill in judging Homer's treatment would carry over to the others.
- His diagnostic: when someone "wakes up" for one author and "goes to sleep" for the rest, he speaks "without any art or knowledge." Mastery of an art as a whole ("poetry is a whole") covers every instance of it.
- Parallel cases he gives from painting, sculpture and music: nobody expounds only Polygnotus, only Daedalus or only Orpheus while having nothing to say about other painters, sculptors or musicians.

chunks.heading: Each art has its own subject matter, so no one expert judges everything
chunks.text:
- Socrates holds that different arts give knowledge of different things: "that which we know with one art we do not know with the other." If two arts gave the same knowledge, there would be no sense in calling them different.
- Test case: the five fingers. Two people know there are five, and they know it by the same art, arithmetic. So the same art has the same subject, and different arts have different subjects.
- Consequence: "he who has no knowledge of a particular art will have no right judgment of the sayings and doings of that art."
- He applies this to passages in Homer:
  - Nestor's advice on rounding the turn in a chariot race: the charioteer judges it better than the physician or rhapsode.
  - Hecamede's posset of Pramnian wine, goat's cheese and onion for Machaon: the art of medicine judges it.
  - The leaden plummet on an ox-horn line among the fishes: the fisherman judges it.
  - Theoclymenus' vision of ghosts and the eagle-and-serpent omen: the prophet judges these.
- Socrates says he can assign each passage to its proper art, and invites Ion to name the passages the rhapsode's own art would judge.

chunks.heading: Pressing the claim that a rhapsode knows a general's art
chunks.text:
- Ion narrows his claim: the rhapsode knows what a man or woman, a free person or slave, a ruler or subject ought to say. Socrates tests each in turn:
  - A pilot knows better than the rhapsode what the ruler of a storm-tossed ship should say.
  - A physician knows better what the carer of a sick man should say.
  - A cowherd knows better how to soothe infuriated cows.
  - A spinning-woman knows better what to say about wool.
- Ion keeps only the general exhorting soldiers. Socrates points out that Ion may possess the general's art in addition to the rhapsode's, as one man may know both horsemanship and the lyre.
- Socrates separates which art a person judges with. A person who judges horses as a horseman and lyre-players as a musician uses a different art in each case.
- Ion then asserts that the rhapsode's and general's arts are "one and the same," so the best rhapsode must be the best general. Socrates draws out the absurdity:
  - If so, the best rhapsode in Hellas would also be the best general in Hellas.
  - Then Ion would not go about as a rhapsode when he could command armies.
- Ion's excuse is that Ephesus is subject to Athens. Socrates answers with foreigners whom the Athenians appointed general after they showed merit (Apollodorus of Cyzicus, Phanosthenes of Andros, Heraclides of Clazomenae).

chunks.heading: Inspiration, not art, explains Ion's gift: the magnet and the chain of rings
chunks.text:
- Socrates's explanation: Ion's gift for speaking about Homer "is not an art, but... an inspiration; there is a divinity moving you."
- His image: Euripides' "magnet," the stone of Heraclea.
  - It attracts iron rings and also gives them the power to attract other rings.
  - A long chain of rings hangs from the original stone, and each ring takes its power from it.
- Applied to poetry:
  - The Muse inspires the poet first.
  - Rhapsodes and actors are the intermediate links.
  - The spectator is the last ring.
  - Through all of them "the God sways the souls of men in any direction which he pleases."
  - Each poet hangs from some Muse (Orpheus, Musaeus, or, for most, Homer). Ion is "possessed by Homer."
- Evidence from Ion's own behavior: he wakes up at Homer and sleeps at any other poet, just as Corybantian revellers respond only to the strain of the god who possesses them.

chunks.heading: Poets compose by divine power, not by rules of art
chunks.text:
- Socrates states that good epic and lyric poets "compose their beautiful poems not by art, but because they are inspired and possessed."
  - He compares them to Corybantian dancers who are not in their right mind, and to Bacchic maidens who draw milk and honey from rivers only while possessed.
  - Poets say they bring songs from "honeyed fountains," like bees flying flower to flower.
  - His description: "the poet is a light and winged and holy thing, and there is no invention in him until he has been inspired and is out of his senses, and the mind is no longer in him."
- Why he says it is not art:
  - A poet good at one kind of verse (dithyramb, hymn, choral strain, epic or iambic) is not good at any other. Had he learned by rules of art, he would know how to treat all themes.
  - "God takes away the minds of poets, and uses them as his ministers, as he also uses diviners and holy prophets," so that listeners know the speaker is God himself, "conversing with us."
- Evidence: Tynnichus of Chalcis wrote nothing worth remembering except one famous paean, "simply an invention of the Muses." Socrates reads this as the god showing, "by the mouth of the worst of poets," that the best songs are divine.
- Ion is persuaded: "your words touch my soul."

chunks.heading: The rhapsode's trance and its effect on the audience
chunks.text:
- Socrates asks Ion if he is in his right mind when recounting Odysseus leaping onto the floor, Achilles rushing at Hector, or the sorrows of Andromache, Hecuba and Priam. Does his soul not seem to be in Ithaca or Troy?
- Ion admits his eyes fill with tears at pity and his hair stands on end and heart throbs at horrors.
- Socrates then asks about a man at a festival, dressed in holiday attire with golden crowns, who weeps or panics before over twenty thousand friendly faces when nobody is robbing or wronging him. Ion concedes such a man "is not in his right mind," and that he produces similar effects on most spectators.
- Ion adds a practical detail he watches from the stage: the audience's pity, wonder or sternness. He says he attends to it closely because "if I make them cry I myself shall laugh, and if I make them laugh I myself shall cry when the time of payment arrives."

chunks.heading: The closing dilemma: dishonest or inspired
chunks.text:
- Socrates says Ion has "as many forms as Proteus," twisting and turning and finally slipping away in the disguise of a general to avoid showing his Homeric art.
- Socrates sets out the choice:
  - If Ion has real art and knowledge about Homer, he is dealing unfairly, because he promised to show it and has not.
  - If he has no art and speaks beautifully under Homer's inspiring influence, Socrates "acquits" him of dishonesty and calls him inspired.
- Ion chooses inspiration as "by far the nobler." Socrates accepts: he will attribute Ion's praise of Homer "to inspiration, and not art."
- Pattern in Socrates's method here:
  - He starts with the person's own claim.
  - He gets agreement to general principles (the unity of an art, the distinct subject of each art).
  - He lets the contradiction between the claim and the principles show.
  - He leaves the person a face-saving alternative.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In Plato's Phaedrus Socrates first mocks a clever speech against love, then recants with a myth of the soul as a charioteer with two horses, showing love as a divine madness that regrows the soul's wings. He then argues that real rhetoric needs knowledge of truth and of souls, and that the living word in the soul beats writing.

chunks.heading: Questioning the world versus knowing oneself
chunks.text:
- Socrates declines to spend time rationalizing myths such as Boreas carrying off Orithyia. He says allegorical explanations take endless "labour and ingenuity" (Hippocentaurs, chimeras, Gorgons, winged steeds).
- His reason: "I must first know myself, as the Delphian inscription says; to be curious about that which is not my concern, while I am still in ignorance of my own self, would be ridiculous."
- He says the common opinion is enough for him on such tales. The question he wants answered is about himself: "am I a monster more complicated and swollen with passion than the serpent Typho, or a creature of a gentler and simpler sort, to whom Nature has given a diviner and lowlier destiny?"
- He calls himself a "lover of knowledge" and says the men in the city are his teachers, "and not the trees or the country." He adds that a book held out in front of him could lead him "all round Attica."
- He claims to "know nothing" of his own invention. He says his speeches come from having been "filled through the ears, like a pitcher, from the waters of another."

chunks.heading: Defining terms first, and the two kinds of madness
chunks.text:
- Socrates' first speech, which he later retracts, opens with a rule for good counsel: "a man should know what he is advising about, or his counsel will all come to nought."
- He says people assume they know the nature of things, skip agreeing on definitions, and so end "contradicting one another and themselves." His remedy is to agree on a definition and keep it in view.
- That speech defines love as irrational desire that overpowers an opinion aiming at the best. He later calls this speech foolish and "to a certain extent, impious," and reproves it as lacking truth or honesty.
- He then gives his recantation, which echoes Stesichorus: "I told a lie." Madness is not simply an evil: "there is also a madness which is a divine gift, and the source of the chiefest blessings granted to men."
- He names four divine madnesses and their gods:
  - prophetic (Apollo)
  - initiatory (Dionysus)
  - poetic (the Muses)
  - erotic (Aphrodite and Eros)
- Examples he gives: the Delphic prophetess and the priestesses of Dodona "when out of their senses have conferred great benefits on Hellas, but when in their senses few or none." He also says the sane man who comes to the door of poetry "by the help of art" is not admitted.
- He argues that if love is a god, as Eros is, "he cannot be evil." He calls the madness of love "the greatest of heaven's blessings."

chunks.heading: The soul: immortal, self-moving, a charioteer with two horses
chunks.text:
- Proof of immortality: what is moved by another ceases to live when the motion ceases. Only the self-moving never stops, and it is the source of motion in all else. Being a beginning, it is unbegotten and indestructible. He concludes that self-motion is "the very idea and essence of the soul."
- Image: the soul is a charioteer driving a pair of winged horses. The gods' horses are all noble. A human has one noble horse and one ignoble, so driving is "a great deal of trouble."
  - The good horse is white, upright, "a lover of honour and modesty and temperance." He needs no whip, "guided by word and admonition only."
  - The bad horse is crooked and dark, "the mate of insolence and pride," "hardly yielding to whip and spur."
- The wing is the part of the body most akin to the divine. It is nourished by "beauty, wisdom, goodness" and wastes away on "evil and foulness."
- Souls follow the gods up to the edge of heaven to see true being: justice, temperance, and knowledge absolute. These are "colourless, formless, intangible," visible only to mind. Souls that fail to see feed on "opinion."
- A soul that falls ranks into human lives by how much it saw. The philosopher, artist, or lover of the Muses ranks first; the tyrant ninth. Wings regrow after ten thousand years, except for the philosopher (and the lover who is not devoid of philosophy), who gets them in three thousand years.
- Learning is recollection. A man must have "intelligence of universals" and proceed "from the many particulars of sense to one conception of reason." Hence "the mind of the philosopher alone has wings," though the crowd thinks him mad.

chunks.heading: Love as the soul growing wings
chunks.text:
- Beauty is the one Form we can see clearly. Sight is "the most piercing of our bodily senses," and beauty "is also the most palpable to sight." Wisdom itself cannot be seen.
- The corrupted or newly arrived lover rushes toward pleasure "like a brutish beast." The one who remembers true beauty feels a shudder and awe and reveres the beloved as an image of a god. Gazing warms the soul, and the wings begin to grow.
- The lover forgets family, property, and propriety. He cannot sleep by night or stay in place by day.
- Each lover follows a god (Zeus, Hera, Apollo, Ares) and seeks a beloved of that god's character. He then tries to shape the beloved into the likeness of the god. Followers of Zeus seek a philosophical nature and "do all they can to confirm such a nature in him."
- The beloved gives back "love for love" (Anteros) and mistakes it for friendship.
- Self-control decides the outcome:
  - If the better elements prevail, the pair live "masters of themselves and orderly," and win "one of the three heavenly or truly Olympian victories." He says "nor can human discipline or divine inspiration confer any greater blessing on man than this."
  - If they yield to the lower life of ambition, they still earn "no mean reward," but their bond is less dear and they lose their wings for the time.
- The non-lover's "worldly and niggardly" prudence, by contrast, sends the soul "bowling round the earth" for nine thousand years.

chunks.heading: Rhetoric must rest on knowledge of truth and of the soul
chunks.text:
- Socrates tests the claim that an orator needs only opinion, not truth. He compares it to praising an ass as a horse to someone who does not know the difference. A speaker ignorant of good and evil, persuading an ignorant city, will reap "the reverse of good."
- Deception works through resemblances, and gradual shifts hide the lie best. He argues that "he who would deceive others, and not be deceived, must exactly know the real likenesses and differences of things."
- Rhetoric has most power where people disagree, as with justice and goodness, unlike iron and silver. So the rhetorician must first divide matters into agreed and disputed kinds.
- He rejects the technical manuals (exordium, statement of facts, witnesses, probabilities, refutation, and recapitulation). He names Theodorus, Evenus, Tisias, Gorgias, Prodicus, Polus, and Protagoras. These are only "the preliminaries" of the art. A man who knows drugs but not "to whom," "when," and "how much" is no physician, and a man who knows only how to make long or short speeches is no tragedian.
- The true art mirrors medicine. Medicine defines the nature of the body; rhetoric must define the nature of the soul. Pericles became the best rhetorician by learning from Anaxagoras: "All the great arts require discussion and high speculation about the truths of nature."
- The three requirements:
  - describe the soul and whether it is simple or multiform
  - explain how it acts and is acted upon
  - classify kinds of souls and kinds of speeches, and show why one soul is persuaded by one argument and another is not
- The learner also needs experience in real life. He must be able to say, "This is the man... who ought to have a certain argument applied to him," and know "when he should speak and when he should refrain."
- He answers Tisias' claim that probability beats truth: probability is "engendered in the minds of the many by the likeness of the truth," so only the knower finds the likenesses. The long and hard road is worth taking because the aim is to "say what is acceptable to God," not to please "fellow-servants."

chunks.heading: Dialectic: collection and division, and the shape of a good speech
chunks.text:
- Socrates names two principles that his two speeches happened to use:
  - Gather scattered particulars into one idea, which gives a definition that is clear and consistent.
  - Divide by species "according to the natural formation, where the joint is, not breaking any part as a bad carver might."
- He says he is "a great lover of these processes of division and generalization; they help me to speak and to think." He follows anyone who can see "a One and Many in nature... as if he were a god," and calls such people dialecticians.
- Every discourse "ought to be a living creature, having a body of its own and a head and feet; there should be a middle, beginning, and end, adapted to one another and to the whole."
- He criticizes the speech of Lysias on these grounds. It never defines love, it begins at the end where the lover would finish, and its parts could be shuffled like the lines of the Midas epitaph.

chunks.heading: Writing versus living speech
chunks.text:
- Socrates tells the story of the Egyptian king Thamus, who rebukes the god Theuth for inventing letters. Letters will "create forgetfulness in the learners' souls" because they will trust external marks. The discovery is "an aid not to memory, but to reminiscence," giving "not truth, but only the semblance of truth." Readers will be "hearers of many things" who "have learned nothing," with "the show of wisdom without the reality."
- He argues writing is like painting. It looks alive, "but if you ask them a question they preserve a solemn silence," gives "one unvarying answer," and cannot defend itself when it is abused or misread.
- The better kind of word is "an intelligent word graven in the soul of the learner, which can defend itself, and knows when to speak and when to be silent."
- The farmer comparison: a sensible man sows seeds in fitting soil and waits months, not in a quick "garden of Adonis" for eight-day show. In the same way, the one who knows the just, good, and honourable writes only "for the sake of recreation and amusement," as reminders for old age. The serious work is for the dialectician, who "finding a congenial soul... sows and plants therein words which are able to help themselves," leaving a seed others can make immortal.
- There is no disgrace in writing as such; "the disgrace begins when a man writes not well, but badly." Disgrace attaches to anyone who writes laws or speeches with false confidence in their clarity while ignorant of justice and injustice, good and evil.
- A writer whose work rests on knowledge of the truth, and who can defend it by spoken argument that leaves the writing "poor in comparison," deserves a higher name. Socrates will not call him wise ("a great name which belongs to God alone") but "lovers of wisdom or philosophers."

chunks.heading: Prayer and the measure of a good life
chunks.text:
- Socrates ends with a prayer to Pan and the local gods: "give me beauty in the inward soul; and may the outward and inward man be at one."
- He adds: "May I reckon the wise to be the wealthy, and may I have such a quantity of gold as a temperate man and he only can bear and carry."
- He says "friends should have all things in common" when Phaedrus asks to share the prayer.
- He predicts that young Isocrates will outgrow Lysias and rhetoric itself: "there is in him a divine inspiration which will lead him to things higher still. For he has an element of philosophy in his nature."
- He says that "to fail in an honourable object is honourable."
- He says conversation beats idleness at midday. The grasshoppers report to the Muses who honours them, and Calliope and Urania favour the philosophers.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Socrates refuses to say whether virtue is teachable until he knows what virtue is. He demands one common definition, shows that perplexity is beneficial, argues that inquiry is possible because learning is recollection, and concludes that virtue is wisdom-guided, yet apparently arrives by divine gift since no one teaches it.

chunks.heading: Virtue needs a single definition before it can be sought or taught
chunks.text:
- Meno answers "what is virtue?" with a list: one virtue for a man (to administer the state, "benefit his friends and harm his enemies"), another for a woman, a child, a slave. Socrates replies that he asked for one virtue and got "a swarm of them."
- He uses the bee: bees do not differ as bees. He looks for the common nature that makes all virtues virtues, the "simile in multis."
- Health, size and strength are the same in man and woman, and so is virtue. Every good person is good through the same temperance and justice.
- He rejects definitions that list parts or use unexplained terms. "Virtue is the power of governing mankind" fails because a child cannot govern a father. "Doing everything with justice" fails because justice is only a part of virtue. "Can any one who does not know virtue know a part of virtue?"
- He insists the whole of virtue be delivered "whole and sound, and not broken into a number of pieces."
- Priority: he would settle "what it is" before asking whether it can be taught, and he says he does not know what virtue is.

chunks.heading: How to define: shape and colour, and answering a friend differently from an opponent
chunks.text:
- To model a good definition he defines figure as "the limit of solid," after first trying "the only thing which always follows colour."
- He says the first definition is true but useless to someone who does not know what colour is. Terms must be ones the questioner already admits.
- With an eristic, antagonistic opponent he would simply state his answer and leave the refuting to the opponent. With friends he uses the dialectician's way: speak the truth, and use premises the other person is willing to admit.
- He notes that his plain answer about figure beats the "orthodox solemn" Gorgias-style definition of colour as an "effluence of form." The solemn one only seems better because Meno is used to hearing it.

chunks.heading: Nobody desires evil: virtue as the power to attain the good
chunks.text:
- Meno proposes "the desire of things honourable and the power of attaining them." Socrates tests it.
- Argument: people who say they desire evils either think those evils are good, in which case they really desire what they take to be good, or they know the evils harm them. Harm makes the possessor miserable, and nobody wants to be miserable. So "there is no one who desires evil."
- Since everyone desires good, no one is better than another in desire. Virtue must lie in the power of attaining good.
- Attaining silver, gold, office or honour counts as virtue only if done justly and piously. Acquiring wealth unjustly is vice, and not acquiring it dishonestly may be virtue. So justice is a part of virtue, and the definition goes in a circle.

chunks.heading: Perplexity as a benefit: the torpedo fish and the slave boy's mistake
chunks.text:
- Meno says Socrates numbs people like a torpedo fish. Socrates answers: "I perplex others, not because I am clear, but because I am utterly perplexed myself."
- The boy asked to double a square of 4 feet confidently says double the side. Socrates shows this gives 16, not 8. The boy then tries 3 feet and gets 9, and finally admits "I do not know."
- Socrates asks Meno: "Is he not better off in knowing his ignorance?" The "torpedo's shock" did the boy no harm.
- Before the shock the boy "would have been ready to tell all the world again and again" that a double space has a double side. Nobody inquires into what he fancies he already knows. Perplexity is what creates the wish to learn.

chunks.heading: Meno's paradox and recollection: inquiry as remembering
chunks.text:
- Meno's challenge: a man cannot inquire into what he knows (no need) or what he does not know (he does not know what to look for, or recognise it if found).
- Socrates calls it a "sophistical argument" that makes us idle and "is sweet only to the sluggard." The alternative makes us "active and inquisitive."
- He cites priests, priestesses and poets such as Pindar: the soul is immortal, is reborn many times, and has seen all things. So "all enquiry and all learning is but recollection," and one recollection can lead to the rest "if a man is strenuous and does not faint." People should live in perfect holiness.
- Demonstration: Socrates only asks questions and does not teach. He asks the boy to say what he thinks. The boy finds that the double square is built on the diagonal. He was never taught geometry, so these were true notions already in him, "stirred up... as in a dream." With repeated questions in different forms he would know as well as anyone.
- Since the knowledge was neither acquired in this life nor always known, the soul must have had it before. Socrates concludes the soul is immortal, but says he is not fully confident of some of this.
- What he will fight for "in word and deed": we will be "better and braver and less helpless" if we believe we ought to inquire into what we do not know.

chunks.heading: Is virtue knowledge? The argument from hypothesis
chunks.text:
- Socrates proposes arguing from a hypothesis, as a geometer does: if virtue is knowledge it can be taught; if not, not.
- Virtue is good and profitable. Health, strength, beauty and wealth help only when used rightly, and harm otherwise. Soul qualities such as courage, temperance and quickness are profitable only with wisdom. Courage without prudence is "only a sort of confidence" and does harm.
- Argument: all else hangs on the soul, and the soul's goods hang on wisdom. Under wisdom everything the soul attempts ends in happiness, and under folly the opposite. So virtue is wholly or partly wisdom.
- If so, the good are not good by nature. If they were, there would be discerners of character who would spot future good people and keep them safe, stamped "far rather than upon a piece of gold."

chunks.heading: Why virtue seems unteachable: no teachers, and the sons of great men
chunks.text:
- Test: anything teachable has teachers and disciples. He has often searched for teachers of virtue and found none.
- Anytus calls the Sophists a "manifest pest." Socrates objects that Anytus condemns them without acquaintance. Protagoras earned more than Pheidias and any ten sculptors and kept his reputation for more than forty years. A cobbler who ruined shoes would be found out within thirty days.
- Gentlemen as teachers fail the test too. Themistocles taught his son Cleophantus horsemanship, but no one calls Cleophantus good. Aristides, Pericles and Thucydides had the same result. Thucydides paid for the best wrestling trainers for his sons but could not make them good men. If virtue could be taught, he would have taught it.
- Meno's own circle disagrees on whether virtue can be taught. Theognis contradicts himself on it. Socrates says people who disagree this much cannot be called teachers.

chunks.heading: Knowledge versus true opinion: Daedalus's statues
chunks.text:
- Socrates corrects his earlier claim that only a person with knowledge can guide well. A person who has never been to Larisa but holds a true opinion about the road guides just as well as one who knows it.
- True opinion is as useful in action as knowledge. The difference is that knowledge always stays right and opinion is sometimes right.
- Image: the statues of Daedalus run away unless tied down. True opinions are "beautiful and fruitful" but flee the soul until "fastened by the tie of the cause." This tying is recollection, and it makes opinion into knowledge. That is why knowledge is "more honourable and excellent."
- Of the claim that knowledge differs from true opinion, he says: "There are not many things which I profess to know, but this is most certainly one of them."

chunks.heading: Conclusion: virtue as a divine gift, and the unfinished question
chunks.text:
- Statesmen like Themistocles did not govern by knowledge, since they could not pass on their virtue. They governed by right opinion, "in politics what divination is in religion." Diviners, prophets and poets say many true things "not knowing what they say." Socrates calls such statesmen "divine."
- His conclusion: virtue is "neither natural nor acquired, but an instinct given by God to the virtuous," not accompanied by reason.
- If someone existed who could educate statesmen, he would be among the living what Tiresias was among the dead, "he alone has understanding; but the rest are flitting shades."
- He says the certain truth cannot be known "until, before asking how virtue is given, we enquire into the actual nature of virtue." He leaves asking Meno to calm Anytus.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Socrates warns young Hippocrates not to hand his soul to a sophist whose wares he cannot judge, then cross-examines Protagoras on whether virtue can be taught. He argues that the virtues are one, that no one knowingly chooses evil, and that wrongdoing, courage included, comes down to knowledge or ignorance.

chunks.heading: Why Socrates examines a teacher before handing him your soul
chunks.text:
