- Socrates tests Hippocrates, who rushes to Protagoras at dawn, by asking what each teacher *makes* of a pupil: a physician makes a physician, a sculptor makes a sculptor. Hippocrates cannot say what a Sophist makes of him, and he blushes at the answer "a Sophist."
- He says knowledge is "the food of the soul." Sophists who sell wisdom praise all their goods alike, without knowing what helps or harms the soul, and so do most of their customers.
- Food bought for the body can be carried home in another vessel and shown to an expert before eating. Knowledge cannot: "when you have paid for them you must receive them into the soul and go your way, either greatly harmed or greatly benefited."
- Practical rule: consult elders, friends and kin for many days before committing the soul, as one would before entrusting the body. Unless you can tell good from evil yourself, "do not hazard your dearest interests at a game of chance."
- His standing test for any teacher is to ask "in what shall I become better, and about what?" Protagoras's vague promise to make pupils "better every day" is not an answer.

chunks.heading: Why Socrates doubts that political virtue can be taught
chunks.text:
- He asks Protagoras to answer concretely what the pupil will improve in. Protagoras replies: prudence in private and public affairs, which Socrates restates as "the art of politics" that "makes men good citizens."
- Evidence against teachability:
  - The Athenian assembly consults specialists on building and shipbuilding, and shouts down any unskilled adviser. On affairs of state it lets carpenter, tinker, cobbler and sailor speak, as if the subject cannot be taught.
  - Pericles taught his sons every subject masters could teach but not virtue. He let them wander "in a sort of hope that they would light upon virtue of their own accord."
  - Cleinias, Alcibiades's younger brother, was sent away by Pericles, and the new guardian Ariphron returned him within six months, not knowing what to do with him.
  - He says he could name "numberless" good men who never made anyone else good.
- Socrates admits he wavers: he first said no human care could make men good, then says he knows better after hearing Protagoras's speech. He wants the question settled by argument, not by speeches.

chunks.heading: Speeches versus short questions and answers
chunks.text:
- Socrates criticizes long orations: great speakers are "like books" or "brazen pots," which keep ringing after being struck, and cannot answer or ask a question.
- He praises question-and-answer as a rare skill, and insists on short answers because of a "bad memory." Discussion "is one thing, and making an oration is quite another."
- He compares himself to a slow runner: "if you want to see Crison and me in the same stadium, you must bid him slacken his speed to mine."
- When Protagoras refuses to keep to short answers, Socrates rises to leave rather than force the conversation. He refuses an umpire: anyone chosen would be inferior, equal, or better than Protagoras, and none of those helps.
- He prefers partners to poets: poets "cannot be interrogated about the meaning of what they are saying," so their interpreters never settle a dispute. Educated people use "their own voices" and "put one another to the proof in conversation," not flute-girls or recited verse.
- He says he asks only to "clear up my own difficulties": "when two go together, one sees before the other," and a discoverer wants someone to confirm his finding.

chunks.heading: Is virtue one, and are its parts distinct?
chunks.text:
- Socrates asks whether justice, temperance, holiness, courage and wisdom are five names for one thing or separate parts. Protagoras says they differ like the parts of a face (eyes and ears), not like pieces of gold.
- Socrates secures agreement that justice is just and holiness is holy, so "justice is either the same with holiness, or very nearly the same."
- An argument from opposites: each thing has only one opposite. Folly is the opposite of wisdom and also of temperance, so wisdom and temperance must be the same.
- He tests the claim that an unjust man can be temperate, using "good sense" and "good counsel." He is also willing to be tested himself: "I who ask and you who answer may both be put on our trial."
- His method: never accept "if you wish" agreements. He wants a conclusion proven for the speakers themselves, "if there be no 'if.'"

chunks.heading: Courage is knowledge of what is and is not to be feared
chunks.text:
- Protagoras claims courage differs from the other virtues, since some very unjust, unholy or ignorant men are courageous. Socrates examines this.
- Divers, skilled horsemen and peltasts are confident because they have knowledge. Ignorant but confident people are mad, not brave, so confidence alone is not courage.
- Socrates concludes that cowards are cowards through ignorance of what is dangerous. Courage is therefore "the knowledge of that which is and is not dangerous," and wisdom is courage.
- Everyone, brave or cowardly, goes toward what he thinks is better. No one willingly goes toward what he believes to be a danger or an evil.
- Protagoras goes silent and will not assent to the last step, then concedes that an ignorant yet courageous man is impossible consistent with the argument.

chunks.heading: No one does wrong willingly: the "power of pleasure" is ignorance
chunks.text:
- Socrates asks whether knowledge is a slave to anger, pleasure, pain, love or fear, as most people think. He and Protagoras hold that knowledge is "a noble and commanding thing" that cannot be overcome if one truly knows good from evil.
- He argues that acting against one's knowledge makes no sense. Pleasures count as evil only because of later pain or lost pleasures, and pains as good only because of later pleasure. Good and evil are measured by pleasure and pain, differing in "more and fewer, greater and less."
- Being "overcome by pleasure" then means choosing a smaller good over a larger one. This is an error of calculation, so it is simply "ignorance, and that the greatest."
- The saving art is measurement. Near pleasures look larger, as near objects do, so "the power of appearance" deceives us. A "weighing" of pleasures and pains by nearness and distance would "teach the soul at last to find rest in the truth, and would thus save our life."
- Conclusions he draws: "no man voluntarily pursues evil, or that which he thinks to be evil." To prefer the worse to the better is not in human nature. The inferiority of a man to himself is ignorance, and superiority is wisdom.

chunks.heading: The upshot: virtue is knowledge, so it can be taught
chunks.text:
- Socrates notes the dialogue's irony: he began by denying that virtue can be taught, yet his argument that all virtues are knowledge implies it can be. Protagoras, who began by claiming it can be taught, argued it is not knowledge, which implies it cannot.
- He wants to continue until they learn "what virtue is, whether capable of being taught or not."
- He prefers Prometheus (forethought) to Epimetheus: he applies "Promethean care of my own life" to these questions.
- He tells the Sophists and the public that if ignorance is the cause of wrongdoing, those who think the art of measurement cannot be taught are mistaken. They neither go to teachers themselves nor send their children, and "the result is that you are the worse off both in public and private life."

chunks.heading: Reading a poet: Simonides and Pittacus
chunks.text:
- When Protagoras accuses Simonides of contradicting himself ("hardly can a man become truly good" versus blaming Pittacus for "hardly can a man be good"), Socrates admits he felt "giddy and faint, as if I had received a blow from the hand of an expert boxer."
- He defends the poem by distinguishing *becoming* good from *being* good. Becoming good is hard but possible. Staying good is impossible for man, because only God has it, and circumstances overpower even the skilled.
- He reads "truly" with "hard," not with "good." The poem is an attack on Pittacus's saying, not a muddle.
- He also claims Spartan and Cretan wisdom lies in terse sayings, like the Delphic "Know thyself" and "Nothing too much."
- Key claim inside his reading: "no wise man... will allow that any human being errs voluntarily"; all who do evil do it against their will.
- He treats the whole exercise partly as mischief and then drops it: quoting poets is like a vulgar party hiring flute-girls. Real conversation tests the speakers themselves.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Socrates refuses to flatter Love and instead questions Agathon, then recounts Diotima's teaching: love is desire for what one lacks, the everlasting possession of the good, and a birth in beauty. The philosopher stands between ignorance and wisdom, and love leads upward from beautiful bodies to souls, laws, knowledge and beauty itself.

chunks.heading: Love as lack: Socrates' claim that he knows only "the art of love"
chunks.text:
- Socrates says he is a master only of "matters of love" and agrees to praise Love only if he may "speak the truth" rather than flatter.
- He objects to the earlier speeches. He had thought praise meant choosing "out of the true" the best things and setting them forth well. He now sees the others attribute "every species of greatness" to Love, "without regard to truth or falsehood", so that Love only appears praised.
- He says such praise fools "those who know him not", but "you cannot impose upon those who know him".
- He will not rival them: "I do not praise in that way; no, indeed, I cannot."
- He starts from a few questions to Agathon, using his admissions as premises, and then retells what the priestess Diotima of Mantineia taught him.

chunks.heading: The elenchus on Agathon: desire implies want
chunks.text:
Socrates' questioning of Agathon runs step by step.

- Love is always love *of* something, as a father is father of a son and a brother is brother of someone.
- Whoever desires something lacks it. "He who desires something is in want of something... absolutely and necessarily true."
- A man cannot desire what he already is. The strong do not desire strength, and the healthy do not desire health.
- When a rich or healthy man says "I desire what I have", he really wants those goods *preserved in the future*, which he does not yet possess.
- Agathon had said Love sets the gods in order through love of the beautiful. So Love lacks beauty. What lacks beauty is not beautiful, and the beautiful is also the good, so Love lacks the good too.
- Agathon concedes: "I cannot refute you, Socrates." Socrates replies: "Say rather, beloved Agathon, that you cannot refute the truth; for Socrates is easily refuted."

chunks.heading: Diotima's correction: Love is neither fair nor foul
chunks.text:
Socrates reports that Diotima corrected his own earlier belief that Love was "a mighty god, and likewise fair".

- Not fair does not mean foul, and not good does not mean evil. There is a mean.
- The parallel she gives is *right opinion*. It lies between knowledge and ignorance, because it cannot give a reason (so it is not knowledge) yet it does reach the truth (so it is not ignorance).
- Gods are happy and possess the good and fair. Love lacks them, so Love is not a god.
- Love is a *daimon*, "a great spirit... intermediate between the divine and the mortal". He interprets between gods and men, carrying prayers up and commands down, and so binds the whole together.
- Socrates' error was a confusion of *love and the beloved*. The beloved is the beautiful and perfect. The lover has "another nature".

chunks.heading: The myth of Love's parentage: Poros and Penia
chunks.text:
- Love was conceived on Aphrodite's birthday. Poros (Plenty), son of Metis (Discretion), fell asleep drunk on nectar in Zeus's garden, and Penia (Poverty) lay with him.
- From his mother Love is always poor: "rough and squalid, and has no shoes, nor a house to dwell in", sleeping on bare ground at doors.
- From his father he is "bold, enterprising, strong, a mighty hunter", "always weaving some intrigue", "fertile in resources", "a philosopher at all times".
- He is neither mortal nor immortal, flourishing in plenty and dying in want. "That which is always flowing in is always flowing out, and so he is never in want and never in wealth."

chunks.heading: Why the philosopher is a lover: wisdom, ignorance and the mean
chunks.text:
- "No god is a philosopher or seeker after wisdom, for he is wise already; nor does any man who is wise seek after wisdom."
- The ignorant do not seek wisdom either. "Herein is the evil of ignorance, that he who is neither good nor wise is nevertheless satisfied with himself: he has no desire for that of which he feels no want."
- Philosophers are therefore those in between, and Love is one of them. Wisdom is among the most beautiful things and Love is of the beautiful, so Love is a philosopher.
- Diotima's point is that desire for wisdom begins with felt lack. This links to Socrates' own profession of ignorance: "my ignorance is the reason why I come to you; for I am conscious that I want a teacher."

chunks.heading: What lovers actually want: the good, forever
chunks.text:
Diotima's questions run in sequence.

- A man who loves the beautiful wants it to be *his*. Putting "good" in place of "beautiful": he wants the *possession of the good*, and the result of that is happiness. No further reason for wanting happiness is needed. "The answer is already final."
- All men desire their own good. Only some are called lovers because the name of the whole is given to one part, as "poet" is given to makers of music and metre though all art is making.
- Against Aristophanes' story that lovers seek their "other half", she says they seek neither half nor whole "unless the half or the whole be also a good". Men would cut off their own diseased hands and feet. "There is nothing which men love but the good."
- Love is therefore "the love of the everlasting possession of the good". Since mortals can only approach this through generation, love is also love of immortality.

chunks.heading: Birth in beauty: why love aims at immortality
chunks.text:
- All people are "pregnant" in body and soul and want to give birth, but only in beauty. Beauty is like the goddess of childbirth: near it the conceiving power is "propitious, and diffusive, and benign"; near ugliness it "frowns and contracts".
- Love is not of the beautiful itself but "of generation and of birth in beauty", because generation is the mortal creature's share of eternity.
- Even one person is never the same: hair, flesh, bones and blood change, and so do habits, opinions, desires, pleasures, pains and fears. Knowledge too is lost and renewed by "recollection". Mortals are preserved by *succession*, leaving a new thing in place of the old.
- This explains why animals will starve and fight to the death for their young.
- It also explains ambition. Men risk more for fame than for children. Alcestis, Achilles and Codrus would not have died without hope of "immortal" memory of virtue, and "the better they are the more they do them".
- Souls "pregnant" more than bodies conceive wisdom and virtue. The greatest, fairest wisdom "is that which is concerned with the ordering of states and families, and which is called temperance and justice".
- Such a person seeks a beautiful, noble, well-nurtured soul, talks to him of virtue and tries to educate him. Their shared "children" are fairer and more immortal than bodily ones, which is why Homer, Hesiod, Lycurgus and Solon are honoured for their offspring.

chunks.heading: The ladder of love (the "greater mysteries")
chunks.text:
Diotima describes the order of going aright, guided by an instructor:

1. Begin in youth by loving one beautiful body and "create fair thoughts" out of it.
2. See that the beauty of one body is akin to that of all, and so abate the "violent love of the one".
3. Value beauty of soul above beauty of body, so that a virtuous soul with little comeliness is still worth loving and tending, and bring forth thoughts that "improve the young".
4. Contemplate the beauty of institutions and laws.
5. Move on to the sciences, no longer a slave "narrow-minded" to one youth or man or institution, but looking on "the vast sea of beauty".
6. Suddenly see the beautiful itself.

This beauty is:
- everlasting, neither growing nor decaying
- not fair in one respect and foul in another, nor fair to some and foul to others
- not found in a face, hands, speech, knowledge or any particular being
- "absolute, separate, simple, and everlasting", imparted to all changing beautiful things without diminishing or changing

The rungs are "steps only": from one to two, to all fair forms, to fair practices, to fair notions, to the notion of absolute beauty, until one "knows what the essence of beauty is".

chunks.heading: The best life and why Socrates endorses love
chunks.text:
- Diotima: the best life is "the contemplation of beauty absolute". Gold, fine clothes and beautiful youths, who now "entrance" Socrates, are nothing beside it.
- Seeing true beauty "with the eye of the mind", one brings forth "not images of beauty, but realities", and so "true virtue". That makes one "the friend of God and... immortal, if mortal man may". She asks: "Would that be an ignoble life?"
- Socrates says he is persuaded and tries to persuade others that "human nature will not easily find a helper better than love". Every man should honour Love "as I myself honour him, and walk in his ways, and exhort others to do the same".

chunks.heading: Socrates as seen by Alcibiades: his temperance, endurance and effect on others
chunks.text:
These points concern Socrates' conduct, as shown by Alcibiades' account, which Socrates invites with "speak the truth" (he allows it to be corrected if false).

- On Alcibiades' offer to give himself in exchange for Socrates' help toward virtue, Socrates answers ironically that Alcibiades would be trading "appearance" for "true beauty", like Diomede swapping gold for brass. He says, "The mind begins to grow critical when the bodily eye fails". They shared a bed and nothing happened; Alcibiades rose "as from the couch of a father or an elder brother."
- Alcibiades reports that Socrates' words alone stir the soul more than the best orators. They make him feel shame and admit that he should not neglect his soul "busying myself with the concerns of the Athenians". He adds that Socrates is "the only person who ever made me ashamed".
- Alcibiades reports that Socrates scorns wealth, beauty and honour, drinks without ever being drunk, and marches barefoot on ice. At Potidaea he stood in thought from dawn through the next morning, and he saved Alcibiades' life and arms in battle.
- Alcibiades also says Socrates' plain talk of "pack-asses and smiths and cobblers and curriers" is like a Silenus statue that opens to reveal "divine and golden images"; the words contain "the whole duty of a good and honourable man". He says Socrates, who began as a lover, ends by being courted by the young.
- At dawn Socrates is shown arguing that the genius of comedy and tragedy is one, and that the true tragic artist is also a comic artist.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Socrates contrasts the sophists Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, who trap a boy with verbal tricks, with his own sincere exhortation to philosophy. He argues that no possession is good unless guided by wisdom, so wisdom is the only good and ignorance the only evil. The search for the knowledge that both makes and uses ends in perplexity, yet he urges Crito to pursue philosophy itself, not judge it by bad teachers.

chunks.heading: The unexamined account of wisdom as the only good
chunks.text:
Socrates argues that all people want to be happy, and that happiness requires having many good things. He first lists the commonly accepted goods: wealth, health, beauty, good birth, power, honours, temperance, justice, courage, wisdom and good fortune.

- Having good things is not enough. They must be used, and "there is no advantage in merely having them."
- Using them wrongly is worse than not using them at all. Non-use is neither good nor evil, while wrong use is an evil.
- A carpenter with plenty of tools and wood who never works gains nothing from them. A man with food and drink who never eats or drinks is not helped by them.
- Only knowledge directs the right use of wealth, health and beauty. In every possession and use of a thing, knowledge gives a man both good fortune and success.
- Socrates concludes that wealth, health, beauty and the rest "are not to be regarded as goods in themselves." Under ignorance they are greater evils than their opposites, because they better serve the evil principle that rules them. Under wisdom and prudence they are greater goods. "In themselves they are nothing."
- So other things are indifferent. Wisdom is the only good and ignorance the only evil.

chunks.heading: Why wisdom counts as good fortune
chunks.text:
Socrates adds good fortune to the list of goods, then argues it is already covered by wisdom: "Surely wisdom is good-fortune; even a child may know that."

- He gives examples: flute-players succeed at playing, scribes at writing and reading, and wise pilots in the dangers of the sea.
- He asks Cleinias whom he would rather go to war with (a wise or a foolish general) and whom he would rather have in a dangerous illness (a wise or an ignorant physician). The answer is always the wise one.
- Reasoning: a wise man would never err, so he acts rightly and succeeds, "or his wisdom would be wisdom no longer." He who has wisdom has no need of fortune.

chunks.heading: Doing less with wisdom beats doing more without it
chunks.text:
Socrates argues that possessions and activity profit a man nothing without good sense.

- If a man does fewer things, he makes fewer mistakes. Fewer mistakes bring fewer misfortunes, and fewer misfortunes make him less miserable.
- It follows that, without wisdom, a poor man does less than a rich man, a weak man less than a strong man, a coward less than a courageous man, and an indolent man less than an active one. In each case the lesser capacity does less harm.
- This is why the goods of fortune only become good "under the guidance of knowledge."

chunks.heading: The exhortation to philosophy
chunks.text:
From these premises Socrates draws a practical conclusion: everyone should try to make himself as wise as he can.

- Since all men desire happiness, and happiness comes from the right use of the things of life, and knowledge gives that right use, "everybody ought by all means to try and make himself as wise as he can."
- Wisdom is a treasure worth far more than money. Asking a father, guardian, friend or suitor to impart it is "not at all dishonourable."
- No service done to anyone, whether a lover or not, is to be blamed if its aim is to get wisdom.
- He notes a question still open between himself and Cleinias: whether wisdom can be taught or comes spontaneously. Cleinias says it can be taught, and Socrates is glad to be spared "a long and tiresome investigation."
- He sets this up as the model of a sincere exhortation: persuade the young person to love wisdom and virtue, then ask which single kind of knowledge makes a person good and happy.

chunks.heading: The knowledge we need must both make and use
chunks.text:
Socrates tests which art could be the knowledge of happiness, and finds that it must be one that uses what it produces.

- Knowing where gold lies hidden, or how to turn stones into gold, would be useless without knowing how to use the gold. The same goes for money-making, medicine, or a knowledge that made men immortal without knowing how to use immortality.
- The makers of lyres and flutes have an art that makes. The player has a different art that uses. The wanted knowledge is "one that uses as well as makes."
- Speech-writing fails the test. Some composers cannot use the speeches they write, and some users cannot compose them. Socrates calls this art a branch of enchantment, charming juries and assemblies as the snake-charmer charms snakes.
- The general's art fails too. Per Cleinias's argument, which Socrates endorses, hunters of every kind (generals, geometers, astronomers, calculators) only catch their prey and hand it to another art to use. A general who takes a city hands it to the statesman.

chunks.heading: The kingly art and the dead end
chunks.text:
Socrates next considers the kingly, or political, art, which seems to command all other arts and so to be the knowledge he seeks.

- It fails when asked what it produces. Medicine produces health and husbandry produces food, but the kingly art cannot name its product.
- Its supposed results (wealth, freedom, tranquillity) are neither good nor evil in themselves. The only good is knowledge, so the kingly art would have to make others wise or good.
- But it cannot say in what it makes them good. It makes others good, who make others good, "without ever determining in what they are to be good." Socrates calls it "the old, old song over again."
- He confesses the inquiry ended in perplexity: "we were like children after larks, always on the point of catching the art, which was always getting away from us." He describes a labyrinth where they "came out again at the beginning."

chunks.heading: Eristic trickery versus real philosophy
chunks.text:
Socrates contrasts his own questioning with the verbal tricks of Euthydemus and Dionysodorus.

- Their puzzles ("do the wise or the ignorant learn?", "you want him to be what he is not, so you want him to perish") trade on ambiguous words. Socrates explains that "to learn" has two senses and that such quibbles are "not serious."
- He says that a man who knew every such trick "would not be at all the wiser; he would only be able to play with men," like someone who pulls a stool away as a man sits down.
- He treats this as a mere preliminary game, "initiation into the correct use of terms," and keeps asking the brothers to turn to serious exhortation.
- He ironically praises their tricks, noting that they can be taught quickly and that an art anyone can pick up cheaply will be undervalued.
- He argues that their doctrines (no falsehood, no contradiction, no ignorance) are self-defeating. If error is impossible, there is nothing for them to teach.

chunks.heading: Judge philosophy itself, not its teachers
chunks.text:
When Crito is put off by a critic who dismissed the sophists' discussion as "making much ado about nothing," Socrates defends philosophy.

- He tells Crito not to mind whether the teachers of philosophy are good or bad, "but think only of philosophy herself."
- In every trade (gymnastics, rhetoric, money-making, generalship) the inferior practitioners are many and worthless, and the good are few and "beyond all price." Crito would not shun those arts or forbid them to his son for that reason.
- Test philosophy honestly. If she is evil, turn all men from her. If she is what Socrates believes, "then follow her and serve her, you and your house... and be of good cheer."
- He also rebuts the orator-politician who claims to stand between philosophy and politics. Something in a mean between two goods that tend to different ends falls short of both. Such people are "third, although they would like to stand first," though he adds that anyone who manfully pursues something like wisdom deserves some affection.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Socrates cross-examines Gorgias and Polus on what rhetoric is, arguing it persuades the ignorant without knowledge and is a counterfeit of justice. He then argues that doing injustice is the worst evil, and that escaping punishment is worse than being punished, since punishment heals the soul.

chunks.heading: Rhetoric is flattery, not an art
chunks.text:
- Socrates asks Gorgias to name his art the way a cobbler names his: by its nature, not its praise. He says Polus "has attended more to the art which is called rhetoric than to dialectic" because Polus praised the art without defining it.
- He gets Gorgias to admit that rhetoric works by persuasion about the just and unjust. It produces belief without knowledge, since "no one can be supposed to instruct such a vast multitude about such high matters in a short time".
- The rhetorician only has to persuade the ignorant that he knows more than those who know. Socrates says that when the rhetorician beats the physician before a crowd, "the ignorant is more persuasive with the ignorant than he who has knowledge".
- Socrates denies that rhetoric is an art. It is "a sort of experience" in producing delight and gratification, and he calls it "the habit of a bold and ready wit, which knows how to manage mankind". He sums it up as "flattery".
- An art can "explain or give a reason of the nature of its own applications". Cookery and rhetoric cannot, and Socrates will not "call any irrational thing an art".

chunks.heading: The four arts and their four counterfeits
chunks.text:
- Socrates sets out two arts for the body and two for the soul, each paired with a flattering imitation:
  - Body: gymnastic (to keep it fit) and medicine (to cure it). Their imitations are tiring (the art of attiring and cosmetics) and cookery.
  - Soul: legislation and justice. Their imitations are sophistry and rhetoric.
- He gives the proportions "after the manner of the geometricians": tiring is to gymnastic as cookery is to medicine; sophistry is to legislation as rhetoric is to justice.
- Flattery "aims at pleasure without any thought of the best". It makes pleasure "the bait of the unwary".
- His test case: if a physician and a cook competed before children, "the physician would be starved to death".
- Rhetoric is "the ghost or counterfeit of a part of politics". He calls it ignoble because it seeks the pleasing, not the good.

chunks.heading: Why the rhetorician must be just, and the contradiction in Gorgias
chunks.text:
- Socrates shows that whoever has learned a thing is what the knowledge makes him: the carpenter, the musician, the physician. So whoever has learned what is just is just.
- The just man always wants to do what is just and will never consent to injustice. A rhetorician who knows justice therefore could not misuse his art.
- This contradicts Gorgias's earlier claim that a teacher should not be blamed if a pupil misuses rhetoric, as with a trainer and a boxer who strikes his father.
- Socrates notes the inconsistency and expects "a great deal of discussion, before we get at the truth of all this".

chunks.heading: Willing the good: why tyrants have no real power
chunks.text:
- Polus says rhetoricians are like tyrants who "kill and despoil and exile any one whom they please". Socrates replies that they have "the least possible power in states".
- Men do not will what they do. They will the end for the sake of which they do it. Examples:
  - Taking painful medicine: they will health.
  - Sailing and trading: they will wealth.
  - Killing or exiling: they will their own good.
- So someone who does what only seems best to him, but is actually bad for him, does not do what he wills. A fool doing what he thinks best has no power, because power is a good only if it benefits the possessor.
- He mocks the idea with a dagger in the Agora: carrying a dagger and being able to kill anyone is not "great power". Such acts bring punishment, and punishment is an evil.
- Killing, exile and confiscation are good "when they are just, and evil when they are unjust".
- He tells Polus not to envy the unjust ruler. Such men are "wretches who are not to be envied, but only to pity".

chunks.heading: Truth over numbers: the single witness
chunks.text:
- Polus points to Archelaus of Macedonia, who murdered his relatives to take the throne. Polus says Archelaus is wicked and yet happy.
- Socrates says he cannot judge whether a man is happy without knowing "how he stands in the matter of education and justice". He claims that "the men and women who are gentle and good are also happy... and the unjust and evil are miserable".
- He rejects courtroom-style refutation by many reputable witnesses: "a man may often be sworn down by a multitude of false witnesses who have a great air of respectability".
- His method needs only the agreement of the person he is arguing with: "I shall produce one witness only of the truth of my words, and he is the person with whom I am arguing."
- He names Nicias, the family of Pericles and others who would side with Polus. He still stands alone, because "who can refute the truth?"
- He says he is "not a public man" and cannot take votes. He will not count heads.
- Whether a man is happy or miserable is, for him, the greatest question, because "what ignorance more disgraceful than this?"

chunks.heading: Doing wrong is worse than suffering it
chunks.text:
- Socrates says it is worse to do injustice than to suffer it. "I should not like either, but if I must choose... I would rather suffer than do." He thinks everyone shares this view, including Polus.
- The argument:
  - Polus admits that doing wrong is more disgraceful than suffering it, though he thinks suffering is the greater evil.
  - Beautiful things are beautiful by reason of pleasure, utility or both. Disgraceful things are disgraceful by pain, evil or both.
  - Doing injustice does not cause more pain than suffering it, so its extra disgrace must lie in greater evil.
  - So doing injustice is the greater evil. No one would choose a greater evil over a lesser one.
- Gorgias's pupil is led to agree that "to do injustice is the greater evil of the two".

chunks.heading: Punishment as medicine, and what rhetoric is for
chunks.text:
- Socrates asks Polus whether being punished is doing or suffering. Polus says suffering. The agent is the punisher, who acts justly, and the one punished suffers justly. What is just is honourable and so good, so the punished man is benefited: his soul is improved.
- There are three parallel evils. Poverty belongs to the estate, disease to the body and injustice to the soul. The soul's evils (injustice, ignorance, cowardice, intemperance) are the most disgraceful and the most hurtful.
- Three arts remove them: money-making cures poverty, medicine cures disease and justice (the judge) cures vice. Justice is the best of the three.
- Being healed is useful but not pleasant. The man who was never ill is happier than the man cured. Order of happiness:
  - First: never having had vice in the soul.
  - Second: being delivered from vice through admonition, rebuke and punishment.
  - Worst: the unjust man who escapes punishment.
- Escaping punishment is like a child so afraid of the knife or cautery that he lets a disease become "the incurable cancer of the soul". Such people gather "money and friends" and "cultivate to the utmost their powers of persuasion" to evade justice.
- Consequences for how to live:
  - Everyone should guard against doing wrong.
  - If he or someone he cares about does wrong, he should go to the judge "as he would to the physician".
  - Rhetoric is useful only to accuse oneself and one's family and friends, so that "the wrong-doer may suffer and be made whole". He should not shrink from "stripes, bonds, fines, exile or death".
  - Rhetoric is useless for excusing injustice. It could serve only someone who wanted an enemy to escape punishment, which Socrates treats as a reductio.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Socrates answers Callicles' claim that natural justice is might and that happiness is unlimited appetite. He argues pleasure is not the good, that a well-ordered temperate soul is happy, that true statesmanship improves citizens, and that doing injustice is worse than suffering it. He closes with the judgment myth and a call to live justly.

chunks.heading: Doing injustice is worse than suffering it, and escaping punishment is worse still
chunks.text:
- Socrates holds that the doer of injustice is worse off than the victim. Being boxed on the ears, robbed or killed wrongfully is not the worst evil. Smiting and despoiling others is "far more disgraceful and evil to the doer of the wrong than to me who am the sufferer."
- There is a greater evil than doing injustice: the unjust man who is not punished.
- He says these conclusions are "fixed and riveted... in words which are like bonds of iron and adamant," unless someone refutes them. He claims he does not know how things are, but has never met anyone who could say otherwise without looking ridiculous.
- Nobody does wrong willingly. Avoiding injustice takes power and art (knowledge), not just good intentions.
- When an argument ends with only one man agreeing, he still wants it finished: "the discovery of the truth is a common good."

chunks.heading: Against Callicles' "natural justice" of the strong: who is "better"?
chunks.text:
- Callicles says nature makes it just for the stronger and better to rule and take more, and that law is a trick of the weak majority. Socrates answers by pressing for a definition of "better."
- If the stronger are the better, then the many are stronger than the one. Their laws, which say justice is equality and doing injustice is more shameful than suffering it, would then be natural and good. Nature and convention would not be opposed, as Callicles claimed.
- Callicles shifts from "stronger" to "wiser" to "wise and courageous in running a state." Socrates charges him with "never saying the same about the same things."
- Socrates tests "the wiser should have more" with concrete cases: a physician with the food, a weaver with the coats, a shoemaker with the shoes, a farmer with the seed. In each, the expert's superiority gives authority over distribution, not a bigger personal share.
- He asks whether the ruler also rules himself. Self-rule means being "temperate and master of himself, and ruler of his own pleasures and passions."

chunks.heading: Temperance against unlimited appetite: the leaky jars
chunks.text:
- Callicles says the happy man lets his desires grow to the utmost and satisfies them all. He calls temperance a virtue invented by the weak, and calls luxury, intemperance and licence "virtue and happiness."
- Socrates tells an image from a Sicilian or Italian thinker. The souls of the ignorant are leaky jars, or a colander, that are never filled. The unrestrained part of the soul is the leaky vessel.
- His two-casks figure compares two men:
  - One has sound casks filled with wine, honey and milk. Once full, he needs no more toil or worry.
  - The other has leaky casks and must fill them night and day, or suffer.
- Callicles replies that a filled cask means no pleasure, "the life of a stone." Socrates answers that the leaky life is that of a cormorant, always hungering and eating.
- He presses the consequences of Callicles' view. If all pleasure is happiness, the man who spends his life scratching an itch is happy, and so is the catamite, which Callicles will not accept.
- Socrates urges Callicles to choose the "orderly and sufficient" life, with due provision for daily needs, over the insatiate one.

chunks.heading: Pleasure is not the good
chunks.text:
- Socrates gets Callicles to agree that good and evil fortune are opposites and cannot be had and lost at the same time, like health and disease of the eyes.
- Hunger and thirst are painful, and drinking while thirsty is pleasant. So pleasure and pain are present together. Thirst and the pleasure of drinking also cease at the same moment, but good and evil do not. Therefore good is not the same as pleasure, nor evil the same as pain.
- A second argument: the good are good by the presence of good. But fools and cowards rejoice as much as the wise and brave, and cowards more in some cases. If pleasure were the good, the bad would be as good as the good or better.
- Callicles concedes that some pleasures are good and some bad. Socrates then states the rule: all actions are done for the sake of the good, so pleasure is to be sought for the sake of the good and not the reverse. Choosing among pleasures takes art and knowledge.

chunks.heading: Flattery versus real care: cookery and medicine, for body and soul
Order in the soul: temperance, justice and the good life
chunks.text:
- Every good thing, whether a house, ship, body or soul, is good through order and arrangement. Order in the body is health and strength. Order in the soul is called "lawful" and "law," which gives temperance and justice.
- A sick body is not given whatever it craves, and a soul in bad state should likewise have its desires restrained. Chastisement is better for such a soul than lack of control.
- The argument in his summary:
  - The soul with order is temperate and good.
  - The temperate man does what is proper toward the gods (holy) and toward men (just).
  - He is also courageous, since he pursues and avoids what he ought and endures when he ought.
  - So he is perfectly good, does well in all he does, and "must of necessity be happy and blessed."
  - The evil man is miserable.
- Practical conclusions:
  - Whoever wants to be happy must pursue temperance and flee intemperance "as fast as his legs will carry him."
  - Best is to live so as not to need punishment. If a person or city does need it, justice must be done and he must accept it.
  - The unrestrained "robber's life" leaves a man "incapable of communion," so he is incapable of friendship and is friend to neither god nor man.
- Socrates cites the philosophers' view that "communion and friendship and orderliness and temperance and justice bind together heaven and earth and gods and men," which is why the universe is a Cosmos. He charges Callicles with neglecting geometrical equality and chasing excess.

chunks.heading: Power, self-defence and tyranny
chunks.text:
- Callicles says Socrates is defenceless: anyone can strike, rob or kill him. Socrates answers that the best defence is never to have said or done wrong toward gods or men. A man who is "his own defence" is well protected. He would be ashamed to fail at that kind of defence, but not to lack flattery or rhetoric.
- To avoid suffering injustice, one must be the ruler, or the equal and companion of the ruler. Like is friend to like, so the tyrant's only real friend is someone with the same likes and dislikes who is subservient to him.
- Imitating the tyrant keeps you safe from harm but leads you to do as much wrong as possible, unpunished. That corrupts the soul, "the greatest evil."
- Socrates also rejects survival as the supreme aim. The pilot, like the pleader, saves bodies and goods for two obols or at most two drachmae (Aegina to Athens, or longer voyages), and is modest about it. He cannot tell whether passengers are better for being saved. For a man with an incurable disease of the soul, life is no benefit.
- "No man who is not an utter fool and coward is afraid of death itself, but he is afraid of doing wrong." To arrive in the next world "having one's soul full of injustice is the last and worst of all evils."
- A man who is truly noble stops caring about living a set length of time. He leaves fate to God and asks how to spend his term well.

chunks.heading: Statesmanship as care for the citizens, and the myth of judgment
chunks.text:
- Socrates argues that a statesman's task is to make citizens better. Before taking on public works, you should ask who taught you and what you have built privately. He does the same with medicine: ask whether anyone was ever cured by you. He asks Callicles whom he has ever made better, and gets no answer.
- Pericles, Cimon, Themistocles and Miltiades supplied ships, walls and docks. They fed appetites like bakers and cooks. Socrates says they left "no room for justice and temperance." He points out that Pericles was convicted of theft, Cimon ostracized, Themistocles exiled and Miltiades nearly put to death.
- Socrates says that, like a trainer who made horses fiercer, Pericles was a bad shepherd of men if the citizens turned savage. A true teacher of virtue could safely leave his pay to his pupils, since having removed injustice from them he has nothing to fear from them.
- He asks whether he should be the physician of the state or its flatterer, and calls himself "the only politician of my time" because he looks to what is best, not to what is pleasant. He expects to be tried like a physician accused by a cook before a jury of children.
- The myth of judgment:
  - Zeus reforms the old practice of judging the living, who came clothed in wealth, rank and witnesses. Now souls are judged naked and dead by the sons Minos, Rhadamanthus and Aeacus.
  - Death is only the separation of soul and body. Each keeps its marks, so a soul bears scars of perjuries and crimes.
  - Punishment has two purposes: to improve the curable, or to be an example to others when the offender is incurable. Most such examples are tyrants and kings, because power allows the worst crimes. The text cites Archelaus, Tantalus, Sisyphus and Tityus. Aristeides, son of Lysimachus, is named as a rare just man in power.
  - A philosopher who has "done his own work" is the likeliest to go to the Islands of the Blessed.
- Socrates' closing position: he renounces worldly honours, wants "to know the truth, and to live as well as I can, and, when I die, to die as well as I can." Of everything argued, what remains unshaken is that doing injustice is more to be avoided than suffering it, that the reality and not the appearance of virtue is to be followed, that the wrongdoer must be chastised, and that flattery of oneself and others must be avoided.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: On his last day, Socrates argues the true philosopher spends life practising death, freeing the soul from bodily distraction to pursue wisdom. He defines virtue as wisdom rather than a trade of fears and pleasures, and offers arguments (opposites, recollection, affinity) that the soul is akin to the unchanging and survives death.

chunks.heading: Why Socrates calls philosophy the practice of dying
chunks.text:
- Socrates tells his friends that true philosophers are "always pursuing death and dying," so they should not grieve when death arrives.
- He defines death as the separation of soul and body. The soul exists "in herself," released from the body, and the body is released from the soul.
- He says it would be a "ridiculous contradiction" to spend a lifetime trying to live as near as possible to a state of death and then complain when it comes.
- On his last day, he says he goes on his way "rejoicing." He hopes to reach what he has pursued all his life, and he believes this holds for anyone whose mind has been made ready and "in a manner purified."
- He defines purification as the soul gathering herself into herself out of the body, dwelling alone, and being released from the body's chains, in this life as far as she can.
- He treats reluctance to die as a test. A man who "repines" at death is "not a lover of wisdom, but a lover of the body," and probably a lover of money or power too.
- He would still be sad about death if he did not believe he is going to wise and good gods, and perhaps to departed men better than those he leaves behind (he is less sure of the second). He has "good hope" that something remains for the dead, "some far better thing for the good than for the evil."

chunks.heading: Why the philosopher turns away from the body
chunks.text:
- Socrates holds that the true philosopher is concerned with the soul and not the body. He does not care for eating and drinking, sexual pleasure, costly clothes or sandals, or anything "more than nature needs."
- He says sight and hearing are "inaccurate witnesses," and that the soul is deceived whenever she inquires through the body.
- Thought is best when the mind is gathered into herself and nothing troubles her: no sounds, sights, pain or pleasure. She "takes leave of the body" and aspires after true being.
- Absolute justice, beauty, good, greatness, health and strength are never seen by the eyes or reached by any bodily sense. The nearest approach to knowing them comes from the person who goes to each "with the mind alone."
- He lists the body's costs to the search for truth:
  - It needs endless feeding.
  - It falls ill.
  - It fills us with "loves, and lusts, and fears, and fancies."
  - It takes away "the power of thinking at all."
  - It breaks in on every inquiry with "turmoil and confusion."
- He traces war to the body. "Wars are occasioned by the love of money, and money has to be acquired for the sake and in the service of the body." Factions and fighting come from the same source.
- His conclusion is that pure knowledge needs the soul to behold things in themselves. We make the nearest approach in this life when we have the least possible intercourse with the body and keep ourselves pure until God releases us.
- He adds that the impure are not permitted to approach the pure.

chunks.heading: Virtue is real only when bought with wisdom
chunks.text:
- Socrates argues that ordinary courage and temperance are contradictions. Most men face death only because they fear greater evils, so they are "courageous from fear," which he calls strange.
- The temperate are the same. They give up some pleasures only because other pleasures, which they fear to lose, rule them. He says they are "made temperate through intemperance."
- Trading one fear, pleasure or pain for another, "as if they were coins," is not the exchange of virtue.
- There is "one true coin for which all things ought to be exchanged," and that coin is wisdom. Only in exchange for wisdom, and in company with it, is anything truly bought or sold, whether courage, temperance or justice.
- True virtue is the companion of wisdom, whatever fears or pleasures come with it. Virtue made of those goods, severed from wisdom, is "a shadow of virtue only," with no "freedom or health or truth" in it.
- Temperance, justice, courage and wisdom are themselves a purging away of fears and pleasures.
- He cites the mysteries: "many are the thyrsus-bearers, but few are the mystics." He reads "mystics" as the true philosophers, and says he has spent his life trying to find a place among them.

chunks.heading: Why a man must not take his own life
chunks.text:
- Socrates says a philosopher will be willing to die but will not kill himself, because suicide is held to be unlawful. He admits this looks inconsistent, since he also says death can be better for some people.
- He gives an argument from a doctrine "whispered in secret" that man is a prisoner who has no right to open the door and run away. He says he does not fully understand this mystery.
- He also believes "the gods are our guardians, and … we are a possession of theirs."
- He asks Cebes whether he would be angry at an ox or an ass that put itself out of the way without being told to. Cebes says yes, so a man should wait until God summons him, "as he is now summoning me."
- Cebes objects. If the wise gladly serve the best of masters, a wise man should be sorry to leave them, and only a fool would be glad to. Socrates is pleased by the objection and treats it as an indictment he must answer in a better defence than he gave the judges.
- He praises Cebes as "always inquiring" and not "easily convinced by the first thing which he hears."

chunks.heading: Pleasure and pain, dreams and poetry
chunks.text:
- Socrates rubs his leg after the chains are removed and observes how strange pleasure is and how it relates to pain. They are never present together, yet whoever pursues one is compelled to take the other. "Their bodies are two, but they are joined by a single head."
- He says Aesop would have made a fable of God trying to reconcile their strife and instead fastening their heads together.
- Cebes asks why he has started writing poetry in prison, turning Aesop's fables into verse and composing a hymn to Apollo. Socrates explains that in his life he has often had a dream saying "Cultivate and make music."
- He had taken this to encourage his philosophy, "the noblest and best of music," like spectators urging a runner already running. Under sentence of death, he decided it was safer to obey the dream in the popular sense too.
- He says a poet must invent stories and that he has "no invention," so he used the Aesop fables that were at hand.
- He sends a message to the poet Evenus: be of good cheer, and come after me "if he be a wise man."

chunks.heading: Arguments that the soul survives death
chunks.text:
- **Opposites.** Socrates asks whether things with opposites are generated from their opposites.
  - The greater comes from the less, the weaker from the stronger, the swifter from the slower, and the more just from the more unjust.
  - Between each pair of opposites runs a process in both directions, such as waxing and waning, or falling asleep and waking.
  - Life and death are opposites like sleep and waking. If the living come from the dead as the dead come from the living, then souls must exist in the world below.
  - He says dying is visible, and that nature should not "walk on one leg only." So there must be a return to life.
  - If generation ran in one direction only, everything would end in the same state. If all living things died and stayed dead, all would at last be "swallowed up in death."
- **Recollection.** He holds that learning is recollecting what the soul knew before birth.
  - Cebes offers the proof from questions: put a question rightly and a person answers truly from himself, as shown with a diagram.
  - Socrates adds that lovers who see a lyre call up the image of the beloved, and a picture of Simmias can recall Cebes.
  - His main example is absolute equality. Equal pieces of wood or stone look equal at one time and unequal at another, but the idea of equality is never unequal.
  - The material equals only "strive to attain" the idea and "fall short of it." To see that, we must already have known equality before our first sense perception.
  - The same holds for beauty, goodness, justice and holiness. We acquired knowledge of these ideas before birth, so the soul existed before it took a human form.
  - He ties the two: if these ideas do not exist, the argument for the soul falls with them. Simmias agrees the ideas are as certain as the soul's prior existence.
- **Combining both.** The soul existed before birth, and she can only be born from death, so she must exist after death too.

chunks.heading: The soul is like the unseen and unchanging, and need not be scattered
chunks.text:
- Socrates says Cebes and Simmias fear, like children, that the wind may blow the soul away on leaving the body, especially in a storm. He tells them to charm away the fear "daily" and to look for a good charmer among all of Hellas and among themselves, "sparing neither pains nor money."
- What can be scattered is the composite. Only the uncompounded can be indissoluble.
- The uncompounded is always the same, like the essences of equality and beauty. The compound, such as the many beautiful horses or garments, is always changing.
- The changing is seen and perceived by the senses; the unchanging is perceived only by the mind. The body is akin to the seen, and the soul to the unseen.
- When the soul uses the body to perceive, she is dragged into the changeable and "wanders and is confused," like a drunkard. When she reflects by herself, she passes into the region of purity and eternity, which is her kindred. This state of the soul is called wisdom.
- Nature makes the soul rule and the body serve, and ruling is akin to the divine. So the soul is like the divine, immortal and unchangeable, and the body like the mortal.
- Even the body lasts a long time after death, for example when embalmed in Egypt, so the invisible soul is unlikely to be blown away at once.
- A soul that is pure at departing goes to the invisible, divine world. A soul that loved the body is weighed down and drawn back to wander near tombs, and is then imprisoned in another body fitting its former life: gluttons and drunkards become asses, tyrants and the violent become wolves, hawks or kites. The merely civic virtuous, whose temperance and justice came from habit "without philosophy and mind," become bees, wasps, ants or men again.
- He describes philosophy as releasing the soul from a body she is "fastened and glued" to. The cause is that each pleasure and pain is "a sort of nail which nails and rivets the soul to the body," so she comes to believe whatever the body affirms.
- That is why philosophers are temperate and brave, he says: not for the world's reasons, but so as not to be left "weaving instead of unweaving her Penelope's web."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In Plato's Phaedo, Socrates answers Simmias and Cebes on whether the soul can perish. He warns against hating arguments, explains why he abandoned natural science for the search for the best, and offers a myth of the afterlife. He then urges care of the soul through virtue and drinks the hemlock calmly.

chunks.heading: Why Socrates will not rely on the argument that the soul outlasts the body
chunks.text:
Simmias and Cebes raise two objections after the first arguments for the soul's survival. Socrates invites them rather than resisting: if they still doubt, "do not hesitate to say exactly what you think," since "there are many points still open to suspicion and attack."

- **Simmias (harmony objection):** the soul might be like the harmony of a lyre. It is invisible and divine, yet it perishes when the strings break, so it may dissolve when the body's hot, cold, wet and dry elements fall out of balance.
- **Cebes (weaver objection):** a weaver outlives many coats yet is outlived by the last one. By analogy, a soul may wear out many bodies and still perish at last. Strength and longevity do not prove immortality, and Cebes says confidence about death is foolish unless the soul is proven "altogether immortal and imperishable."
- Socrates calls Simmias's point forceful ("there is force in his attack upon me") and asks Cebes to state his difficulty before answering either.
- He compares his own calm to the swans, who sing most "lustily" before dying, and says he would not go out of life "less merrily than the swans."
- Simmias gives a standard for hard questions: either discover or be taught the truth, or take "the best and most irrefragable of human theories" as a raft to sail through life on, "not without risk."

chunks.heading: Avoiding misology: hatred of arguments
chunks.text:
When the company is shaken by the objections, Socrates warns against becoming "misologists," haters of ideas. He says nothing worse can happen to a man.

- **Misanthropy comes from inexperience.** A person trusts others too much, is betrayed again and again, and ends by hating everyone. Experience shows "few are the good and few the evil, and the great majority are in the interval between them."
- Extremes are rare in everything (very large or very small men, swift or slow, fair or foul), and "if there were a competition in evil, the worst would be found to be very few."
- **Misology works the same way.** A person without skill in dialectic believes an argument, then finds it false, then another, until he decides all arguments are unsound. Great disputers think they alone see that everything is "going up and down in never-ceasing ebb and flow," like the currents of the Euripus.
- The error is to blame arguments instead of oneself: "Rather say that we have not yet attained to soundness in ourselves." A man who does this "should lose truth and the knowledge of realities."
- Socrates calls the loss of faith in reasoning "very melancholy" and urges that one struggle "manfully" to gain health of mind.

chunks.heading: Arguing to convince himself, not to win
chunks.text:
Socrates says he does not have "the temper of a philosopher" here but is like a partisan, and explains the difference.

- A partisan cares nothing for the rights of the question and only wants to convince his hearers.
- Socrates seeks first "to convince myself; to convince my hearers is a secondary matter."
- He argues that he gains either way. If the soul survives, he does well to believe the truth. If nothing follows death, he will not distress his friends with lamentations in the time left, and "my ignorance will not last, but will die with me."
- He asks the others to think "of the truth and not of Socrates": agree if he speaks truly, and "withstand me might and main" if not, so that he does not deceive them and himself "like the bee, leave my sting in you before I die."
- He restates each objection accurately before answering, to make sure nothing escapes the discussion.

chunks.heading: Refuting the soul-as-harmony theory
chunks.text:
Socrates answers Simmias with several arguments, using Simmias's own commitments.

- **Contradiction with recollection.** Simmias still holds that knowledge is recollection and that the soul existed before the body. A harmony comes after its parts (lyre, strings, sounds exist first, "and then harmony is made last of all, and perishes first"), so the soul cannot both pre-exist the body and be its harmony. Simmias keeps recollection because it rests on demonstration, while the harmony theory "rests only on probable and plausible grounds." He adds that arguments from probability are "impostors."
- **Harmony follows, the soul leads.** A harmony cannot act against its parts or "lead" them, only follow. Yet the soul opposes the body constantly: she resists drinking when the body is thirsty and eating when it is hungry, and she disciplines desires, passions and fears.
- Homer is cited as seeing this: Odysseus "beat his breast, and thus reproached his heart: Endure, my heart."
- **Degrees.** A harmony can be more or less fully harmonized, but no soul is more a soul than another. If virtue were harmony and vice discord, no soul would have more vice or virtue than another, and every soul of every creature would be equally good. That is plainly false.
- Socrates concludes the soul is no harmony, but "a far diviner thing," ruler of the body and especially "the wise soul."

chunks.heading: His intellectual history: from natural science to the Forms
chunks.text:
To answer Cebes, Socrates tells how he came to his method.

- As a young man he pursued the study of nature: what the causes of generation and destruction are, whether we think with blood, air, fire or the brain. He became so confused that he "forgot" things he thought self-evident, such as that eating makes a man grow.
- He could no longer explain simple things: why one plus one makes two (addition?) while dividing one also makes two (separation?).
- He hoped Anaxagoras, who said mind orders all things, would show that each thing is as it is because that is best. He "would not have sold [these hopes] for a large sum of money."
- He was disappointed: Anaxagoras fell back on air, ether and water. Socrates compares this to explaining why he sits in prison by his bones and muscles and joints, forgetting the true cause: "the Athenians have thought fit to condemn me, and accordingly I have thought it better and more right to remain here and undergo my sentence."
- **Cause versus condition.** Bones and muscles are conditions without which he could not act, but they are not the cause. The many, "feeling about in the dark," mistake one for the other. They ignore "the obligatory and containing power of the good."
- Failing to find the cause of things, he took a "second best" course: avoid blinding the soul by looking at things directly through the senses, as one avoids damaging the eyes by staring at an eclipse, and look at them through thought and reasoning (the "image reflected in the water").

chunks.heading: The method of hypothesis and the safe answer about causes
chunks.text:
Socrates explains the method he adopted.

- Assume the strongest principle (an absolute beauty, goodness, greatness), affirm whatever agrees with it, and reject what disagrees.
- **The "safe" answer:** things are beautiful only by participating in absolute beauty: "by beauty beautiful things become beautiful." He is unsure how participation works but is "assured" it is the cause. Colour or shape as the source of beauty only confuses him.
- The same applies to size: A is not taller than B "by a head," since the head is small and the same for both. Ten exceeds eight by number, not by two, and two comes about by participating in duality, not by addition or division.
- When challenged, do not argue with the challenger until you have checked whether the consequences of the principle agree with one another. If asked for an explanation of the principle, assume "a higher principle, and a higher, until you found a resting-place in the best of the higher."
- Do not confuse principle with consequences "like the Eristics," who enjoy turmoil in their ideas and do not care about reality.
- A refinement: instead of the "safe and stupid" answer (heat makes things hot), give the "far superior" one: fire makes things hot, fever makes the body diseased, the monad makes odd numbers.

chunks.heading: The final proof that the soul is immortal
chunks.text:
Socrates builds the proof on opposites that exclude each other.

- Essential opposites never admit their contrary: greatness will not become small. Some things that are not themselves opposites still carry an opposite and will not admit its contrary. Three is not oddness, yet it is always odd and "will endure annihilation or anything sooner than be converted into an even number." Fire resists cold, snow resists heat, and each either withdraws or perishes.
- The soul brings life to whatever she possesses. Life's opposite is death, so the soul will never admit death. What does not admit death is "the immortal."
- If the odd were imperishable, three would be imperishable, and the snow and the fire would retreat unharmed. So if the immortal is also imperishable, the soul, "attacked by death," cannot perish but retires safe and sound.
- Cebes is convinced. Simmias still feels uncertain "when I think of the greatness of the subject and the feebleness of man."
- Socrates answers that first principles, "even if they appear certain, should be carefully considered," and then one may follow the argument with "a sort of hesitating confidence in human reason."

chunks.heading: Care of the soul and the myth of the afterlife
chunks.text:
Socrates draws the practical consequences of the soul's immortality.

- If death were the end, the wicked would have "a good bargain" in being quit of their evil. Since the soul is immortal, "there is no release or salvation from evil except the attainment of the highest virtue and wisdom," and the soul takes with her only "nurture and education."
- The care owed to the soul covers eternity, not only "the portion of time which is called life."
- Souls are guided after death. The wise and orderly soul follows the straight path. The soul that desired the body "wanders in extremity of evil" and no one will be her companion.
- Judgment divides souls: the incurable (great sacrilege, foul murders) go to Tartarus and never leave. Those with great but curable crimes, such as violence to a parent done in anger and repented for life, suffer a year in Tartarus and must then win pardon from the victims on the Acherusian lake. Those pre-eminent for holiness go to a purer earth, and those who purified themselves with philosophy live "altogether without the body."
- He does not claim the details are exactly true: "A man of sense ought not to say, nor will I be very confident." But given that the soul is immortal, he may think that "something of the kind is true. The venture is a glorious one."
- Hence he tells a man to be of good cheer if he has cast away bodily pleasures and adorned the soul "in her own proper jewels, temperance, and justice, and courage, and nobility, and truth." His conclusion: "Fair is the prize, and the hope great!"

chunks.heading: His last instructions and his death
chunks.text:
Socrates' final words and conduct show the same convictions in practice.

- To Crito, who asks what to do for his children and how to bury him: "take care of yourselves; that is a service which you may be ever rendering to me and mine." Burial may be as they like, but Crito mistakes the dead body for Socrates. He should say he is "burying my body only," since "false words are not only evil in themselves, but they infect the soul with evil."
- He bathes beforehand so that the women need not wash his body. He sends the weeping women away, saying "a man should die in peace."
- When Crito urges delay because the sun is still on the hills, he refuses: he would be "ridiculous in my own eyes for sparing and saving a life which is already forfeit."
- He treats the jailer kindly, calling him "charming," and prays to the gods to prosper his journey, then drinks the poison "quite readily and cheerfully."
- When his friends break into tears, he rebukes them: "Be quiet, then, and have patience."
- His last words: "Crito, I owe a cock to Asclepius; will you remember to pay the debt?"
- Phaedo's verdict is that he was "the wisest and justest and best" of the men of his time.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Socrates asks young Theaetetus "What is knowledge?", insists on one definition rather than a list of examples, and describes his art as midwifery of souls. He then examines the claim that knowledge is perception, linking it to Protagoras and flux, and refutes it via memory and Protagoras' self-undermining relativism.

chunks.heading: Socrates's midwifery: drawing out and testing other people's ideas
chunks.text:
- Socrates says he is the son of a midwife, Phaenarete, and practises midwifery himself, but on men's souls instead of women's bodies. He attends them "when they are in labour" and examines whether what the mind brings forth is "a false idol or a noble and true birth."
- He compares his own situation to the midwives' own. Artemis lets only women past childbearing be midwives, and Socrates is "barren" of wisdom. He says: "the god compels me to be a midwife, but does not allow me to bring forth."
- He admits the common reproach that he asks questions and never answers them is "very just." He claims "I am not myself at all wise, nor have I anything to show which is the invention or birth of my own soul."
- The test is whether the offspring is real or a "wind-egg." After a birth he proposes to "run round the hearth" with the child and decide whether it is "worth rearing" or "only a wind-egg and a sham."
- Like a midwife who also knows the best matches, he can tell who is not pregnant with ideas. He sends such people on to other teachers, "many of them I have given away to Prodicus."
- The pain is part of the work. Those who consort with him suffer "perplexity and travail" day and night, which he says is worse than the pangs of childbirth.

chunks.heading: Why Socrates will refute a cherished idea, and how he wants it taken
chunks.text:
- He warns Theaetetus not to "quarrel with me" if his first conception is exposed as "a vain shadow." Some people were "ready to bite me when I deprived them of a darling folly."
- He says he acts "from goodwill," because "no god is the enemy of man." It would be wrong for him "to admit falsehood, or to stifle the truth."
- He says that disciples who learn from him learn nothing from him. "It is quite clear that they never learned anything from me; the many fine discoveries to which they cling are of their own making." He and the god only deliver them.
- Some pupils left early out of self-conceit or bad company. They lost what he had delivered and "stifled whatever else they had in them." They ended "seeing themselves, as others see them, to be great fools." Aristeides, son of Lysimachus, is one. Truants often return and ask to start again, and he takes them back only "if my familiar allows."
- He denies that the theories he lays out are his own. "None of these theories come from me; they all come from him who talks with me. I only know just enough to extract them from the wisdom of another, and to receive them in a spirit of fairness."

chunks.heading: "What is knowledge?": ask for the one nature, not a list of examples
chunks.text:
- Socrates opens with a puzzle he says he "can never solve to my satisfaction": what knowledge is. He first gets agreement that learning is growing wiser, that wisdom is what makes the wise wise, and so wisdom and knowledge are the same.
- Theaetetus first lists geometry, astronomy, harmony, calculation, and the crafts such as cobbling. Socrates says this is "Too much" and gives many things when he asked for "one simple thing."
- Listing the subject matter of each art does not answer the question. "We wanted to know not the subjects, nor yet the number of the arts or sciences... but... the nature of knowledge in the abstract."
- His illustration: asked "What is clay?", it is absurd to answer with "a clay of potters, a clay of oven-makers, a clay of brick-makers." The short answer is "clay is moistened earth."
- He argues that you cannot understand a name without knowing the nature of the thing. Someone who does not know what knowledge is has no real knowledge of shoemaking or any other craft.
- He wants Theaetetus to repeat the move he made with square roots. Theaetetus had grouped the endless roots under one scheme, splitting numbers into square (equal factors) and oblong (unequal factors) numbers, with roots of the second kind called "powers." Socrates says "try and bring the many sorts of knowledge under one definition."
- He encourages the failure to find an answer: the task "would task the powers of men perfect in every way." Missing it does not make the praise of Theaetetus false, just as a boy runner beaten by a man is still a fast boy.

chunks.heading: Wonder as the beginning of philosophy, and how to teach with questions
chunks.text:
- When Theaetetus says he is amazed and dizzy at the puzzles about size and change, Socrates replies that this shows his nature: "wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, and philosophy begins in wonder."
- He cites the genealogy that Iris, the messenger of heaven, is the child of Thaumas, "wonder."
- He tells the young man to "take courage," "quit yourself like a man," and say what he thinks, and he praises a brave answer: "that is the way in which you should express your opinion." He does not let Theaetetus escape by saying "I cannot tell."
- He softens a refutation with encouragement. After a good answer he says there will be no dispute "because I want you to grow."
- He explains his reason for the long discussion: he and Theaetetus "have no professional aims" and only want to see "whether they are consistent with each or not." He prefers to "calmly and patiently review our own thoughts" over a "sparring-match."
- He asks that people who have never practised the question-and-answer method be coaxed in. Theodorus, who is "unused to your game of question and answer," is pushed to "strip" and wrestle with an argument, and Socrates says doing so "will do yourself good as well as me."

chunks.heading: Test of the claim "knowledge is perception" (Protagoras)
chunks.text:
- Theaetetus claims that knowledge is perception. Socrates links it to Protagoras: "Man is the measure of all things." Things are to each person as they appear, as with a wind that feels cold to one and not to another. Appearing and perceiving are the same, so perception is always of what is and is "unerring."
- Socrates lays out the supporting "Heracleitean" view, which he does not endorse as his own. Everything is motion and becoming, nothing "is," and a colour belongs to neither eye nor object but to what passes between them for each perceiver.
- He then gives the objections that arise. Dreams, illnesses and madness produce false perceptions, and nobody can prove we are awake rather than dreaming. Truth cannot be settled by how long a state lasts.
- A key argument: knowing and seeing cannot be the same. A man who has seen a thing and now closes his eyes still remembers it, so he would know it while "not seeing" it, which the theory makes impossible. So "knowledge and perception are one" involves "a manifest impossibility," and they "must be distinguished."
- Letters and foreign speech: we know and perceive the shape and colour of unfamiliar letters, and the pitch of foreign sounds. We do not perceive by sight or hearing what grammarians and interpreters teach about them.
- He also points out that if each person is the sole judge of what is true for them, nobody needs Protagoras as a teacher, and "the whole art of dialectic" and midwifery would be a "tedious and enormous piece of folly."

chunks.heading: Where Protagoras undermines himself, and the line between disputing and dialectic
chunks.text:
- Everyone thinks others are wiser or more ignorant than they are in some matters. In danger at sea, in war or in sickness, people "look up to their commanders as if they were gods" for their knowledge. This belief in wisdom and ignorance as true or false opinion contradicts the claim that all opinions are true.
- If everyone's opinion is true, then the many who think Protagoras is wrong are right. "His truth is more untrue than true" in proportion as the many outnumber the one, and his own thesis becomes "true neither to himself nor to any one else."
- Socrates will not pretend that every opinion is equally good. He grants that on immediate sensations such as hot, dry or sweet each person's appearance stands. But about health, and about what is expedient for a city, some people and some counsellors are wiser than others.
- He lets Protagoras speak in his own defence and says that the wise man replaces bad impressions with better ones, as a physician does with drugs or a farmer with plants. Socrates shows he wants the strongest version of the opposing view argued before rejecting it.
- He separates sophistic disputation from dialectic. He criticises himself and Theaetetus for "being satisfied with mere verbal consistency," "like a good-for-nothing cock" that crows without winning the victory.
- A paid fighter in argument can trap a young person by tripping him on words and make him pay "the sum to be paid for your release." By contrast, the dialectician "will be in earnest, and only correct his adversary when necessary," so that the person "will lay the blame of his own confusion and perplexity on himself," love the questioner, and "escape from himself into philosophy, in order that he may become different from what he was."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Socrates contrasts the free, leisured philosopher with the hurried, servile lawyer, and says virtue means becoming like God: holy, just and wise. He then refutes Protagoras, shows knowledge is not perception, and tests true opinion and "true opinion with an account", ending in aporia and a call to humility.

chunks.heading: The philosopher and the lawyer: leisure, freedom and the soul
chunks.text:
Socrates contrasts those trained in philosophy with those trained in the law courts, as a freeman differs from a slave.
- The philosopher has leisure. He "has his talk out in peace," wanders from subject to subject, and does not care whether his words are many or few. "His only aim is to attain the truth."
- The lawyer is always hurried by the water clock and bound by the indictment. He argues before a master who holds the verdict, and the trial usually concerns his own life.
- This makes him keen and shrewd, skilled at flattering his master in word and deed. But "his soul is small and unrighteous." Fear and deception in youth leave him "stunted and warped," and he thinks himself a master of wisdom.
