- Socrates adds that the philosopher looks foolish in court because he is untrained in trivial matters. He knows no scandal and cannot answer insults.
- Socrates says the lawyer gets dizzy and stammers when pulled up to questions about justice, injustice and human happiness. Anyone not brought up a slave sees this.

chunks.heading: The philosopher's detachment and what he laughs at
chunks.text:
Socrates describes the philosopher as present in the city only in body, while his mind measures earth and heaven.
- He does not know the way to the agora, the courts or the assemblies. He ignores clubs, banquets and the gossip about who has disgraced his family.
- The story of Thales is the model. He fell into a well while watching the stars, and a Thracian maid joked that he could not see what was at his feet. Socrates says the jest applies to every philosopher: he hardly knows whether his neighbor is a man or an animal, and he asks what the nature of man is.
- He laughs at praise of tyrants and kings. To him they are like herdsmen praised for the milk they squeeze from a harder animal to manage, and they are as uneducated as shepherds because they have no leisure.
- He sees ten thousand acres as a trifle, since he is used to thinking of the whole earth.
- He sees pride in a long pedigree as poverty of ideas. Every man has had thousands of ancestors, rich and poor, kings and slaves, Greeks and barbarians, and "a little arithmetic" would cure the vanity.

chunks.heading: Becoming like God: why virtue is pursued
chunks.text:
Socrates says evils can never pass away, because something must always oppose good. So a man should "fly away from earth to heaven as quickly as we can."
- "To fly away is to become like God, as far as this is possible; and to become like him, is to become holy, just, and wise."
- He rejects the common reason for virtue, which is only seeming good, calling it "an old wives' fable." God is perfect righteousness, and the most righteous man is most like him.
- Knowing this is true wisdom and virtue, and ignorance of it is folly and vice. The cleverness of politicians and of the arts is "coarse and vulgar" by comparison.
- The unjust man does not know the real penalty of injustice. It is not blows or death, which wrongdoers often escape, but a penalty that cannot be escaped.
- Two patterns are always set before men, one blessed and divine and one godless and wretched. Evildoers grow like the second, and live in the likeness of their own evil selves with evil friends.
- Socrates notes that such clever men, if they stay in private argument, grow discontented with themselves. "Their rhetoric fades away, and they become helpless as children."

chunks.heading: Refuting Protagoras on the future and on expert judgment
chunks.text:
Socrates argues against "man is the measure of all things" using the future and expertise.
- Laws aim at expediency, which concerns the future. States often fail in this aim, so a state's belief about what is good does not make it so.
- If each man is his own judge of what will be, a layman and a physician would both be right about whether a fever is coming. Socrates calls this ludicrous.
- Examples of experts who judge the future better: the vinegrower on the coming vintage, the musician on what will sound harmonious, the cook on the pleasure of a dinner in preparation.
- Protagoras sold his teaching as superior judgment of what will persuade a court. That admits one man is wiser than another, and so a wise man is the measure.
- Socrates adds that he, "who know nothing," has no obligation to accept the honor of being a measure of anything.

chunks.heading: Why knowledge is not perception
chunks.text:
Against the flux theory, Socrates argues that if everything is always changing, no word such as "white" or "seeing" can be used rightly. Every answer would be equally right, and the theory would need a new language, perhaps the word "no how."
- Knowledge is not perception, because the senses are instruments, and perception is through the eyes and ears, not with them. Different senses meet in one mind.
- The mind grasps things the senses cannot: being and not-being, likeness and unlikeness, sameness and difference, unity and number, the noble and the base, good and evil.
- The soul reaches these "by a power of her own," comparing past, present and future. Their meaning is "slowly and hardly gained, if they are ever gained, by education and long experience."
- Without grasping being, a man cannot attain truth, and without truth there is no knowledge. So "knowledge does not consist in impressions of sense, but in reasoning about them."

chunks.heading: Thinking as the soul's silent conversation, and the puzzle of false opinion
chunks.text:
Theaetetus then offers "true opinion" as knowledge. Socrates takes up how false opinion is possible.
- He defines thinking: "the conversation which the soul holds with herself," asking and answering, affirming and denying. Opinion is "a word spoken," silently, to oneself.
- Puzzle: a thing is known or unknown. A man cannot mistake one known thing for another known thing, nor think of what is not, since that is thinking of nothing.
- Treating false opinion as swapping one thing for another fails too. No one tells himself that an ox is a horse or that odd is even.
- His first model is a wax block in the soul, with memory as the seal. Error comes from fitting a present perception to the wrong impression, "like a bad archer" who misses the mark. Deep, clean, well-tempered wax makes men wise. Hard, soft or muddy wax makes them confused and ignorant.
- It fails on pure numbers: people do mistake five plus seven for eleven. That error would involve no perception.
- His second model is an aviary of knowledges. A man can possess a bird without having it in hand, and error is catching the wrong bird. This too collapses into a circle.
- Socrates concludes that it is shameless to explain the verb "to know" before knowing what knowledge is, and that "that must be first ascertained; then, the nature of false opinion."

chunks.heading: Knowledge as true opinion with an account, and why each version fails
chunks.text:
Socrates tests the idea that knowledge is true opinion plus a rational account.
- True opinion alone is not knowledge. Orators and lawyers persuade judges of events no one witnessed. The judges may reach a true opinion "without knowledge," but cannot be taught the facts in the time of a water clock.
- The "dream" theory says the simple elements can only be named, and complexes are known by combining names. Socrates tests it with letters and syllables.
- A man who knows the syllable "SO" must know S and O. If the syllable is a single form with no parts, it is as unknowable as a letter. So either way the theory fails. Socrates says elements are more certainly known than compounds, as shown by learning to read and by the harp-player who knows each note.
- Three meanings of "account" fail in turn:
  - Giving verbal expression of one's thought. Everyone who has a right opinion can do this, so it does not separate knowledge from opinion.
  - Listing the elements, as a wagon is wheels, axle, body, rims and yoke. A learner who spells "Theaetetus" correctly once but misspells it another time has right opinion and an enumeration, yet not knowledge.
  - Naming the mark that distinguishes a thing from all others, as the sun is the brightest body in the heavens. This is circular, because it demands a right opinion of the differences we are supposed to be explaining, so we "go round and round."
- Socrates ends without a definition. Knowledge is neither sensation, nor true opinion, nor true opinion with an account.

chunks.heading: Socratic midwifery and what failed inquiry is for
chunks.text:
Socrates closes by describing what his questioning does.
- His art is midwifery: "The office of a midwife I, like my mother, have received from God; she delivered women, I deliver men."
- He tests whether what is born is real or "wind." Here the offspring of Theaetetus's brain were "not worth bringing up."
- The benefit of a failed inquiry: if Theaetetus conceives again, he will be better for it. If not, "you will be soberer and humbler and gentler to other men, and will be too modest to fancy that you know what you do not know."
- Socrates states the limits of his art: he claims no knowledge of what great and famous men know.
- Earlier he praised boldness in answering, because "either we shall find what we seek, or we shall be less likely to think that we know what we do not know."
- He ends by leaving for the porch of the King Archon, where he is to meet Meletus and his indictment.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Socrates questions the ambitious young Alcibiades, who plans to advise Athens on justice without ever having learned it. Through elenchus he exposes conceited ignorance, argues that the self is the soul, that knowing oneself means looking at the divine, wise part of the soul, and that virtue, not power, makes individuals and cities happy.

chunks.heading: Socrates's claim: no one can advise a state without knowledge, and Alcibiades lacks it
chunks.text:
- Socrates tells the young Alcibiades he is about to advise the Athenian assembly. He asks whether Alcibiades knows the matter better than they do.
- A man is a good adviser because of knowledge, not riches, beauty or birth. Whether the counsellor is "rich or poor" does not matter. Athenians deliberating on health only require that he be a physician.
- Alcibiades learned only writing, the lyre and wrestling. None of these is the business of the assembly. He admits he cannot advise on building, divination or shipbuilding, since others know those better.
- Socrates says anyone who tries "teaching what you do not know, and have not taken any pains to learn, is downright insanity."
- Almost all Athenian statesmen are in the same position, "with the exception, perhaps of your guardian, Pericles."

chunks.heading: How Socrates exposes conceit of knowledge: the justice test
chunks.text:
- Socrates asks what "better" means in deciding war and peace. Alcibiades cannot say, though he would readily say "more wholesome" about food. Socrates calls it disgraceful to profess knowledge and fail to answer.
- The answer comes to justice: whom to fight, when, and for how long. Alcibiades has no teacher of justice and never discovered it.
- Alcibiades thought he knew justice as a child, shouting that a playmate had cheated at dice. He never passed through a time of knowing he was ignorant, so he never inquired.
- Learning and discovery both require admitting ignorance first. A man will not examine what he thinks he already knows.
- The "many" cannot teach justice. Good teachers must agree with one another, and the many agree about wood and stone but quarrel about justice. Socrates cites the Iliad and Odyssey, and the battles of Tanagra and Coronea, where Alcibiades' father Cleinias died.
- Men do not go to war over the principles of health. They kill one another over justice, so the many clearly do not understand it.
- Socrates points out that in a question-and-answer exchange the answerer is the speaker. Alcibiades, not Socrates, said he knew nothing of the just and unjust.

chunks.heading: Perplexity as a sign of ignorance, and the worst kind of ignorance
chunks.text:
- Alcibiades is asked whether the just is expedient. Through his own answers he concludes that it is:
  - All just things are honourable.
  - Honourable things are good, since a rescue in battle is honourable as courage and evil only in the wounds or death it risks.
  - The good is expedient.
- Alcibiades then admits: "I do not know what I am saying." He is "of different minds in successive instants."
- Socrates says the cause of self-contradiction is ignorance. Nobody wavers about whether he has two eyes or two hands.
- People are not perplexed about what they know they do not know, such as cookery or steering a ship. They leave it to the cook or the pilot.
- Only those who do not know and think they know make mistakes. That is "ignorance of the disgraceful sort which is mischievous."
- It is most disgraceful and harmful when it concerns the greatest matters: the just, the honourable, the good and the expedient.
- Socrates says Alcibiades is "wedded to ignorance of the most disgraceful kind" and rushes into politics before he is educated.

chunks.heading: Why Alcibiades must train: his real rivals are Sparta and Persia
chunks.text:
- Alcibiades says he can beat the uneducated politicians "by the light of nature." Socrates replies that the contest is not with fellow citizens.
- A pilot must look to the enemy, not to the crew. Alcibiades' true rivals are the Spartan and Persian kings.
- Socrates describes the training of a Persian prince:
  - At seven he rides and hunts.
  - At fourteen he is given four royal teachers, the wisest, the justest, the most temperate and the most valiant.
  - They teach him the worship of the gods and the duties of kingship, to speak the truth, never to let any pleasure be lord over him, and to be fearless.
  - By contrast Pericles gave Alcibiades a slave, Zopyrus the Thracian, "past all other work."
- Spartan and Persian wealth far exceeds Athenian. Socrates says Alcibiades' mother's wardrobe was "not worth fifty minae" and Alcibiades has a 300-acre patch at Erchiae.
- Socrates imagines Persian queens being astonished that an uneducated youth, not yet twenty, relies on beauty, stature and birth against kings.
- He ends the passage by urging: "hear the Delphian inscription, 'Know thyself'," since rivals can only be overcome "by pains and skill."

chunks.heading: What it means to take care of oneself
chunks.text:
- Socrates says all people greatly need "pains and care," himself included, and the pair must take counsel together.
- To take care of something means to improve it. Care of a thing differs from care of its belongings: shoemaking tends the shoe, gymnastic tends the foot.
- Taking care of one's possessions is therefore not taking care of oneself.
- One cannot know the art that makes a man better without knowing what a man is. So self-knowledge is the necessary start.
- Socrates admits it is unclear whether self-knowledge is easy or hard, but says "there is no other way."
- He argues that the user of a thing differs from the thing used. A shoemaker is not his tools or his hands, and a man uses his whole body.
- A man is therefore not his body, and neither the body nor the body and soul together can rule. So "the soul is man."
- Following this, Socrates says "he who bids a man know himself, would have him know his soul."
- It follows that:
  - A physician or trainer, as such, knows only the things of the body, not himself.
  - He who cherishes his body cherishes not himself, and he who cherishes money is further removed still.
  - These bodily arts are "vulgar" and not what a good man would practise.

chunks.heading: True love loves the soul, and warnings about the people
chunks.text:
- Whoever loves Alcibiades' body loves only what belongs to him, and leaves when youth fades.
- The lover of the soul "goes not away, as long as the soul follows after virtue."
- Socrates says he loves Alcibiades for his own sake, "whereas other men love what belongs to you." Alcibiades' beauty is fading "just as your true self is beginning to bloom."
- Socrates' main fear is that Alcibiades will "become a lover of the people" and be ruined by them, as many a noble Athenian has been. The demus looks fair but "you should see him naked."
- His remedy is to learn what he ought to know before entering politics, which works as an antidote.

chunks.heading: Self-knowledge, wisdom and the mirror of the soul
chunks.text:
- Socrates uses an analogy to sight. The eye sees itself only by looking into another eye, at the pupil where sight resides.
- The soul likewise must look at the soul, especially the part where wisdom and knowledge reside. That is the most divine part, so one who looks there and at things divine will best know himself.
- Self-knowledge is wisdom. Without it, one cannot know one's own good and evil.
- Not knowing oneself means not knowing one's belongings, other people's affairs, or the affairs of states. Such a man "can never be a statesman" or economist, will not know what he is doing, will err and be miserable, and so will those he governs.
- Socrates concludes that "not he who has riches, but he who has wisdom, is delivered from his misery."

chunks.heading: Virtue, not power, should be the aim of men and cities
chunks.text:
- Cities do not need walls, triremes, docks, numbers or size "without virtue." A man cannot give citizens virtue he does not have.
- Anyone who wants to govern himself and the state must first acquire virtue. He needs "not power or authority" but "justice and wisdom."
- Power without understanding is dangerous, like a sick man free to do as he likes but without a physician's mind, or a ship's captain with no skill in navigation. All aboard will perish.
- Therefore "not tyrannical power... should be the aim either of individuals or states, if they would be happy, but virtue."
- Until a person has virtue, being commanded by a superior is better. Vice suits a slave and virtue a free man, so the slavery to be escaped is the slavery of ignorance and vice.
- Socrates says a man who acts justly and wisely acts "according to the will of God," and that he will be "security" for Alcibiades' happiness if he does.
- When Alcibiades says he will escape by Socrates' help, Socrates corrects him: it is "by the help of God."
- Alcibiades vows to follow Socrates as a disciple. Socrates replies that his love "breeds another love," then adds that he fears "the power of the state, which may be too much for both of us."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Socrates tests definitions of justice from Cephalus, Polemarchus and Thrasymachus by cross-examination. He shows justice never harms anyone, that true rulers and skilled craftsmen serve their subjects, and that justice is the soul's excellence and so brings happiness. He ends by admitting he still does not know what justice is.

chunks.heading: Socrates tests "paying debts and telling the truth" as a definition of justice
chunks.text:
- Cephalus offers justice as "to speak the truth and to pay your debts."
- Socrates tests it with a counter-example. If a friend left weapons with you while sane and asks for them back when mad, returning them is wrong, and so is telling him the truth.
- His conclusion: truth-telling and debt-paying "is not a correct definition of justice."
- He treats a definition as something to be tested against exceptions, not accepted because it sounds right.
- He says he likes talking with the old because they are travellers on a road he may also have to take. He asks Cephalus whether the way is "smooth and easy, or rugged and difficult."
- Cephalus says old age is bearable for a calm, good-natured man whatever his wealth. Socrates draws out that the chief value of money is peace of mind: no need to deceive or defraud anyone, and no debts to men or offerings owed to the gods.

chunks.heading: Socrates refutes "justice is doing good to friends and harm to enemies"
chunks.text:
Polemarchus, defending Simonides, reworks the definition into "justice is the art which gives good to friends and evil to enemies." Socrates takes it apart in four steps.

- **Art analogy.** Medicine gives drugs and food to bodies, and cookery gives seasoning. Socrates asks what justice gives. The physician helps friends in sickness and the pilot at sea. Justice would help friends and harm enemies in war and alliances.
- **Uselessness in peace.** If justice is useful only in war, it is useless in peace. Polemarchus says it serves in contracts and partnerships. Socrates shows that in every real partnership an expert is better: the draughts-player, the builder, the horse expert, the shipwright.
- **Safekeeping.** The just man is preferred only when money is "to be kept safely" and not used. Socrates concludes justice is "useful when money is useless," and so "not good for much."
- **The thief.** The best guard of anything is also the best thief, as the best boxer is best at warding off blows. So the just man who keeps money well would be good at stealing it. Socrates jokes that justice becomes "an art of theft," which Homer's Autolycus "excellent above all men in theft and perjury" would approve.

chunks.heading: Why harming anyone, even an enemy, can never be just
chunks.text:
- **Appearance versus reality.** People often misjudge who is good or bad. If justice means helping friends and harming enemies as they seem, the just would end up harming the good. Polemarchus admits "the doctrine is immoral."
- **Repair.** Polemarchus fixes it: help friends only if they are good, and harm enemies only if they are wicked.
- **Harm degrades.** Socrates asks whether injured horses and dogs get better or worse at their own excellence. They get worse. Injured men likewise get worse in "the proper virtue of man," which is justice, so harming them makes them more unjust.
- **No art does the opposite of its aim.** The musician cannot make men unmusical, the horseman cannot make bad riders, and heat cannot produce cold. So the just man cannot, by justice, make men unjust: "the good cannot harm any one."
- **Conclusion.** Harming anyone, friend or enemy, is "the act of the opposite, who is the unjust."
- **Origin of the saying.** Socrates suggests it belongs to a rich and mighty man with a high opinion of his own power, such as Periander, Perdiccas, Xerxes or Ismenias, not to a wise man like Simonides, Bias or Pittacus.

chunks.heading: Answering and questioning: Socrates on Thrasymachus' demand
chunks.text:
- Thrasymachus bursts in, accusing Socrates of only asking and refusing to answer. He also bans the answers "duty, advantage, profit, gain, interest."
- Socrates replies that a seeker of justice is like a seeker of gold. Two men looking for it together do not "knock under" to each other, since justice is "more precious than many pieces of gold."
- He gives the twelve example: if you ask what makes twelve and forbid "twice six, three times four, six times two, four times three," no one can answer. Even a forbidden answer, if it seems true, should be given.
- He says of himself that he "knows just nothing," and cannot be expected to speak when told by a man of authority not to utter his half-formed notions.
- He learns from others and pays for it "in praise, which is all I have."
- Socrates asks Thrasymachus to accept the hearers' pity, not anger, since they "cannot" find the answer.
- He says he does not ask in order to injure or trick Thrasymachus, and would "as well shave a lion" as try to cheat him.
- He prefers answering one another by admissions, so the inquirers "unite the offices of judge and advocate in our own persons." The alternative is rival set speeches that need outside judges.
- He asks only for consistency: "if you change, change openly and let there be no deception."

chunks.heading: Refuting "justice is the interest of the stronger"
chunks.text:
Thrasymachus holds that every government makes laws in its own interest, and that obeying those laws is justice. Socrates answers in two stages.

- **Rulers can err.** Thrasymachus admits rulers sometimes mistake their own interest, and that subjects must obey. Then subjects are sometimes commanded to do what harms the stronger, so justice is "the reverse" of the stronger's interest.
- **The strict-sense ruler.** Thrasymachus retreats: a ruler "in the strictest sense" never errs, as a true physician or arithmetician does not err while practising the skill.
- **Arts serve their subject.** Socrates accepts that standard. Every art has an interest, which is the perfection of its subject. Medicine considers the body, horsemanship the horse. No art serves itself, since arts are complete and have no needs.
- **Rulers as artists.** The true physician is a healer, not a money-maker. The true pilot is a captain, not a mere sailor. So no ruler "in so far as he is a ruler" considers his own interest, only that of his subject. The arts rule over the weaker and serve them.
- **Shepherd.** Thrasymachus says shepherds fatten sheep for their own table. Socrates replies that this treats the shepherd as a diner or trader, not as a shepherd. The shepherd's art concerns only the flock.

chunks.heading: Why rulers need payment, and why good men rule reluctantly
chunks.text:
- **Pay is a separate art.** Each art has its own function and good. Medicine gives health, building gives houses. Pay comes from the additional art of payment. A man who works for nothing still confers benefit, so the benefit comes from the art and not from the pay.
- **Why rulers are paid.** No one wants to reform others' evils without remuneration, so rulers must be induced in one of three ways: money, honour, or a penalty for refusing.
- **Good men.** Good men do not want to be called hirelings or thieves, and they care nothing for honour. So they rule from fear of punishment: "the worst part of the punishment is that he who refuses to rule is liable to be ruled by one who is worse than himself."
- **A city of good men.** In such a city avoiding office would be fought over as office is now. Everyone would "rather receive a benefit from another than have the trouble of conferring one." This shows the true ruler is not meant to seek his own interest.

chunks.heading: Justice as wisdom and virtue, injustice as ignorance
chunks.text:
Thrasymachus now claims the unjust life is more profitable, and calls injustice "discretion" and justice "sublime simplicity." Socrates argues from the arts that the just man is wise and good.

- **Reaching beyond.** The musician and the physician do not try to exceed those with the same skill, only the unskilled. Whoever has knowledge tries to do the same as his like. The ignorant try to outdo both the knowing and the ignorant.
- **Mapping to justice.** The just man tries to outdo only the unjust. The unjust tries to outdo both just and unjust. So the just man resembles the wise and good, and the unjust resembles the ignorant and evil.
- **Reluctance.** Thrasymachus gives these admissions with "extreme reluctance," sweating on a hot day, and Socrates sees "what I had never seen before, Thrasymachus blushing."

chunks.heading: Injustice divides; the work of the soul; justice is happiness
chunks.text:
- **Injustice cannot unify.** A state, army, band of robbers or any gang could not act together if they injured one another. Injustice "creates divisions and hatreds," while justice "imparts harmony and friendship." Within one person, injustice makes him "not at unity with himself" and an enemy to himself, to the just and to the gods.
- **Even thieves keep some justice.** Evildoers who act together must have "some remnant of justice" in them. Utterly unjust men "would have been utterly incapable of action."
- **Function and excellence.** Everything has an end that nothing else can fulfil as well: the eye sees, the ear hears, the pruning-hook prunes. It fulfils that end by its proper excellence and fails through its defect. A blind eye cannot see.
- **The soul.** The soul's functions are "to superintend and command and deliberate," and life itself is among them. Its excellence is justice, and its defect is injustice. So the just soul lives well and the unjust lives ill.
- **Conclusion.** Living well is being blessed and happy, so "the just is happy, and the unjust miserable." Happiness is profitable, so "injustice can never be more profitable than justice."

chunks.heading: Socrates admits he has not found what justice is
chunks.text:
- He closes by comparing himself to an epicure who snatches a taste of every dish without enjoying the first.
- He moved from asking what justice is to whether it is virtue and wisdom, and then to whether it is more advantageous. He never finished the first question.
- His verdict: "the result of the whole discussion has been that I know nothing at all."
- Without knowing what justice is, he says, he cannot know whether it is a virtue, nor whether the just man is happy or unhappy.
- He still says "no light matter is at stake, nothing less than the rule of human life."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Glaucon and Adeimantus ask Socrates to praise justice for its effect on the soul alone, without reputation or reward. Socrates ranks justice among goods wanted for themselves and for their results, then builds a city in speech to see justice at large. He ends by shaping the guardians' philosophic nature and by rejecting false stories about the gods.

chunks.heading: Glaucon's challenge: why Socrates must praise justice for itself
chunks.text:
- Socrates first ranks goods into three classes: those wanted for their own sake (harmless pleasures), those wanted for themselves and their results (knowledge, sight, health), and those that are burdensome but done for the reward (gymnastic, medical treatment, money-making).
- He places justice in the highest class, "among those goods which he who would be happy desires both for their own sake and for the sake of their results."
- Glaucon says the many put justice in the burdensome class, pursued for rewards and reputation, and that Socrates' answer to Thrasymachus has not shown what justice does "inwardly... in the soul."
- Glaucon asks Socrates to praise justice with rewards and reputation set aside. Socrates answers that he would "wish really to persuade you, if I could."
- Adeimantus adds that parents, poets and teachers only commend justice for its reputation and rewards. He asks Socrates to show "what effect they have on the possessor of them," "whether seen or unseen by gods and men."
- Socrates calls the brothers' ability to argue for injustice without being convinced by it "truly divine." He says he cannot refuse to help: "I am afraid that there would be an impiety in being present when justice is evil spoken of and not lifting up a hand in her defence."
- He warns that the inquiry "would require very good eyes."

chunks.heading: The challenge Socrates agrees to answer: Gyges, the unjust man and the just man
chunks.text:
Socrates does not state these arguments himself, but he takes them on as the challenge to be answered.

- **Origin of justice:** Glaucon presents the common view that justice is a compromise between doing injustice with impunity (best) and suffering it without redress (worst). It is "tolerated not as a good, but as the lesser evil."
- **Gyges' ring:** a shepherd finds a ring that makes him invisible, then seduces the queen, kills the king and takes the kingdom. Glaucon claims no one would "stand fast in justice" with such a ring, so people are just only of necessity.
- **Isolating the two lives:** the perfectly unjust man has the reputation of justice, while the perfectly just man "wishes to be and not to seem good" and is thought the worst of men. Glaucon says the second will be scourged, racked and impaled.
- Adeimantus notes that the young learn that appearance "tyrannizes over truth." Hence, if they can hide their wrongdoing and buy off the gods with sacrifices, they have no reason to be just.
- Glaucon and Adeimantus ask Socrates to show that justice is the greatest good of the soul and injustice its greatest evil. Without that, each person must watch others, whereas "every one would have been his own watchman."

chunks.heading: Method: find justice in the city first, then in the individual
chunks.text:
- Socrates compares the inquiry to a short-sighted person asked to read small letters from a distance, who is lucky to find the same letters written larger elsewhere.
- Justice is the virtue of an individual and also of a State. The State is larger, so "the quantity of justice is likely to be larger and more easily discernible."
- He proposes to inquire into justice "first as they appear in the State, and secondly in the individual, proceeding from the greater to the lesser and comparing them."
- He proposes building a city in thought, since watching it grow should show how justice and injustice grow.

chunks.heading: Origin of the city: need and the division of labour
chunks.text:
- A State arises "out of the needs of mankind; no one is self-sufficing." Necessity is "the mother of our invention."
- The first needs are food, then a dwelling, then clothing. The minimal city has four or five people: a husbandman, builder, weaver and shoemaker.
- Principle: people differ in nature, so each is suited to a different occupation. A work is done better "when he has only one" occupation, and it is spoilt if not done at the right time. Things are produced "more plentifully and easily and of a better quality when one man does one thing which is natural to him."
- The city grows as each trade needs tools and trades. Carpenters, smiths, herdsmen, importers and exporters, merchants, sailors, a market-place and money-tokens follow. Retailers (often the physically weakest) and hirelings who sell their labour are added.
- Socrates guesses justice and injustice arise "in the dealings of these citizens with one another."
- Their way of life is simple: barley and wheat cakes, wine, garlands, hymns to the gods, and families kept within their means. Socrates takes salt, olives, cheese, roots, herbs, figs, peas and beans as the relish. He says they would live "in peace and health to a good old age."

chunks.heading: The healthy city versus the luxurious city
chunks.text:
- Glaucon objects that this is "a city of pigs" and wants sofas, tables, sauces and sweets.
- Socrates calls the simple city "the true and healthy constitution of the State" but is willing to examine "a State at fever heat." Luxury here means furniture, perfumes, courtesans, cakes, painters, embroiderers, gold and ivory.
- The city swells with callings "not required by any natural want": hunters, actors, poets, rhapsodists, dancers, tutors, nurses, barbers, cooks and swineherds. It also needs many more physicians.
- The land then becomes too small, and the city must take a slice of the neighbours' land. They will do the same to it, once they "exceed the limit of necessity" and give themselves up "to the unlimited accumulation of wealth." So war arises.
- Socrates says war springs from "the causes of almost all the evils in States, private as well as public." He leaves open whether war does good or harm.

chunks.heading: Guardians: why they need training and what nature they need
chunks.text:
- War is an art as demanding as shoemaking. By the same principle that no one can practise many arts well, a soldier must be a full-time guardian, not a part-time husbandman or artisan. Tools will not make a skilled workman of someone who has not learned to use them.
- The higher the duty of the guardian, the more "time, and skill, and art, and application" it requires, and natural aptitude as well. So the guardians must be selected.
- A noble youth is like a well-bred dog: quick to see, swift to catch, strong to fight. He must also have spirit, which makes the soul "fearless and indomitable."
- Difficulty: spirited natures turn savage toward everyone, but guardians must be "dangerous to their enemies, and gentle to their friends." Socrates resolves it by noting the well-bred dog is gentle to familiars and fierce to strangers.
- He calls the dog "a true philosopher." It tells friend from enemy "only by the criterion of knowing and not knowing." Since loving learning is loving wisdom, the guardian must unite "philosophy and spirit and swiftness and strength."

chunks.heading: Education of the young: stories, the censorship of poets, and the nature of God
chunks.text:
- Traditional education has gymnastic for the body and music (including literature) for the soul. Music comes first, because stories are told before gymnastics can be taught, and "the beginning is the most important part of any work." Character is formed when the child is "young and tender."
- Socrates would set up a censorship of fiction. Mothers and nurses may tell only approved tales, "fashion the mind with such tales, even more fondly than they mould the body with their hands."
- He faults Homer and Hesiod for telling "a bad lie" about gods and heroes, as a painter might paint a portrait with no likeness. His examples are Uranus and Cronus, and Hephaestus bound and thrown out by Zeus.
- A young person "cannot judge what is allegorical and what is literal," so such tales must not be told, because they become "indelible and unalterable." The tales should be "models of virtuous thoughts" and teach that quarrelling is unholy.
- As founders, Socrates and Adeimantus set only the forms poets must follow; making the tales is not their business.
- **First rule:** God is good, the good does no harm, and what does no harm cannot cause evil. So God is "the cause of a few things only," the good ones. The causes of evil are to be sought elsewhere. Poets may not say God is "the author of evil to any one," and punishment may be shown only as benefiting the punished.
- **Second rule:** God does not change. Whatever is best is least altered from without, and God would not change himself for the worse. So no tales of gods who "take the disguise of strangers." Such stories also make cowards of children.
- **The true lie versus the lie in words:** the "true lie" is ignorance and deception in the soul about the highest realities. Everyone hates it. The lie in words is only "a shadowy image" of that state. It can be useful against enemies, as medicine for a friend gone mad, or in myths about ancient times. God has no such reason to lie, so he is "perfectly simple and true both in word and deed."
- Guardians should be "true worshippers of the gods and like them." Socrates would deny a chorus to poets who say otherwise, such as Aeschylus on Apollo's false promise to Thetis, and would not let teachers use them.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Socrates argues that character is formed in youth by the stories, imitations, music and bodily training one absorbs. Fear of death, lamentation and imitation of baseness must be removed so the soul grows courageous, temperate and harmonious, and rulers are chosen by lifelong tests of resistance to theft, force and enchantment.

chunks.heading: Why Socrates censors tales of the afterlife and of grieving heroes
chunks.text:
- Socrates argues that no one can be courageous while fearing death. Someone who believes the world below is "real and terrible" will not choose death in battle over defeat and slavery.
- He would strike lines such as "I would rather be a serf on the land of a poor and portionless man than rule over all the dead who have come to nought", plus the shrieking-shades and bat-in-a-cave images and names like Cocytus and Styx.
- The reason is not that these passages are unpoetical. Socrates says "the greater the poetical charm of them, the less are they meet for the ears of boys and men who are meant to be free, and who should fear slavery more than death."
- Poets should be asked to "commend the world below" rather than revile it.
- He grants that such tales may have some use, but warns they could make the guardians' nerves "too excitable and effeminate".

chunks.heading: The good man's equanimity and why laments are cut
chunks.text:
- Socrates' principle is that a good man will not think death terrible for a good comrade, so he will not mourn a departed friend as if something terrible had happened.
- Such a man is "sufficient for himself and his own happiness", so he needs other people least. The loss of a son, a brother or his fortune therefore hits him least.
- He will lament least and bear misfortune with the greatest equanimity.
- Socrates would give the laments of famous men to women (not even good ones) and baser men, so that the guardians scorn to do likewise.
- He objects to Achilles rolling in ashes, Priam grovelling in the dirt, and gods lamenting over Sarpedon or Hector.
- If youth watch such unworthy scenes instead of laughing at them, they will excuse the same behaviour in themselves. They will lose shame and self-control and become men "always whining and lamenting on slight occasions."
- Excessive laughter should also be avoided, since it produces a violent reaction. Gods overcome by "inextinguishable laughter" are excluded too.

chunks.heading: Truth, the physician's lie and obedience to rulers
chunks.text:
- Socrates says truth should be highly valued. A lie is useless to the gods and useful to men only as a medicine, so its use is restricted to physicians.
- If anyone may lie, it is the rulers, and only "for the public good", whether with enemies or their own citizens.
- A private man lying to the rulers is a worse fault than a patient hiding his illness from his physician, or a sailor hiding the state of the ship from the captain.
- Any craftsman caught lying (priest, physician or carpenter) is to be punished, because lying subverts a ship or a state.
- Temperance, as he defines it, consists mainly of obedience to commanders and self-control over sensual pleasures.
- He approves of "Friend, sit still and obey my word" and of soldiers marching in silent awe of their leaders. He rejects insults to rulers such as "O heavy with wine, who hast the eyes of a dog".
- He also rejects praise of feasting, Zeus overcome by lust, and tales of gods in adultery.
- He approves of tales of endurance, such as "Endure, my heart; far worse hast thou endured!"

chunks.heading: Against love of money and divine misconduct
chunks.text:
- Guardians must not be "receivers of gifts or lovers of money". Socrates rejects the line "Gifts persuading gods, and persuading reverend kings".
- He rejects Phoenix advising Achilles to take the Greeks' gifts. He also rejects the idea that Achilles took payment for returning Hector's body, or defied Apollo and the river-god, or dragged Hector round the tomb.
- Achilles, he says, cannot be both mean and avaricious and also contemptuous of gods and men.
- Poets must not claim that heroes such as Theseus and Peirithous did dreadful things. They must say either that the deeds were not done, or that the heroes were not sons of gods.
- Stories that gods cause evil or that heroes are no better than men let people excuse their own vices and "engender laxity of morals among the young."
- On the happiness of the wicked, Socrates says poets who claim injustice pays when undetected, or that justice is "a man's own loss and another's gain", must be commanded to say the opposite. He will not settle this until it is found "what justice is, and how naturally advantageous to the possessor, whether he seem to be just or not."

chunks.heading: Imitation, narration and the single-role principle
chunks.text:
- Socrates splits poetry into three styles: simple narration, where the poet speaks as himself (the dithyramb); pure imitation, where characters speak (tragedy and comedy); and a mix (epic).
- He rests his rule on the earlier principle that one man can do only one thing well. No one can imitate many things as well as one, and the same people cannot succeed at both tragedy and comedy.
- Guardians should imitate only the "courageous, temperate, holy, free". They should avoid imitating baseness, "lest from imitation they should come to be what they imitate".
- Imitations that begin in youth "grow into habits and become a second nature, affecting body, voice, and mind."
- They must not imitate women quarrelling or grieving, slaves, cowards, drunkards, madmen, smiths, or the neighing of horses, thunder or the sea.
- The good man will narrate mostly in his own voice and imitate a good man freely. He will imitate a worse character only briefly, or in jest.
- The worse a man is, the more he will imitate anything, including thunder, hail, dogs and sheep, "in right good earnest".
- The wholly imitative "pantomimic" poet would be anointed with myrrh, crowned with wool and sent to another city. The city keeps the "rougher and severer" poet who imitates only the virtuous.

chunks.heading: Music: harmonies, rhythms and the soul
chunks.text:
- A song has three parts: words, melody and rhythm. The melody and rhythm must follow the words, not the reverse.
- The mournful Lydian harmonies are banished. The "relaxed" Ionian and Lydian are also banned as drinking harmonies.
- Socrates keeps only the Dorian (the strain of necessity, misfortune and courage) and the Phrygian (the strain of freedom, good fortune and temperance).
- He therefore needs no multi-stringed, many-scaled instruments and no flute-makers. Only the lyre and harp are allowed in the city, with a pipe for shepherds in the country. He prefers Apollo's instruments to Marsyas'.
- For rhythms he defers to Damon. He says rhythms should express "a courageous and harmonious life", and the foot and melody should fit the words.
- He holds that grace or its absence follows from good or bad rhythm, and style follows the temper of the soul. Beauty of style, harmony and grace depend on "the true simplicity of a rightly and nobly ordered mind", not the "simplicity" that is a euphemism for folly.
- The same standard applies to painting, weaving, architecture and sculpture. Guardians should not "grow up amid images of moral deformity, as in some noxious pasture", gathering "a festering mass of corruption in their own soul."
- Musical training is the most potent because "rhythm and harmony find their way into the inward places of the soul". A well-trained youth will love the good and hate the bad before he knows why. When reason arrives he will "recognise and salute the friend with whom his education has made him long familiar."
- The musical person must learn the forms of temperance, courage, liberality and magnificence, and their opposites, wherever they appear. Socrates compares this to knowing the letters of the alphabet so that one recognises them in any size or reflection.

chunks.heading: Love of beauty and the limits of pleasure
chunks.text:
- Socrates says a beautiful soul in a beautiful form is the fairest of sights. The man of harmony loves the lovely, but he will tolerate a merely bodily defect in someone he loves, though not a discordant soul.
- Excess of pleasure is no ally of temperance or virtue. It deprives a man of his faculties as much as pain does.
- Sensual love is the keenest pleasure and the "madder".
- "True love is a love of beauty and order—temperate and harmonious", and intemperate pleasure must never come near the lover and beloved.
- He would make the lover treat the beloved as a father treats a son, for a noble purpose and with the other's consent. Going further would be coarseness and bad taste.
- Music should end in "the love of beauty".

chunks.heading: Gymnastic, simple living and why a city full of doctors and lawyers is a sign of decay
chunks.text:
- Socrates believes the good soul improves the body, not the reverse. So he leaves detailed bodily care to the trained mind.
- Guardians must not get drunk. Ordinary athletes, who "sleep away their lives" and are endangered by small departures from regimen, are the wrong model. The guardians should be like "wakeful dogs", able to withstand changes of food, water and climate on campaign.
- His model is Homer's soldiers, who eat roast meat with no fish, no boiled dishes and no sweet sauces. He rejects Syracusan dinners, Sicilian cookery, Corinthian girls and Athenian confectionery.
- Simplicity in music breeds temperance of soul, and simplicity in gymnastic breeds health of body. Complexity breeds licence in the one and disease in the other.
- When intemperance and disease multiply, "halls of justice and medicine are always being opened". Needing first-rate lawyers and doctors even among the liberally educated is a disgrace. Prideful litigiousness is worse, because "to order his life as to be able to do without a napping judge is a far higher and nobler sort of thing."
- Men who fill themselves "with waters and winds, as if their bodies were a marsh" force doctors to invent names like flatulence and catarrh. Herodicus, a sickly trainer, invented "lingering death" and spent his life tending his illness.
- A carpenter wants a quick cure (emetic, purge, cautery or knife) because he has "no time to be ill" and his work gives his life its profit. Wealthy people think they have no such work.
- Excessive care of the body is "most inimical to the practice of virtue". It blocks management of a house or office, and "study or thought or self-reflection", since every headache is blamed on philosophy.
- Asclepius cured only those who were basically healthy and left the incurably sick, as he did not want to "lengthen out good-for-nothing lives". Socrates concludes that the city's medicine and law should serve better natures and let the bodily diseased die, and "the corrupt and incurable souls they will put an end to".

chunks.heading: Good judges, good physicians and the harmony of spirit and philosophy
chunks.text:
- Socrates separates physicians from judges. The best physicians learn through experience of disease, even their own, because they cure the body with the mind.
- A judge governs mind by mind, so he should have had no experience of evil in his own soul when young. Good men seem simple in youth and are easily fooled for just that reason.
- The judge should be older and know evil "not from his own soul, but from late and long observation of the nature of evil in others: knowledge should be his guide, not personal experience."
- The clever criminal is shrewd among his own kind. Among honest men he looks foolish, because he has no pattern of honesty in himself. As Socrates puts it, "vice cannot know virtue too, but a virtuous nature, educated by time, will acquire a knowledge both of virtue and vice."
- Music and gymnastic are not for soul and body respectively. Both aim chiefly at improving the soul.
- Exclusive gymnastic yields hardness, ferocity and ignorance, a man who hates philosophy and "never uses the weapon of persuasion". Exclusive music yields softness and effeminacy.
- Spirit, if rightly educated, gives courage. Gentleness, rightly educated, makes a man moderate.
- The harmonious soul is temperate and courageous, and the inharmonious one is cowardly and boorish. Soft, melancholy music first tempers spirit like iron, then melts and wastes it.
- Two principles in human nature, the spirited and the philosophical, are matched by the two arts. The person who blends music and gymnastic in the fairest proportions is "the true musician and harmonist" and is always needed for a lasting government.

chunks.heading: Choosing rulers, testing guardians and the noble lie
chunks.text:
- The elder should rule the younger, and the best should rule. The best guardians are those with the character of guardians, who love their city most because they regard its interests as identical with their own.
- Guardians are chosen as those who "show the greatest eagerness to do what is for the good of their country". They must be watched at every age to see that they never lose that conviction.
- A conviction can be lost willingly (one learns better) or unwillingly (one is deprived of truth). Socrates names three causes of unwilling loss: theft (argument or time steals it), force (pain or grief), and enchantment (pleasure or fear).
- Candidates are tested in youth with actions where they might forget or be deceived, then with toils and conflicts, then with terrors and pleasures, "more thoroughly than gold is proved in the furnace."
- Those who pass at every age become full guardians (rulers) and receive the highest honours in life and death. Those who fail are rejected. The younger soldiers become auxiliaries.
- Socrates proposes "one royal lie" which he is ashamed to tell. Citizens are told that their upbringing was a dream and that they were formed in the earth, so they must defend their land as a mother and treat fellow citizens as brothers.
- The second half is the myth of metals. God mixed gold into rulers, silver into auxiliaries, and brass and iron into farmers and craftsmen. Children usually resemble their parents, but sometimes a golden parent has a silver child, or the reverse.
- Rulers must guard the purity of the race, and if a child has an admixture of brass or iron, they must demote him without pity. Likewise, children of artisans with gold or silver in them are raised. The oracle says the state is destroyed if a man of brass or iron guards it.
- Socrates admits the present generation will not believe the tale, but their sons and descendants may. The belief will make them "care more for the city and for one another."

chunks.heading: Guardians' way of life: no property, no gold
chunks.text:
- The auxiliaries must not become wolves among sheep. Socrates compares them to watch-dogs that, from poor discipline or hunger, turn on the flock. The best safeguard is true education, which should "civilize and humanize them."
- Their way of life is communal. They own nothing beyond what is necessary, have no private house or store closed to others, and live together in a mess like soldiers in a camp.
- They receive from the citizens a fixed rate of pay, enough for the year and no more.
- They are told that they have divine gold and silver in their souls, so they need no earthly coin. They alone may not touch or handle gold or silver, wear it, drink from it, or live under the same roof with it.
- This will be "their salvation", and they will be "the saviours of the State".
- If they acquire homes, lands or money they will become "housekeepers and husbandmen instead of guardians, enemies and tyrants instead of allies" of the citizens.
- They would then live in greater terror of internal enemies than of external ones, and ruin would follow.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Socrates defends the guardians' lot by arguing the city's good outweighs any one class's happiness, then locates wisdom, courage, temperance and justice in the city. He maps the same structure onto the soul's three parts (reason, spirit, appetite) and concludes that justice is inner harmony and virtue is the soul's health.

chunks.heading: Fixing the budget: wealth and poverty corrupt crafts
chunks.text:
- Adeimantus objects that the guardians are made miserable: they own nothing, are fed but not paid, and cannot travel or spend on luxuries. Socrates answers that the guardians "may very likely be the happiest of men", but that the city was founded for "the greatest happiness of the whole", not the disproportionate happiness of one class.
- He compares this to painting a statue. You do not paint the eyes purple because purple is the most beautiful color; you give each feature its due proportion so the whole is beautiful.
- If every class were given easy luxury, the farmer would stop farming and the potter would stop potting, and the city would lose its distinct classes. Pretense is harmless among cobblers, but when guardians are only "seemingly and not real guardians" they "turn the State upside down".
- He names two causes that make the arts deteriorate: wealth and poverty. A rich potter grows "indolent and careless" and becomes a worse potter. A poor one cannot afford tools and teaches his sons and apprentices worse.
- Wealth is "the parent of luxury and indolence" and poverty "of meanness and viciousness, and both of discontent". The guardians must watch for both, because they creep into a city unobserved.

chunks.heading: Why a poor city can still win wars and how large it should be
chunks.text:
- Asked how a city without money can fight a rich enemy, Socrates says trained warriors fighting an army of rich men have the advantage. He compares them to a single expert boxer who can retreat, turn and strike, and overturn more than one stout opponent.
- He suggests sending an embassy to one of two rival cities: "Silver and gold we neither have nor are permitted to have, but you may; do you therefore come and help us in war, and take the spoils of the other city." No one would choose to fight "lean wiry dogs" rather than side with them against "fat and tender sheep".
- Other cities are not single states. Any city, however small, is two cities, the poor and the rich, at war with each other. Treat them as many and you will "always have a great many friends and not many enemies".
- His limit on size: let the city grow only "so far as is consistent with unity". It should be "neither large nor small, but one and self-sufficing". He says such a city could be the greatest in deed and truth with no more than a thousand defenders.

chunks.heading: Education as the one great thing, and the danger of musical innovation
chunks.text:
- Socrates says the rules he sets are "trifles" if care is taken of "the one great thing", which he would call sufficient rather than great: education and nurture. Well-educated, sensible citizens will work out questions like marriage and child-rearing for themselves, following the proverb that friends have all things in common.
- A well-started city "moves with accumulating force like a wheel". Good nurture implants good constitutions, which improve further when rooted in good education.
- Rulers must preserve music and gymnastic in their original form and allow no innovation. He cites Damon: "when modes of music change, the fundamental laws of the State always change with them."
- Adeimantus describes how lawlessness enters through play. It looks harmless, then seeps into manners and customs, then contracts, then laws and constitutions, ending in "an overthrow of all rights, private as well as public".
- Children who gain habits of order through well-regulated play carry them into all their actions. Socrates holds that the direction in which education starts a man "will determine his future life", because like attracts like.

chunks.heading: Why detailed legislation is pointless: the sick man and the political quack
chunks.text:
- Educated good men will find out for themselves what rules they need for the market, contracts, juries, harbour dues and manners. Written rules about dress, hair and deference to elders are unlikely to last.
- Socrates compares cities that endlessly mend their laws to invalids with no self-restraint. They are "always doctoring and increasing and complicating their disorders", trying every nostrum and treating as an enemy the man who tells them the truth: unless they give up "eating and drinking and wenching and idling", no drug, cautery, spell or amulet will help.
- He mocks ill-ordered cities that forbid changing the constitution on pain of death, yet honor whoever flatters the citizens and anticipates their humors as "a great and good statesman".
- He is kinder to politicians deluded by popular applause: when a man cannot measure and many others who cannot measure say he is four cubits high, he will believe them.
- Reformers who try to end fraud in contracts by legislation are "cutting off the heads of a hydra". The true legislator does not bother with such enactments. They are useless in a bad city and easy to devise in a good one.
- The greatest matters, temples, sacrifices, the service of gods and heroes, and burial rites, he leaves to Apollo at Delphi, since "these are matters of which we are ignorant ourselves".

chunks.heading: Method for finding justice: the four virtues, wisdom and courage
chunks.text:
- Socrates proposes to find justice by assuming the rightly ordered city is perfect, so it is wise, valiant, temperate and just. Find three of the virtues and justice is the residue.
- **Wisdom** is good counsel, a kind of knowledge. Knowing carpentry, bronze-working or farming does not make a city wise. The knowledge that does is the knowledge of the whole: how the city deals with itself and other cities. It belongs to the perfect guardians, the smallest class. The whole city is wise through its smallest part.
- **Courage** resides in the fighting class. It is "a kind of salvation", the preservation under all circumstances of the law-implanted opinion about what is and is not to be feared, in pleasure or pain, desire or fear.
- His dyeing illustration: dyers prepare the white wool carefully so the sea-purple becomes a fast color that no lye can wash out. Education in music and gymnastic prepares soldiers to take the dye of the law. Pleasure is a "mightier agent far in washing the soul than any soda or lye", and sorrow, fear and desire are the strongest solvents.
- He excludes the uninstructed courage of a wild beast or a slave. The courage he means is the courage "of a citizen".

chunks.heading: Temperance as harmony, and justice as doing one's own business
chunks.text:
- **Temperance** is the ordering and control of certain pleasures and desires. "Master of himself" is a paradoxical phrase, since the master is also the servant. It means the better principle in the soul rules the worse; when bad education leaves the better principle overwhelmed, the man is "slave of self".
- Complex, manifold desires are found mostly in children, women, servants and the lowest, most numerous class. Simple, moderate desires guided by reason belong to the few, best born and best educated. The temperate city lets the few hold the many down.
- Unlike wisdom and courage, which sit in one part, temperance runs through the whole like a scale. It is agreement between the naturally superior and inferior about who should rule, in cities and individuals alike.
- With three virtues found, Socrates hunts justice like a huntsman, then realizes it was "tumbling out at our feet" from the start, like people looking for what they hold in their hands. It is the founding principle: each person does the one thing their nature suits best, "doing one's own business, and not being a busybody".
- Justice is the condition and preserver of the other three virtues. Courts also reflect it: a man may "neither take what is another's, nor be deprived of what is his own".
- A carpenter doing a cobbler's work does little harm. The ruin comes when a trader, "lifted up by wealth or strength or the number of his followers", forces his way into the warrior class, or a warrior into the guardians. Meddling between the three classes is "the greatest harm to the State" and is injustice; each class doing its own work is justice.

chunks.heading: The three parts of the soul
chunks.text:
- Socrates tests whether the individual's justice matches the city's. He admits the method is not fully adequate and that "the true method is another and a longer one".
- His principle: the same thing cannot act or be acted upon in the same part, in relation to the same thing, at the same time, in contrary ways. Contradiction shows the things are different. A spinning top is at rest at its axis and in motion at its circumference.
- A thirsty man may refuse to drink. So something bids him drink and something else forbids him. The forbidding principle is **reason**; the bidding one is **appetite**, the irrational part that loves, hungers and thirsts. They must be two.
- **Spirit** (anger) is a third. The story of Leontius, who saw corpses by the Piraeus wall, wanted to look, and was disgusted. He forced his eyes open and said "Look, ye wretches, take your fill of the fair sight", angry at himself. Spirit fights desire and sides with reason.
- A noble man who thinks he has wronged another does not resent the punishment, but when he is the one wronged he "boils and chafes", on the side of justice, until reason, the shepherd, calls his dog off.
- Spirit is distinct from reason too: children are full of spirit at birth, some never reach reason, and animals have spirit. Socrates cites Homer's line of Odysseus striking his breast and rebuking his heart.

chunks.heading: Justice and injustice as health and disease of the soul
chunks.text:
- The just individual is wise through the ruling reason, which knows what is good for each part and the whole. He is courageous when spirit holds to reason's commands about what to fear, in pleasure and pain. He is temperate when all three parts agree that reason should rule.
- Music and gymnastic bring reason and spirit into accord: noble words and lessons strengthen reason, harmony and rhythm soothe the wildness of spirit. Together they guard the appetitive part, "the largest part of the soul and by nature most insatiable of gain", lest it enslave the others and overturn the whole life.
- Justice concerns "not the outward man, but the inward, which is the true self". The just man does not let his parts interfere with each other. He "sets in order his own inner life, and is his own master and his own law, and at peace with himself", binding the three parts like the high, low and middle notes of a scale until he is "no longer many, but has become one".
- Just actions preserve this harmony and are called just and good; the knowledge presiding over them is wisdom. Actions that impair it are unjust, and the opinion presiding over them is ignorance.
- Injustice is "a rebellious subject against a true prince": strife, meddling and the rising of a part of the soul against the whole. It is the same as intemperance, cowardice, ignorance "and every form of vice".
- Justice and injustice are to the soul what health and disease are to the body. Virtue is "the health and beauty and well-being of the soul, and vice the disease and weakness and deformity of the same". Good practices lead to virtue and evil practices to vice.
- Glaucon says it would be ridiculous to argue that life is worth living with all wealth and power if the soul itself is corrupted, answering the old question of whether injustice pays if unpunished. Socrates agrees but proposes to look at the forms of vice. Virtue is one while vice has innumerable forms, and there are five forms of state and five of soul. The first is what they have described, called monarchy or aristocracy, one form either way if the rulers are trained as supposed.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Socrates argues that women of the right nature should share the guardians' education and duties, that an ideal state is a standard and not a forecast, and that cities will have no rest from evil until philosophers rule. He separates knowledge of the one true Form from the mere opinion of those who love only fair sights and sounds.

chunks.heading: The ideal city and the limits of what words can prove
chunks.text:
Socrates treats the model city as a pattern, not a forecast. He compares it to a painter who draws a perfectly beautiful man and is "none the worse" for being unable to show that such a man ever lived.

- The earlier inquiry into justice aimed to build an ideal, so the just man could be judged by how closely he resembles it. It was never meant to prove the ideal could exist.
- He asks: "whether ideals are ever fully realized in language? Does not the word express more than the fact?" The actual always falls short of the ideal.
- So he asks only for an approximation. If a city can be governed nearly as described, the possibility has been shown.
- He asks for the fewest and slightest changes, ideally one thing, or two at most.
- He admits the proposals are hard to defend. He is "a hesitating enquirer", and to carry on an argument that way is "a dangerous and slippery thing". His fear is not ridicule but that he will "miss the truth where I have most need to be sure of my footing, and drag my friends after me in my fall".
- He says he would rather risk being "a deceiver about beauty or goodness or justice in the matter of laws" among enemies than among friends. He thinks deceiving about these things is worse than involuntary homicide.
- He compares those who daydream about their wishes with those who skip the question of possibility. They assume the wish is granted and plan from there, which does little good for "a capacity which was never good for much".

chunks.heading: Different natures: why women can be guardians
chunks.text:
Socrates argues that women can take the same pursuits as men by examining what "sameness of nature" means.

- The objection is that different natures need different pursuits, and men's and women's natures differ. Socrates replies that this is a verbal contradiction. Many people argue from words because they "cannot define and divide, and so know that of which [they are] speaking".
- He says "glorious is the power of the art of contradiction!" Disputing in a spirit of contention is not reasoning.
- He gives a test case: bald and hairy men are different, but it would be a jest to forbid hairy men to be cobblers if bald men are. Nature differs only where the difference affects the pursuit in question.
- A physician and one who is "in mind a physician" share a nature. A physician and a carpenter do not.
- The sexes differ only in that women bear children and men beget them. That is no reason to give them different education.
- The real tests of a gifted nature are these: one person learns easily and another with difficulty, one discovers much from a little learning, and one has a body that serves the mind rather than hindering it.
- Some women have a gift for healing, music, gymnastic, philosophy or spirit, and others do not. Men and women have the same qualities of a guardian, "they differ only in their comparative strength or weakness".
- Women who have these qualities should be chosen as companions and colleagues of men like them.
- Socrates grants Glaucon the general claim that women are weaker, but not that any pursuit is closed to them. The lighter labours go to the women.
- His dog analogy: guard dogs, male and female alike, share in hunting and watching, and the only difference is strength. The same duties require the same nurture and education, namely music and gymnastic.

chunks.heading: Custom, ridicule and the standard of the good
chunks.text:
Socrates expects the proposals to look ridiculous, such as women exercising naked with the men. He answers by pointing out that the standard of laughter changes while the standard of the good stays fixed.

- The Hellenes once thought a naked man ridiculous, as barbarians still do. When the Cretans and then the Lacedaemonians introduced the custom, wits mocked them.
- Experience showed that uncovering was better. Reason prevailed over the "ludicrous effect to the outward eye".
- The man who mocks anything but folly and vice is a fool. A man should not weigh the beautiful by any standard but the good.
- Of the one who laughs at women exercising "from the best of motives", he says he is "plucking a fruit of unripe wisdom". He does not know what he is laughing at.
- His maxim: "the useful is the noble and the hurtful is the base."
- He argues the practice is beneficial as well as possible. The same education makes men and women good guardians, the guardians are the best citizens, and "there can be nothing better" for the State than that men and women be as good as possible.
- The present practice of excluding women is "a violation of nature". Their virtue "will be their robe".

chunks.heading: Unity as the greatest good: common wives, children and property
chunks.text:
Socrates asks what the legislator's chief aim should be. He answers that discord is the greatest evil and the bond of unity the greatest good.

- A city is unified when citizens share pleasures and pains. Disunity comes from disagreement about "mine" and "not mine".
- The best-ordered State is the one where the greatest number apply "mine" and "not mine" to the same things.
- His model is the body. When a finger is hurt, the whole frame feels it and we say the man has a pain in his finger. Likewise, when one citizen fares well or badly, the whole State should rejoice or grieve with him.
- Names matter, but only if they are meant. In other States rulers are masters and the ruled are slaves. In his city the people are "saviours and helpers" and the rulers "maintainers and foster-fathers". Guardians call one another fellow-guardians and treat every citizen as brother, sister, parent or child. They must act in the spirit of those names, "for what can be more ridiculous than... to utter the names of family ties with the lips only".
- Common wives and children, together with common property, are meant to make the guardians "more truly guardians". The proposal is that no parent knows his own child, nor any child his parent.
- Socrates says this would end suits, quarrels over money or children, and flattery of the rich by the poor. He also says it would end the burdens of finding money to raise a family, and trials for assault.
- Equals defending themselves against equals is honourable. Elders rule and chastise the younger, and the younger are held back by shame and fear. Shame restrains them from striking those like parents, and fear that others will rescue the injured one.
- He claims the guardians' life will be blessed "as the life of Olympic victors and yet more blessed", since their victory is the salvation of the whole State.
- He repeats that the city aims at the happiness "not of any particular class, but of the whole". A guardian who tries to appropriate the city for himself will learn Hesiod's saying, "half is more than the whole".
- He admits his main proposals are open to doubt, and he handles utility first and possibility second. He notes that the possibility of common wives and children "will be very much disputed".

chunks.heading: Breeding, marriage regulation and the use of useful falsehood
chunks.text:
Here Socrates describes a controlled system of mating for the guardian class, modelled on the breeding of dogs and birds.

- If breeders take care to pair the best with the best, "what consummate skill will our rulers need if the same principle holds of the human species".
- He says rulers will need "a considerable dose of falsehood and deceit" for the good of their subjects, as a doctor uses medicine rather than mere regimen. The best of either sex should unite as often as possible and the inferior as seldom as possible.
- The arrangement must stay secret to the rulers, or the guardians may rebel. Mating takes place at festivals with sacrifices and hymns. "Ingenious... lots" are drawn by the less worthy so they blame luck and not the rulers.
- The braver youth get more access to women, and such fathers "ought to have as many sons as possible".
- The offspring of good parents go to a nursery with nurses in a separate quarter. Inferior offspring, or those that are deformed, are put away "in some mysterious, unknown place". Mothers are not allowed to recognise their own children.
- The prime of life is about twenty years for a woman (bearing children from age twenty to forty) and thirty for a man (from twenty-five to fifty-five). Those outside these ages who beget children without rulers' sanction are said to act unholily, raising a bastard "uncertified and unconsecrated".
- After those ages people may range freely, except for parent-child and grandparent-grandchild unions. Any embryo conceived must not be allowed to see light, and any child that does is not to be maintained.
- Kinship is by birth timing. Children born in the seventh to tenth month after a wedding are called sons and daughters by the husband of that wedding. Those born then are brothers and sisters and generally may not marry, though the lot and the Pythian oracle may permit it.

chunks.heading: War and the conduct of Hellenes towards Hellenes
chunks.text:
Socrates sets rules for guardians in war, built on the distinction between discord among kin and war against foreigners.

- Children should be taken to war as spectators, as a potter's boy watches before touching the wheel. The presence of their young is "the greatest incentive to valour" in parents. Risk is acceptable if it makes them better.
- They go only on safe expeditions under experienced veterans, and are mounted on tractable, swift horses so they can escape.
- A soldier who deserts his rank or throws away his arms is degraded to husbandman or artisan. One who is captured is given to the enemy. A hero is crowned by comrades and given the right hand of fellowship. Anyone he wishes to kiss may not refuse while the expedition lasts. He is also honoured with seats of precedence, meats and full cups. Those who die gloriously are "of the golden race" and are revered at their graves.
- Hellenes should not enslave Hellenes, and should spare Hellenic cities, "considering the danger... that the whole race may one day fall under the yoke of the barbarians".
- They should not strip the dead beyond the armour. Despoiling gives cowards an excuse to skulk, and robbing a corpse is "illiberality and avarice". He compares it to a dog quarrelling with the stones that strike it. The dead should not be hindered from burial, and spoils taken from Hellenes should not be offered at temples.
- He forbids devastating Hellenic land or burning houses, and would "take the annual produce and no more".
- His distinction: Hellenes and barbarians are natural enemies, so their fighting is "war". Hellenes fighting Hellenes are natural friends, so it is "discord". In discord they act as "correctors, not enemies" and fight "as those who intend some day to be reconciled".
- He argues the guilt of war is confined to a few and the many are friends. Hostility lasts only until the innocent sufferers compel the guilty few to give satisfaction.

chunks.heading: Philosophers must rule: the third wave
chunks.text:
Socrates names the proposal he thinks will be received with the greatest laughter and holds that it is the one change that could reform the State.

- His statement: "Until philosophers are kings, or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy, and political greatness and wisdom meet in one, and those commoner natures who pursue either to the exclusion of the other are compelled to stand aside, cities will never have rest from their evils,—nor the human race, as I believe."
- Only then will his State "have a possibility of life and behold the light of day". He believes that in no other State can there be happiness, private or public.
- He braces for anger. Glaucon warns that many respectable people will run at him with weapons, and he agrees to defend the claim by saying whom he means by a philosopher. Some natures should study philosophy and lead, and others are born to be followers.

chunks.heading: Who is a true philosopher: knowledge, opinion and the many beautiful things
chunks.text:
Socrates defines the philosopher by love of the whole of wisdom and by the ability to see the one form behind the many particulars.

- A true lover loves the whole of what he loves, not a part. Socrates gives parallels: a lover of the young finds a reason to like every flower of youth, a lover of wine takes any wine, and an ambitious man takes any honour. Likewise the philosopher desires "the whole" of wisdom, has a taste for every sort of knowledge, is curious to learn and "is never satisfied".
- Someone who dislikes learning, especially in youth, is not a philosopher, like one who refuses food and is not hungry.
- Glaucon objects that sight-lovers and music-lovers are curious too. Socrates says they are "only an imitation". True philosophers are "lovers of the vision of truth".
- The distinction is between the many and the one. Beauty and ugliness are two, and each is one. Just and unjust, good and evil are also each one, but in combination with actions and things they appear many.
- Lovers of sounds and sights love fine tones, colours and forms, but their minds cannot see or love absolute beauty. Few can attain it.
