- The one who knows beautiful things but not absolute beauty is "a dreamer", one who "likens dissimilar things, who puts the copy in the place of the real object". The one who distinguishes the idea from the objects that participate in it is "wide awake".
- Knowledge and opinion are separate faculties with separate subject-matters. He defines a faculty by its sphere and its result, and the same sphere and result make the same faculty.
- Knowledge is "the mightiest of all faculties" and is infallible. Opinion can err. Knowledge is of being, and the utterly non-existent is utterly unknown.
- Opinion is neither knowledge nor ignorance. It lies between them: "darker than knowledge, but lighter than ignorance". Its objects lie between being and not-being.
- The many beautiful things are always also ugly in some respect, and the many doubles are also halves. These are like riddles told at feasts, which cannot be fixed as being, not-being, both, or neither. This is the "intermediate flux" caught by opinion.
- So those who see many just things but not absolute justice have opinion but not knowledge. Those who see the "absolute and eternal and immutable" know.
- He calls the former "lovers of opinion" and the latter lovers of wisdom. He tells them not to be angry, because "no man should be angry at what is true".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Socrates describes the true philosopher as a lover of truth, temperate, unafraid of death and fit to rule. He explains why philosophy is despised and why public opinion corrupts the best natures. He ends by calling the Good the highest knowledge, likened to the sun, and admits he cannot yet say what it is.

chunks.heading: Why the philosopher's nature is the one fit to rule
chunks.text:
- Socrates argues that guardians of a state must be able to see the truth of each thing. Those who lack knowledge of true being are "simply blind", because they have no clear pattern in their souls to look to and cannot "order the laws about beauty, goodness, justice" here by looking at the original.
- Where the philosopher equals others in experience and virtue and also knows "the very truth of each thing", he must have first place.
- Philosophers love the eternal nature that does not vary through generation and corruption. They love all true being and will renounce no part of it, large or small, honoured or not.

chunks.heading: Marks of the true philosophical nature
chunks.text:
- **Truthfulness:** a lover of wisdom cannot also love falsehood, since nothing is more akin to wisdom than truth. He desires all truth from youth and detests intentional falsehood.
- **Temperance:** desire drawn toward knowledge is like a stream diverted into another channel. It weakens bodily pleasure, so the philosopher is temperate and not covetous.
- **No meanness:** a soul that longs for "the whole of things both divine and human" has no corner of illiberality. A mind that surveys all time and existence does not think much of human life and does not fear death.
- **Justice and gentleness:** a harmonious man who is not covetous, boastful or cowardly cannot be unjust or hard in dealings. Socrates says rude, unsociable behaviour in youth distinguishes the unphilosophical from the philosophical.
- **Pleasure in learning and a good memory:** no one loves what brings pain and little progress, and a forgetful soul is "an empty vessel" that ends hating itself and its fruitless labour.
- **Proportion:** truth is akin to proportion, so he needs a well-proportioned, gracious mind that moves of itself toward the true being of everything.
- Only men with these gifts, perfected by years and education, should be entrusted with the state.

chunks.heading: The ship of state: why philosophers look useless
chunks.text:
- Adeimantus objects that philosophers become "strange monsters, not to say utter rogues", or useless. Socrates agrees that people say this and answers with a parable.
- A shipowner is strong but a little deaf, short-sighted and ignorant of navigation. The sailors quarrel over the helm, though none has learned the art and they claim it cannot be taught. They drug the captain and take over.
- They praise as "able seaman" whoever helps them seize command, and call the true pilot, who studies the seasons, sky, stars and winds, a "prater" and "star-gazer".
- Socrates concludes that philosophers' uselessness is the fault of those who will not use them. As with the physician, the sick man must go to the doctor: "he who wants to be governed" goes to the one able to govern. The true ruler should not beg subjects to be ruled by him.

chunks.heading: How great natures get corrupted
chunks.text:
- Philosophical natures are rare, and they are destroyed by their own virtues (courage, temperance) and by the goods of life: beauty, wealth, strength, rank, connections.
- A seed that lacks proper soil is more damaged the more vigorous it is, so the best natures suffer most in a bad environment. Great crimes spring from "a fulness of nature ruined by education"; weak natures are capable of neither great good nor great evil.
- Socrates denies that private Sophists corrupt the young. The public are "the greatest of all Sophists": in assemblies, courts, theatres and camps the uproar of praise and blame sweeps a young man's sense of good and evil along. They back it with "attainder or confiscation or death".
- He says no one has been trained in virtue by public opinion alone. Whatever is saved in the present evil state of governments "is saved by the power of God".
- Hired Sophists teach only the opinions of the many. He compares them to a keeper who learns the moods of a great beast and calls its likes "good" and its dislikes "evil", with no notion of what the words mean.
- The crowd cannot believe in absolute beauty rather than the many beautiful, so it cannot be philosophical. Flattering friends who want the young man's future power also turn him away from philosophy.

chunks.heading: Pretenders, the rare few, and the right education
chunks.text:
- Philosophy is dishonoured by unworthy pretenders: cleverest craftsmen who leap into it like prisoners "running out of prison into a sanctuary". Socrates likens them to a bald little tinker, newly rich, marrying his master's daughter. Their offspring are "sophisms captivating to the ear".
- The worthy disciples are a small remnant: the exiled, those born in mean cities, those who leave arts they despise, or those held back by illness, as with Theages. Socrates mentions his own "internal sign" as a rare monitor.
- Such a man, among wild beasts, shelters "under the shelter of a wall" and lives pure from injustice. This is great work but not the greatest, because only in a suitable state could he be its saviour.
- Socrates says no existing government is worthy of the philosophic nature.
- On education, he criticises studying philosophy only when young, in spare time from moneymaking, and dropping it when dialectic gets hard. Instead:
  - In childhood and youth, study suited to tender years and chief care for the body.
  - As the intellect matures, "increase the gymnastics of the soul".
  - When civic and military duties are past, let them range freely.
- He urges gentleness toward the multitude. The harsh feeling toward philosophy comes from pretenders who "make persons instead of things the theme of their conversation". True philosophers have no time for envy; their eyes are on fixed, orderly things, which they imitate.

chunks.heading: Philosopher-rulers as painters of constitutions
chunks.text:
- Cities will not rest from evil until the few philosophers termed useless but not corrupt are compelled to take charge and the state is compelled to obey them. Alternatively, kings or their sons must be inspired with a true love of philosophy. Neither is impossible, only difficult.
- "One is enough": a single philosopher-ruler with an obedient city could bring the ideal polity into being.
- Such rulers would wipe the tablet clean, sketch the constitution, then look "upwards and downwards" between absolute justice, beauty and temperance and the human copy. They would erase some features and keep others, making human ways agreeable to the ways of God.
- Guardians must be tested by pleasures, pains, labours and dangers, and "like gold tried in the refiner's fire". Quick intelligence and steadfastness rarely grow together, so they must also be tested in many kinds of knowledge.

chunks.heading: The Form of the Good: the highest knowledge
chunks.text:
- A merely fair measure of the virtues is not enough: "nothing imperfect is the measure of anything". Guardians must take the longer circuit to the highest knowledge, the idea of good, by which all else becomes useful.
- Without the good, no possession or knowledge profits us. Whoever does not know how the just and beautiful are good will be "but a sorry guardian" of them.
- He rejects both common answers:
  - Pleasure: its defenders must admit some pleasures are bad, so good and bad would be the same.
  - Knowledge: its defenders can only say it is knowledge of the good, which is circular.
- Many will accept the appearance of justice, but no one is satisfied with the appearance of good.
- On his own view, Socrates says "all mere opinions are bad, and the best of them blind", and that no one has a right to say positively what he does not know. He declines to state what the good is, offering only its "child", the sun.

chunks.heading: The sun analogy and the divided line
chunks.text:
- The many things are seen but not known, and the ideas are known but not seen. Sight needs a third thing, light, and the sun is its lord. The sun is not sight but its author, and the eye is the most sun-like of the senses.
- As the sun is to sight and visible things, the good is to mind and intelligible things. The soul resting on truth and being is radiant with intelligence; turned to the twilight of becoming and perishing, it has opinion only.
- The good gives truth to the known and the power of knowing to the knower. It is more beautiful than knowledge and truth. As the sun gives generation and growth, the good gives being and essence to things known, though it "far exceeds essence in dignity and power".
- The divided line has four sections, each matched to a faculty, with clearness proportional to truth:
  1. Images (shadows, reflections): perception of shadows.
  2. Visible things (animals, plants, artefacts): faith or conviction. The copy is to the original as opinion is to knowledge.
  3. Mathematical objects: understanding. Geometers use hypotheses and diagrams but think of "the absolute square and the absolute diameter".
  4. The ideas, reached by dialectic: reason. Hypotheses serve as "steps and points of departure" to the first principle of the whole, then the soul descends through ideas alone.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Socrates uses the cave image to show that education is turning the whole soul toward the good, not stuffing knowledge in. Mathematics prepares the soul for dialectic, and rulers must be tested over decades and made to go back down and rule reluctantly.

chunks.heading: The allegory of the cave: what the "unenlightened" nature looks like
chunks.text:
Socrates offers an image of "how far our nature is enlightened or unenlightened."
- Prisoners sit chained in an underground den from childhood. They can only face forward and cannot turn their heads.
- A fire burns behind them. Between the fire and the prisoners runs a raised way with a low wall, "like the screen which marionette players have," over which men carry statues and figures of animals made of wood and stone.
- The prisoners see only the shadows these objects cast on the wall. If they could talk, they would take the names they use to refer to the real things. An echo would make them think the passing shadows were the ones speaking.
- Socrates concludes: "to them, the truth would be literally nothing but the shadows of the images." He says plainly that they are "like ourselves."
- Prisoners honour whoever is quickest at spotting which shadow comes before or after another and best at predicting what follows. Socrates treats this "wisdom of the den" as cleverness about appearances.

chunks.heading: The painful ascent: why truth is hard to see and hard to accept
chunks.text:
Socrates describes what happens when a prisoner is freed and turned toward the light.
- At first he suffers sharp pains and glare. He cannot make out the realities whose shadows he knew, and he would think the shadows "far truer" than the objects now shown to him.
- If forced to look straight at the light, he turns back to what he can see. If dragged up a steep, rugged ascent into the sun, he is "pained and irritated" and dazzled.
- Sight must be acquired by habit, in stages: shadows first, then reflections in water, then the objects themselves, then the moon and stars by night, and last the sun "in his own proper place," as it is.
- The freed man would reason that the sun gives the seasons and years and is guardian of the visible world. He would pity his former companions and refuse their honours. He would say with Homer that it is better "to be the poor servant of a poor master, and to endure anything, rather than think as they do and live after their manner."
- Returning to the den, his eyes are full of darkness. He looks ridiculous in contests of measuring shadows. The prisoners say it is better not to ascend, and that anyone who tries to free and lead them up should be put to death.

chunks.heading: The idea of the good, and how to read the allegory
chunks.text:
Socrates gives his interpretation, "whether rightly or wrongly God knows."
- The prison is the world of sight, the fire is the sun, and the ascent is "the ascent of the soul into the intellectual world."
- In the world of knowledge the idea of the good "appears last of all, and is seen only with an effort." Once seen, it is inferred to be "the universal author of all things beautiful and right," source of light in the visible world and of reason and truth in the intellectual.
- Anyone who would act rationally, "either in public or private life," must keep his eye fixed on it.
- Those who reach this vision are unwilling to descend to human affairs, which is natural. Someone coming from contemplation into a courtroom, arguing about "the images or the shadows of images of justice" before people who have never seen absolute justice, will blink and look foolish.
- Bewilderment of the eyes has two causes: coming out of the light and going into it. A sensible person asks which has happened before laughing. If he must laugh, there is more reason to laugh at the soul rising into the light than at the one returning from it.

chunks.heading: Education as turning the soul, not filling it
chunks.text:
Socrates rejects the claim of "certain professors of education" that they can "put a knowledge into the soul which was not there before, like sight into blind eyes."
- The power and capacity to learn already exist in the soul. Just as the eye cannot turn from dark to light without the whole body, the instrument of knowledge turns toward being only by "the movement of the whole soul."
- Education is therefore an art of conversion: it does not implant sight but turns a faculty that is "looking away from the truth" in the right direction, and it must do so in the easiest and quickest way.
- Other virtues resemble bodily qualities and can be implanted later by habit and exercise. The virtue of wisdom contains "a divine element which always remains," made useful or harmful by which way it faces.
- The "clever rogue" shows this. His keen intelligence is "the reverse of blind," but it is forced into the service of evil, so he is "mischievous in proportion to his cleverness."
- If such natures were released in youth from the pleasures of eating and drinking, "like leaden weights" dragging the soul down, the same faculty would see truth as keenly.
- Turning the soul is "not the turning over of an oyster-shell." It is the passage from a day "little better than night" to the true day of being.

chunks.heading: Why philosophers must rule, and must be made to descend
chunks.text:
Socrates argues that neither the uneducated nor the endlessly educated make able ministers of state. The first have "no single aim of duty" guiding their actions. The second will not act unless compelled, thinking they already dwell "in the islands of the blest."
- The founders' task is to compel the best minds to ascend to the good, and then to make them go back down among the prisoners "and partake of their labours and honours, whether they are worth having or not."
- To Glaucon's objection that this is unjust, Socrates replies that the lawgiver aimed at the happiness of the whole city, not of one class. He binds citizens by persuasion and necessity, making them benefactors of one another.
- He tells the philosophers they have been educated better than others "to be rulers of the hive." Each must go down in turn and get "the habit of seeing in the dark," after which they will see "ten thousand times better" because they know the beautiful, just and good in their truth.
- Key political claim: "the State in which the rulers are most reluctant to govern is always the best and most quietly governed, and the State in which they are most eager, the worst."
- Rulers must have a better life than ruling to look forward to. Only those "rich, not in silver and gold, but in virtue and wisdom" will rule well. Men who come to office "poor and hungering after their own private advantage" fight over it and ruin themselves and the state.
- "The only life which looks down upon the life of political ambition is that of true philosophy." Those who govern should not be lovers of the task, or "there will be rival lovers, and they will fight."

chunks.heading: The curriculum: arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, harmony
chunks.text:
Socrates looks for studies that draw the soul "from becoming to being." Gymnastic concerns generation and decay, and music built habit through harmony and rhythm but gave no science. The useful trades are "mean." What remains is what all arts share: number and calculation.
- **What provokes thought:** Sense objects that give a clear answer, like a finger being a finger, do not invite thought. Those where the senses report opposites at once (large and small, hard and soft, light and heavy) perplex the soul, which then summons calculation and intelligence and asks "What is great?" and "What is small?" This is where the visible and the intelligible separate.
- **Arithmetic:** Unity appears as both one and a multitude, which stirs the question "What is absolute unity?" Arithmetic has a double use: the soldier needs it to array troops, and the philosopher needs it to "rise out of the sea of change and lay hold of true being." It must be studied "not like merchants or retail-traders" but "in the spirit of a philosopher, and not of a shopkeeper," until the nature of numbers is seen "with the mind only." Mathematicians refuse to divide absolute unity, because they speak of numbers "realised in thought." Even dull students become quicker for it, and it is hard to find a more difficult study.
- **Geometry:** Beyond the little needed for war, its value is as knowledge "of the eternal, and not of aught perishing and transient." Practitioners wrongly talk of "squaring and extending and applying." Socrates notes that solid geometry is neglected because no government patronises it and students lack a director; with state backing, disciples and discoveries would follow.
- **Astronomy:** Socrates denies that gazing at the sky makes the soul look up. Whoever studies "the fretted ceiling" or seeks particulars of sense is looking downward, "whether he floats, or only lies on his back." The visible heavens should serve as a pattern, like skilled work by Daedalus: a geometer would admire it but never look there for "the true equal or the true double." So "employ problems, and let the heavens alone."
- **Harmony:** Musicians who put their ears to strings and compare audible notes labour in vain. Even the Pythagoreans fall short, because they "never attain to problems," never asking why some numbers are harmonious and others not. This is useful only "if sought after with a view to the beautiful and good."
- All these studies have value only when brought into "inter-communion" and seen in their mutual affinities. They are "but the prelude" to dialectic.

chunks.heading: Dialectic as the coping-stone, and who may study it, and when
chunks.text:
Dialectic is the "hymn" for which the sciences are the prelude. Socrates says "I have hardly ever known a mathematician who was capable of reasoning," and that men unable "to give and take a reason" cannot have the needed knowledge.
- **What dialectic does:** It proceeds by reason alone, without the senses, until pure intelligence perceives the absolute good, ending the intellectual journey as seeing the sun ends the visible one. It alone goes "directly to the first principle" and "does away with hypotheses." Geometry and similar sciences only "dream about being," since they leave their hypotheses unexamined. If a man "knows not his own first principle," his conclusions are built "out of he knows not what."
- **Four divisions of knowing:** science, understanding, belief, and perception of shadows. The first two are intellect, concerned with being; the last two are opinion, concerned with becoming. "As being is to becoming, so is pure intellect to opinion."
- **The test of knowing the good:** Someone who cannot define the idea of good and "run the gauntlet of all objections," disproving them "not by appeals to opinion, but to absolute truth, never faltering at any step," knows neither the good nor any good. He apprehends a shadow and is "dreaming and slumbering" through life. Rulers must not be "like posts, having no reason in them," so they need training in "asking and answering questions."
- **Who qualifies:** Natures that are steady, brave, quick, with good memory, and "an unwearied" lover of labour. Industry must not be "lame": a man who loves exercise and hunting but hates learning, or one who hates deliberate lies yet tolerates ignorance "like a swinish beast in the mire," is half-sound. Philosophy fell into disrepute because such "bastards" take it up instead of true sons.
- **Method for the young:** Start in childhood, but "a freeman ought not to be a slave in the acquisition of knowledge." Knowledge gained under compulsion "obtains no hold on the mind," so early education should be "a sort of amusement" that reveals each child's natural bent. Solon was wrong that the old can learn much; "youth is the time for any extraordinary toil."
- **The staged path:**
  - Around age 20: those selected see the sciences brought together and their kinship with true being. "The comprehensive mind is always the dialectical."
  - Age 30: a further selection, tested by dialectic.
  - Five years of philosophy, then sent back down into the den to hold military or other offices and be tested by temptation.
  - Fifteen years of that, until age 50.
  - At 50, the survivors who excelled in every action and branch of knowledge finally behold the absolute good and use it as the pattern for ordering the state and their lives. They rule when their turn comes "simply as a matter of duty," and when they have trained successors they depart to the Islands of the Blest.
  - Women with the same natures share this life.

chunks.heading: The danger of dialectic taken up too early
chunks.text:
Socrates warns that dialectic has introduced "lawlessness" among its students.
- His image is a supposititious son raised in wealth among flatterers. He honours his supposed parents until he learns they are not his real ones; once he cannot find his true parents, he turns to the flatterers.
- Likewise, someone raised on inherited maxims of justice and honour is questioned until arguments leave him believing "nothing is honourable any more than dishonourable, or just and good any more than the reverse." Having lost the old beliefs and not yet found true ones, he drifts to the life that flatters his desires and becomes a lawbreaker. Socrates calls this natural, "most excusable," and "pitiable."
- Youngsters who first taste argument "argue for amusement," contradict everyone, and "like puppy-dogs, they rejoice in pulling and tearing at all who come near them." They end up believing nothing and give philosophy a bad name.
- Older men do not fall into this. They imitate "the dialectician who is seeking for truth, and not the eristic, who is contradicting for the sake of amusement."
- Hence the care: only orderly, steadfast people, not "any chance aspirant or intruder," and only at age 30 or later after careful selection.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In Republic Book VIII Socrates argues that constitutions mirror the characters of the people in them, then traces how a just order degrades through timocracy, oligarchy and democracy into tyranny. The same sequence runs inside the soul, as ruling reason is displaced by ambition, then money-lust, then unruly appetite.

chunks.heading: Why cities and souls decline: Socrates' five constitutions and their matching characters
chunks.text:
- Socrates holds that "governments vary as the dispositions of men vary" and that there are as many constitutions as there are types of soul.
- Cities are not made "of 'oak and rock'" but out of the human natures in them, which "turn the scale and draw other things after them." In his words: "the States are as the men are."
- He lists five constitutions, each with a matching soul:
  - Aristocracy, rule of the best, matching the just and good man.
  - Timocracy (Crete and Sparta), rule of honour, matching the contentious and ambitious man.
  - Oligarchy, a state that "teems with evils," matching the money-lover.
  - Democracy, matching the man of unordered freedom.
  - Tyranny, "the fourth and worst disorder of a State," matching the tyrant.
- His method is to take the city first, then the individual, then compare the most just life with the most unjust. This tests whether to pursue injustice, as Thrasymachus advises, or justice, and whether the best man is also the happiest.
- Political change begins in divisions among those who hold power: "a government which is united, however small, cannot be moved."

chunks.heading: From aristocracy to timocracy: discord, neglect of music, and the metals
chunks.text:
- Socrates says everything that has a beginning has an end, so even the ideal city will dissolve.
- Decline starts when rulers, using calculation mixed with sense-perception, misjudge the timing of births and breed children who are unfortunate.
- These unworthy children take over as guardians, and they neglect the Muses: "first by under-valuing music," then gymnastic, so the young become less cultivated.
- The new rulers lose the power to test the metals of the gold, silver, brass and iron races. Iron mixes with silver and brass with gold, producing "dissimilarity and inequality and irregularity, which always and in all places are causes of hatred and war."
- Discord splits the classes:
  - The iron and brass types turn to acquiring money, land, houses, gold and silver.
  - The gold and silver types incline toward virtue and the old order.
- The compromise is private ownership of land and houses. The rulers also enslave the people they once protected as free citizens and make them subjects.
- The resulting timocracy is a mean between aristocracy and oligarchy:
  - It keeps honour for rulers, common meals, a warrior class that avoids farming, crafts and trade, and a focus on gymnastics and military training.
  - It fears putting philosophers in power, since they are no longer simple and earnest, and prefers spirited characters suited to war.
  - Its rulers secretly hoard gold in private treasuries and are "stealing their pleasures," like children running from their father, the law.
- They were "schooled not by gentle influences but by force," having neglected "the true Muse, the companion of reason and philosophy."
- One element dominates: "the spirit of contention and ambition," the spirited part of the soul.

chunks.heading: The timocratic man: how a quiet father produces an ambitious son
chunks.text:
- This man is self-assertive, less cultivated yet a friend of culture, a good listener but no speaker, rough with slaves, courteous to free men, and obedient to authority.
  - He loves power and honour and claims rule on the strength of military feats, not eloquence.
  - He loves gymnastics and hunting.
- He despises riches when young but grows more avaricious with age, "having lost his best guardian": "Philosophy, tempered with music, who comes and takes her abode in a man, and is the only saviour of his virtue throughout life."
- His origin is a grave father in an ill-governed city who declines office, avoids lawsuits and waives his rights to escape trouble.
- Outside voices then pull the son the other way:
  - His mother complains that her husband has no place in government and is "only half a man."
  - Old servants urge the son to retaliate against his father's debtors and be "more of a man."
  - In the city, those who mind their own business are called simpletons, while busybodies are honoured.
- The father waters the rational principle in the boy, while the others feed the spirited and appetitive parts. The boy, not originally bad but in bad company, settles in the middle and hands "the kingdom which is within him" to contentiousness and passion.

chunks.heading: Oligarchy: how love of wealth destroys virtue and splits the city in two
chunks.text:
- Oligarchy is "a government resting on a valuation of property, in which the rich have power and the poor man is deprived of it."
- Timocracy turns into it as private hoards of gold build up and people invent illegal ways to spend:
  - One man sees another grow rich and rivals him, until most citizens become money-lovers.
  - "When riches and virtue are placed together in the scales of the balance, the one always rises as the other falls."
  - What is honoured is cultivated and what is dishonoured is neglected, so virtue and the virtuous lose standing.
  - A property qualification for citizenship is then set by law, enforced by arms or intimidation.
- He lists its defects:
  - Choosing rulers by wealth is like choosing pilots by property: a poor but better pilot would be refused the helm, and the ship would be wrecked. Ruling a city is the hardest case of all.
  - The state is two cities, rich and poor, on one spot and always conspiring against each other.
  - It cannot wage war: arming the multitude makes the rich fear them more than the enemy, and not arming them leaves "few to fight as they are few to rule." Its rich also dislike paying taxes.
  - The same people are farmer, tradesman and soldier at once.
  - A man can sell everything and remain in the city as "only a poor, helpless creature," belonging to no class.
- Socrates calls the spendthrift who is neither ruler nor subject a drone, "the plague of the city as the other is of the hive."
  - Stingless drones end as paupers.
  - Stinging drones become the criminal class.
  - Where there are paupers, there are hidden thieves, cutpurses and temple robbers. He traces this to "want of education, ill-training, and an evil constitution of the State."

chunks.heading: The oligarchic man: saving, fear and a divided soul
chunks.text:
- This man's origin is a timocratic father who is ruined by the state, perhaps tried by informers and stripped of office and property.
  - The son, taught by fear, throws ambition and passion off their throne.
  - Humbled by poverty, he saves and works until he has a fortune.
  - He seats the appetitive, covetous element as great king and makes reason and spirit sit on the ground beside it.
  - Reason may only calculate how small sums become larger, and spirit may only admire wealth and the wealthy.
- He satisfies only necessary appetites, subdues his other desires as unprofitable, and is the "shabby fellow" who saves from everything and whom the crowd applauds.
- His honesty is "enforced virtue." He restrains his bad desires "by necessity and fear," not by reason, because he trembles for his possessions.
  - To see his real nature, watch him where he can cheat safely, such as guardianship of an orphan, or when he spends money that is not his.
  - He is "two men, and not one," at war with himself. He is more respectable than most, but "the true virtue of a unanimous and harmonious soul will flee far away and never come near him."
- He is a poor competitor for honours because he will not spend on glory, fighting "with a small part only of his resources."
- Lack of education shows: had he been educated he would not have made "a blind god director of his chorus."

chunks.heading: Oligarchy into democracy: ruinous lending, the "stings", and a remedy
chunks.text:
- Oligarchic rulers refuse to limit the extravagance of spendthrift youths because they profit by lending to them and buying up their estates.
- Socrates says "the love of wealth and the spirit of moderation cannot exist together in citizens of the same State to any considerable extent."
- Ruined men of good family stay in the city, armed with grievances and ready to sting. They are in debt or stripped of citizenship, hate those who took their property, and want revolution.
- Money-men, who pretend not to see their victims, keep lending to the unwary and multiply the original sum many times over, so drones and paupers abound.
- He proposes a milder remedy than banning extravagance: let every voluntary contract be entered "at his own risk." This would reduce scandalous money-making and push citizens to look to their characters.
- The rulers' young men live in luxury and idleness of body and mind. On campaign, a tough, sunburnt poor soldier beside a puffing rich one concludes that the rich are only rich because nobody has the courage to despoil them. They say privately, "Our warriors are not good for much."
- A weak state, like a diseased body, falls ill at the slightest touch and goes to war with itself.
- Democracy arises when the poor win, killing or banishing some opponents and sharing "an equal share of freedom and power" with the rest. Magistrates are commonly chosen by lot.

chunks.heading: Democracy and the democratic man: freedom as the only good, and desires without order
chunks.text:
- Democracy is free and frank, and "a man may say and do what he likes." It holds the greatest variety of human natures, an "embroidered robe" spangled with flowers. Socrates says it is like a bazaar of constitutions where a founder could pick one.
- Nobody must rule, obey, fight or hold office unless he fancies it. This is "supremely delightful," but he adds "for the moment."
- Democracy tramples the principles of the ideal city, including that a good man must be raised from childhood among beautiful things. It promotes anyone who professes to be "the people's friend," and gives "a sort of equality to equals and unequals alike."
- The democratic man is the oligarch's son, raised miserly and then drawn into the unnecessary pleasures. Socrates distinguishes:
  - Necessary desires cannot be got rid of and benefit us. Eating simple food for health and strength is one.
  - Unnecessary desires can be removed by training from youth and do no good or harm. Delicate food and luxuries are examples.
  - The oligarch serves only the necessary ones, while the drone-like spendthrift serves the unnecessary ones.
- The change begins when the young man tastes "drones' honey" among crafty companions who supply endless pleasures.
  - Desires from outside ally with desires inside, as like helps like in a city.
  - Reverence and a father's advice may briefly restore order.
  - Fresh desires then multiply, because he does not know how to educate them, and seize his soul's citadel, which is "void of all accomplishments and fair pursuits and true words."
  - False and boastful conceits take over, and he lives among the lotus-eaters.
  - Modesty is renamed silliness and temperance unmanliness. Insolence is called breeding, anarchy liberty, waste magnificence and impudence courage.
- He gives each desire its turn. He rejects the advice that some pleasures are noble and should be honoured while others are evil and should be mastered, and says they are all alike. His life is "motley and manifold," with no law or order, and he calls it "joy and bliss and freedom."
  - He drinks and plays the flute, then drinks only water.
  - He trains in gymnastics, then idles, then plays at philosophy.
  - He dabbles in politics and copies warriors or businessmen.

chunks.heading: From democracy to tyranny: excess of freedom, drones and the protector who becomes a wolf
chunks.text:
- Oligarchy fell by its insatiable desire for wealth, and democracy falls by its insatiable desire for freedom. Socrates says "the excess of liberty, whether in States or individuals, seems only to pass into excess of slavery."
- A democracy thirsty for freedom with "evil cupbearers" punishes rulers as "cursed oligarchs" unless they pour freely. It sneers at loyal citizens as slaves who "hug their chains."
- Anarchy spreads everywhere:
  - Fathers fear their sons, and sons have no reverence for parents.
  - Resident foreigners, citizens and visitors are equal.
  - Teachers flatter pupils, and the old imitate the young.
  - Slaves are as free as their buyers, and even animals "march along with all the rights and dignities of freemen."
  - Citizens "chafe impatiently at the least touch of authority" and stop caring even for written or unwritten laws.
- The doctor-lawgiver should treat idle spendthrifts as the plague of every city, "what phlegm and bile are to the body," and keep them out like a wise bee-master.
- Democracy has three classes:
  - Drones, now nearly the entire ruling power, with the keener speaking and acting while the rest buzz about the platform and allow no opposition.
  - The orderly, wealthy class, which the drones squeeze for honey.
  - The working people, the largest and most powerful class, who gather only for a little honey.
- Leaders strip the rich and give the people a share while keeping the larger part. The rich are accused of plotting against the people. Driven by deceived majorities and the drones' stings, they become oligarchs in fact.
- The people then set a champion over them. This is "the root from which a tyrant springs" and he first appears as a protector.
- He turns into a tyrant by shedding kinsmen's blood through false accusation, hinting at cancelling debts and redistributing land. Socrates compares him to the Arcadian tale of the man who tasted human entrails and became a wolf.
- He then asks for a bodyguard "lest the people's friend be lost to them," is exiled, returns, and finally becomes tyrant.

chunks.heading: The tyrant in power: war, purges and a ruler's dependence on bad company
chunks.text:
- At first he smiles, greets everyone, and promises debt relief and land.
- Once foreign enemies are dealt with, he stirs up wars so the people need a leader. War also impoverishes them with taxes, which keeps them busy with daily needs, and lets him expose anyone suspected of favouring freedom.
- Growing unpopular, he must remove the brave, high-minded, wise and wealthy among his own backers. This is the reverse of a physician's purge, which removes the worse and leaves the better. Socrates calls his position "a blessed alternative": to dwell with the many bad who hate him, or not to live.
- The more hated he is, the more guards he needs. He hires drones from many lands and frees citizens' slaves to enrol them in his bodyguard. They admire him, while the good avoid him.
- Socrates quotes Euripides, "Tyrants are wise by living with the wise," and says poets who praise tyranny as godlike would not be admitted to his city. They attract mobs, hire persuasive voices and draw cities toward tyranny and democracy.
- To pay his followers he confiscates sacred treasures and attainted persons' fortunes, then lives off the people and finally off his father's estate, meaning the people. If they try to expel him, he beats them with force. The tyrant is a parricide, and the people escaping "the smoke which is the slavery of freemen" fall "into the fire which is the tyranny of slaves."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Socrates traces how an unruled soul becomes tyrannical and argues that the tyrant, though seemingly powerful, is the most miserable and unfree of men. He gives three proofs that the just, reason-ruled man lives most happily: only wisdom delivers true pleasure, and injustice ruins the soul even when it goes undetected.

chunks.heading: The tyrannical soul is formed when one master passion enslaves the rest
chunks.text:
- Socrates holds that everyone, even good people, has a lawless "wild-beast nature" that "peers out in sleep." It is the set of unnecessary, unlawful appetites that wake when reason is asleep.
- In the self-controlled person these appetites are banished or left few and weak. In the unruly person they are strong and numerous.
- The tyrannical man is built in stages. A son grows up under a democratic father, is pulled into what seducers call "perfect liberty," and then has a single master passion planted in him as lord over his idle lusts.
- Socrates images this passion as "a sort of monstrous winged drone." Madness becomes captain of its guard.
- The passion drives out any good opinions, appetites and shame in the soul until temperance is purged and madness fills it.
- He links this to old sayings: love is called a tyrant, and a drunk or deranged man fancies he can rule even the gods.
- The tyrannical man appears when nature, habit or both make him "drunken, lustful, passionate."

chunks.heading: How the tyrannical man lives, and why he ends up a criminal
chunks.text:
- Desire is the lord of his house. Feasts and revelry spend his money, then comes debt, and then his desires cry out "like young ravens" for more.
- He needs money "no matter how" to escape pain, so he takes from his parents. He cheats them first, then uses force, and feels no compunction about it.
- Socrates notes the irony of him preferring a new, dispensable lover over his mother and father, his "ancient friends" and most necessary ones. He says "a tyrannical son is a blessing to his father and mother."
- He moves on to burglary, stealing cloaks and robbing temples. His childhood opinions about good and evil are overthrown by the freed passions, which now guard love's empire.
- What he once did only in dreams (murder, forbidden acts) he now does awake.
- When such men are many and feel their strength, they pick the one with the most tyrant in his own soul and make him tyrant of the city. If the city resists, he beats his fatherland as he beat his parents.
- As private men they flatter and fawn when they need something and drop people once satisfied.
- Socrates' verdict: "They are always either the masters or servants and never the friends of anybody; the tyrant never tastes of true freedom or friendship." They are treacherous and utterly unjust.
- He calls the tyrant "the waking reality of what we dreamed," and says the longer he lives the more tyrant he becomes.

chunks.heading: The tyrant is a slave, poor and afraid, and the real tyrant is the most miserable of all
chunks.text:
- Socrates sets the city and the soul side by side. A city under a tyrant is enslaved, poor, full of fear, and rich in lamentation. The tyrannical soul is the same.
- That soul is a slave's, because its best parts are enslaved and a small, maddest part rules.
- It is least able to do what it wants, goaded by a gadfly and full of remorse.
- It is poor and insatiable, "full of fear."
- He then argues that the man who is tyrannical by nature and also rules as a public tyrant is more miserable than a private tyrant.
- Analogy: a rich man with some fifty slaves lives without fear because the whole city protects every owner. Carry him into a wilderness with no freemen to help him and he must flatter and cajole his own slaves. Surround him with neighbours who would kill a slave-master and his plight is worse still.
- The tyrant lives in exactly that prison. He cannot travel or see what free citizens see. He "lives in his hole like a woman hidden in the house" and envies anyone who goes abroad.
- He must "be master of others when he is not master of himself," like a paralytic forced to fight other men.
- Socrates concludes: "He who is the real tyrant, whatever men may think, is the real slave," forced into servility and flattery of the vilest people.
- Power makes him worse: more jealous, faithless, unjust, friendless and impious, "the purveyor and cherisher of every sort of vice."
- Judge by someone with insight who has seen the tyrant at home "stripped of his tragedy attire" and in public danger, not by the pomp that dazzles outsiders like children.

chunks.heading: Proclaiming the verdict: the five regimes ranked, and the first proof
chunks.text:
- Socrates has Glaucon rank the five regimes and the matching souls by virtue and vice, happiness and misery: royal, timocratic, oligarchic, democratic, tyrannical.
- The announcement: "the son of Ariston (the best) has decided that the best and justest is also the happiest," the man "most royal" and "king over himself." The worst and most unjust is the most miserable, "he who being the greatest tyrant of himself is also the greatest tyrant of his State."
- He adds that this holds "whether seen or unseen by gods and men."
- This is his first proof, resting on the parallel between city and soul.
- He calls the question of good and evil "the greatest" of all questions and insists the answer should be reasoned out, not conjectured.

chunks.heading: Second proof: three parts of the soul, three kinds of people, and who is qualified to judge pleasure
chunks.text:
- The soul has three principles, each with its own pleasure, desire and rule:
  - the part that learns, which loves wisdom and knowledge
  - the spirited part, which loves ruling, conquering and honour
  - the appetitive part, which loves money and gain because money satisfies its desires
- So there are three kinds of people: lovers of wisdom, honour and gain. Each praises his own life as pleasantest and dismisses the others.
- Socrates asks how to decide, since the question is which life is more pleasant, not more honourable. The criterion he picks is "experience and wisdom and reason."
- On experience, the philosopher has tasted the other pleasures from childhood. The lover of gain has hardly tasted the sweetness of knowing truth.
- Honour comes to the rich, brave and wise alike, so all have tasted it. Only the philosopher knows the delight of knowing true being.
- On the instrument of judgment, reason is the philosopher's own tool, not the covetous or ambitious man's.
- Result: the pleasure of the intelligent part is pleasantest, the life of the honour-lover comes second and the gain-lover's last. In his words, "the wise man speaks with authority when he approves of his own life."
- This is the second time the just man has overthrown the unjust.

chunks.heading: Third proof: true pleasure versus shadow pleasure
chunks.text:
- Socrates notes there is a neutral state of rest between pleasure and pain. The sick say nothing is pleasanter than health, and people in pain say nothing is pleasanter than being rid of it.
- Rest cannot be both pleasure and pain, since pleasure and pain are motions of the soul and the neutral state is not motion. So relief from pain only appears pleasant by contrast. It is "an appearance only and not a reality."
- Many pleasures have no antecedent pain, such as smells. They come and go without leaving pain, which shows pure pleasure is not mere cessation of pain.
- The strong bodily pleasures are mostly reliefs of pain, as are anticipations of pleasures and pains.
- Illustration: a man carried from the lower to the middle region thinks he has gone up. Someone who has never seen the true upper region mistakes the middle for it. Likewise, people inexperienced in truth mistake freedom from pain for pleasure, "like contrasting black with grey instead of white."
- Hunger and thirst are emptiness of the body. Ignorance and folly are emptiness of the soul. Food fills the one and wisdom the other.
- What is filled with things of more real being (true opinion, knowledge, mind, virtue) is more truly filled and enjoys truer pleasure than what is filled with perishable things.
- Those who know no wisdom or virtue and live for gluttony and sensuality "go down and up again as far as the mean" and never reach the true upper world.
- He compares them to cattle with eyes always on the ground and heads at the dining-table. They fatten, breed, and "kick and butt at one another with horns and hoofs which are made of iron," killing one another from insatiable lust.
- Their pleasures are shadows mixed with pain, fought over as the Greeks fought over the shadow of Helen at Troy.
- The spirited part too goes wrong when it pursues honour or anger "without reason or sense."
- Lovers of money and honour who follow reason get the truest pleasures available to them. When the whole soul follows the philosophical principle, each part does its own work, is just, and enjoys its own best pleasures.
- The more a desire departs from law and order, the further it is from reason, so the tyrant lives farthest from true pleasure and the king nearest.

chunks.heading: The 729 calculation: how much more pleasantly the king lives
chunks.text:
- Socrates counts the steps from true pleasure. The tyrant is third from the oligarch, who is third from the royal man, so the tyrant is removed from true pleasure by a number three times three.
- His "shadow pleasure" is a plane figure (length by width), and raised to a solid it is cubed.
- Result: "the king is parted from the tyrant in truth of pleasure... living 729 times more pleasantly, and the tyrant more painfully by this same interval."
- He remarks that the number "nearly concerns human life," since it can be set against days, nights, months and years.
- He adds that the just man's superiority in propriety of life, beauty and virtue is "immeasurably greater" still.

chunks.heading: The image of the soul, and why injustice never profits
chunks.text:
- To answer the claim that injustice pays for a man reputed to be just, Socrates builds an image of the soul. It has a many-headed beast that can grow heads of tame and wild animals, a lion, and a man, all joined and wrapped in a single human shape.
- The defender of injustice is in effect saying it pays to feed the monster and strengthen the lion while starving the man and letting the three bite and devour each other.
- The defender of justice says to give the man within complete mastery. Like a good husbandman, he should cultivate the gentle heads, stop the wild ones growing, make the lion his ally, and unite all the parts with one another and with himself.
- Socrates tests the unjust man with questions. The noble is what subjects the beast to the man, "or rather to the god in man." The ignoble subjects the man to the beast.
- Taking gold to enslave the best part of oneself to the worst is worse than selling a son or daughter into slavery to evil men. It is selling "his own divine being to that which is most godless." He compares it to Eriphyle taking the necklace for her husband's life.
- Common blame maps onto the image:
  - Intemperance means the monster is let loose.
  - Pride and bad temper mean the lion and serpent grow too strong.
  - Luxury and softness weaken the lion.
  - Flattery and meanness mean the lion is trained for money until he becomes a monkey.
- Mean trades and manual arts are a reproach because the higher principle is so weak that the person must flatter the creatures within.
- On rule, it is better for everyone to be ruled by divine wisdom within, or failing that by an outside authority, so all are "friends and equals." This, he says, is not for the servant's injury, answering Thrasymachus.
- He sees the same purpose in law, and in how children are not freed until a ruling principle has been set up in them.
- Injustice never profits: "He who is undetected only gets worse, whereas he who is detected and punished has the brutal part of his nature silenced and humanized." The soul is perfected by justice, temperance and wisdom more than the body is by beauty, strength or health.

chunks.heading: How the man of understanding lives
chunks.text:
- He honours studies that shape his soul and ignores others.
- He trains his body to preserve the soul's harmony, so he treats even health as secondary. His aim is not to be fair or strong or well unless that brings temperance.
- He gets wealth by a principle of order and will not be dazzled by the world's applause or heap up riches to his own harm.
- He looks at "the city which is within him," guards against disorder from excess or want, and gains or spends accordingly.
- He accepts honours that will make him better and avoids those, public or private, that would disorder his life.
- On politics, he will not be a statesman in his native land "unless he have a divine call," but he will rule in the city of the founders' own making.
- That city exists only in idea: "In heaven... there is laid up a pattern of it, methinks, which he who desires may behold, and beholding, may set his own house in order." Whether it ever exists matters little, since he lives by its manner and no other's.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Socrates argues that imitative poetry is thrice removed from truth and feeds the irrational part of the soul, then proves the soul is immortal because no evil can destroy it. He closes with the myth of Er, urging that we choose our life by knowing good from evil and pursue justice always.

chunks.heading: The Socratic critique of imitative poetry: three removes from truth
chunks.text:
Socrates opens Book X by saying the rejection of imitative poetry is the part of the city's order that pleases him most, now that the parts of the soul have been distinguished. He claims "all poetical imitations are ruinous to the understanding of the hearers, and that the knowledge of their true nature is the only antidote to them."

- He admits a lifelong awe and love of Homer, "the great captain and teacher of the whole of that charming tragic company", but says "a man is not to be reverenced more than the truth."
- He starts his usual way: where many things share a name, assume there is one idea or form. There are many beds and tables but only one form of each.
- A craftsman makes a particular bed "in accordance with the idea", but no artisan makes the idea itself.
- That gives three beds and three makers: the one bed in nature, made by God; the carpenter's bed; and the painter's bed.
- God made only one bed, because a second would imply a third form behind both, so He is the natural maker of the essential bed.
- The painter is an imitator, "third in the descent from nature". The tragic poet, like every imitator, is "thrice removed from the king and from the truth."

chunks.heading: Imitation yields appearances, not knowledge
chunks.text:
Socrates argues the imitator knows only appearances, and so can "do all things" only in a shallow sense.

- A mirror turned round and round "makes" the sun, earth and yourself, but only as appearances. The painter is "a creator of appearances".
- Painting reproduces a bed as it appears from one angle, not as it is. It aims at appearance, not reality.
- A painter can paint a cobbler or carpenter without knowing their arts, and fool children or simple people from a distance.
- Anyone who claims someone knows all the arts has probably met a wizard or actor and could not "analyse the nature of knowledge and ignorance and imitation."
- He applies this to the claim that Homer and the tragedians know every art and all virtue and vice. Either they were fooled by imitators, or they truly know their subjects. His test follows below.
- Three arts relate to any object: the one that uses it, the one that makes it, and the one that imitates it.
- The user has knowledge. The maker gets only correct belief, learned from the user. A flute player tells the flute maker what makes a good flute.
- The imitator has neither knowledge nor right opinion about whether his images are good, so he copies "that which appears to be good to the ignorant multitude." Imitation is "a kind of play or sport".

chunks.heading: Testing Homer: what did he ever actually do?
chunks.text:
Socrates asks what claim Homer has to be an educator, if he had real knowledge rather than imitation. He focuses on the "chiefest and noblest subjects": military tactics, politics and education.

- No city was ever better governed through Homer. Lacedaemon owes its order to Lycurgus, and Italy and Sicily boast of Charondas. Solon is renowned at Athens. Even the Homerids do not call Homer a legislator.
- No war was won by his counsel, and no useful invention is credited to him, unlike Thales or Anacharsis.
- He left no private following or "Homeric way of life", unlike Pythagoras, whose order endures. Tradition says even his companion Creophylus neglected him.
- Sophists like Protagoras and Prodicus tell people they cannot manage their house or state without them as educators, and their companions all but carry them on their shoulders. If Homer or Hesiod could have made people virtuous, nobody would have let them wander as rhapsodists. People would have kept them "as unwilling to part with them as with gold."
- Conclusion: the poets copy "images of virtue and the like" but never reach the truth.
- Poetry persuades through melody, metre and rhythm. Stripped of music and recited in prose, the tales look like faces that "were never really beautiful, but only blooming", with the bloom of youth gone.

chunks.heading: Why imitation harms the soul: reason versus the passions
chunks.text:
Socrates ties poetry to a conflict within the soul.

- Optical illusions (a stick bent in water, big and small by distance) show that perception can contradict itself. Measuring, numbering and weighing "come to the rescue", and these belong to the calculating, rational part of the soul.
- One faculty cannot hold contrary opinions about the same thing at once, so the part that opposes measure is a lower part. The better part trusts measure and calculation.
- Imitation is "an inferior who marries an inferior, and has inferior offspring": it consorts with the part of the soul far from reason.
- Grief shows the same split. A good man who loses a son will moderate his sorrow, and more so when seen by others than when alone. Law and reason bid him resist, while his feeling pushes him to indulge.
- Reason's counsel is to be patient, since we cannot know whether such things are good or evil. Grief stands in the way of what is needed, namely to "take counsel about what has happened, and when the dice have been thrown order our affairs in the way which reason deems best." We should not behave like children who hold the part struck and howl.
- The fretful, complaining part is easy to imitate, while the calm, wise temperament is hard to imitate and hard for a festival crowd to appreciate.
- So the popular poet is drawn to the passionate and fitful character. Like the painter, he deals in inferior truth and appeals to an inferior part of the soul.
- This is why the poet is refused admission to a well-ordered state: "he awakens and nourishes and strengthens the feelings and impairs the reason." It is like letting the evil rule a city while pushing the good aside.

chunks.heading: The "heaviest count": poetry corrupts even good people
chunks.text:
Socrates says poetry's gravest charge is its power to harm even the good.

- The best of us delight in a hero's long lament and praise the poet who stirs us most. Yet in our own sorrow we pride ourselves on being quiet and patient, and call the other behavior womanly. It is inconsistent to praise in a stage hero what we would be ashamed to do ourselves.
- The explanation: the natural hunger to weep, held in check in our own troubles, is satisfied by the poets. The better part, not yet trained by reason or habit, relaxes its guard because the sorrow is someone else's.
- The spectator thinks he loses nothing. He does not see that "from the evil of other men something of evil is communicated to themselves." Pity fed at the theatre is hard to restrain in our own misfortunes.
- Comedy works the same way. Jokes you would be ashamed to make yourself, you enjoy on stage, and you end up "playing the comic poet at home."
- The same goes for lust, anger and every desire, pleasure and pain: "poetry feeds and waters the passions instead of drying them up; she lets them rule, although they ought to be controlled, if mankind are ever to increase in happiness and virtue."
- His verdict on Homer's admirers: they may be excellent people, and Homer is the greatest poet and first of the tragedians. But only "hymns to the gods and praises of famous men" should be admitted. Otherwise pleasure and pain will rule instead of law and reason.

chunks.heading: The ancient quarrel and the terms for poetry's return
chunks.text:
Socrates frames the ban as a regretful, reasoned judgment, not hostility.

- He cites the "ancient quarrel between philosophy and poetry", with phrases like "the yelping hound howling at her lord" and "the mob of sages circumventing Zeus."
- He is charmed by poetry himself, especially Homer. He proposes that she may return from exile if she can defend herself in verse, and that her lovers who are not poets may defend her in prose. They must show she is useful to states and human life, not merely pleasant.
- If the defence fails, we must give her up "after the manner of lovers", who restrain a desire that opposes their interest, though "not without a struggle."
- Meanwhile he prescribes a charm to repeat while listening: poetry is not to be taken seriously as attaining truth, and the listener, "fearing for the safety of the city which is within him," should guard against her seductions.
- The stakes: "great is the issue at stake, greater than appears, whether a man is to be good or bad." Nothing, including honour, money, power or the excitement of poetry, should lead a person to neglect justice and virtue.

chunks.heading: The argument for the soul's immortality
chunks.text:
Socrates says the greatest rewards of virtue come over eternity, since seventy years is "nothing" beside it, and an immortal being should think of the whole. Glaucon is astonished when told the soul is immortal; Socrates says the proof is easy.

- Every thing has its own evil that destroys it: ophthalmia for the eyes, mildew for corn, rot for timber, rust for iron. Good cannot destroy a thing, and neither can what is neither good nor evil.
- The soul's evils are unrighteousness, intemperance, cowardice and ignorance. None of them wastes the soul away and separates it from the body. The unjust man does not die of his injustice.
- If the soul's own inherent evil cannot destroy it, an external evil cannot either. Bad food harms the body only by producing bodily disease, which is the body's own corruption.
- So fever, the knife at the throat, or cutting the body into pieces cannot destroy the soul, unless the soul is shown to become more unjust as a result. Nobody will show that death makes souls more unjust.
- Glaucon adds that injustice often keeps the murderer "alive, aye, and well awake too", so it is far from a "house of death".
- Conclusion: a soul that cannot be destroyed by internal or external evil must exist forever. The number of souls stays constant, since none are destroyed and increase would have to come from something mortal.
- The soul in its true nature cannot be a "variety" of many elements. We see her like the sea-god Glaucus, whose original form is crusted over with seaweed, shells and stones. To see her truly, look at her love of wisdom, her kinship with "the immortal and eternal and divine", and how she would be if freed from the sea of earthly things.

chunks.heading: Justice's rewards, and the Myth of Er: choosing a life
chunks.text:
Having shown justice is best for the soul in itself "whether he have the ring of Gyges or not", Socrates asks that justice be given back her good reputation. The just are loved by the gods, and everything works out for good for them in life and death. Their aim is "to be like God, as far as man can attain the divine likeness, by the pursuit of virtue."

- Clever unjust people are like runners who start fast but do not finish, while the true runner is crowned. Even if the unjust escape in youth, most are found out and end old, miserable and mocked.
- He then tells the tale of Er of Pamphylia, who was killed in battle and revived on the funeral pyre on the twelfth day. Souls are judged and sent up or down. For every wrong they suffer tenfold, over a thousand-year journey (a hundred years counted as a lifetime, paid ten times). Rewards for justice follow the same proportion. The tyrant Ardiaeus, who murdered his father and elder brother, is refused re-entry and dragged off to be punished.
- Souls travel to the spindle of Necessity, where Lachesis, Clotho and Atropos sing the past, present and future. A prophet announces: "Your genius will not be allotted to you, but you choose your genius... Virtue is free, and as a man honours or dishonours her he will have more or less of her; the responsibility is with the chooser. God is justified."
- Lots decide the order of choosing, and the available lives include tyrannies, famous and obscure lives, and animal lives. The prophet adds, "Even for the last comer, if he chooses wisely and will live diligently, there is appointed a happy and not undesirable existence. Let not him who chooses first be careless, and let not the last despair."
- The first chooser grabs the greatest tyranny without thinking it through and finds he is fated to devour his own children. Then he blames chance and the gods instead of himself. He came from heaven and had lived in a well-ordered state, but his virtue was "a matter of habit only, and he had no philosophy". Souls returning from suffering on earth chose more carefully.
- Choices follow past experience: Orpheus picks a swan, Ajax a lion, Agamemnon an eagle, and Thersites a monkey. Odysseus, cured of ambition, takes the last lot and finds the quiet life of a private man with no cares, which everyone else neglected, and says he would have chosen it even if first.
- Socrates calls this "the supreme peril of our human state". Each person should leave every other kind of knowledge and seek only to "discern between good and evil, and so to choose always and everywhere the better life." The standard: call a life evil if it makes the soul more unjust, and good if it makes the soul more just; "all else he will disregard."
- Take into the next world "an adamantine faith in truth and right", and "choose the mean and avoid the extremes on either side."
- The souls then drink from the river of Unmindfulness (forgetfulness), and those not saved by wisdom drink more. Er alone was kept from drinking.
- His closing counsel to Glaucon: "hold fast ever to the heavenly way and follow after justice and virtue always, considering that the soul is immortal and able to endure every sort of good and every sort of evil." Then we shall "live dear to one another and to the gods" and fare well in this life and the thousand-year pilgrimage.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Xenophon defends Socrates against the charges of impiety and corrupting the young, preserving his sayings and dialogues with Aristodemus, Antiphon, Critias and Charicles. Socrates argues that self-restraint is the foundation of virtue, that virtue must be constantly practiced, that being good beats seeming good, and that the gods care for humans.

chunks.heading: Socrates on piety, divination and the limits of human knowledge
chunks.text:
- Socrates sacrificed often, at home and at the state's common altars, and relied on divination. His saying "A divinity gives me a sign" was known to everyone. Xenophon notes it was no stranger than other people's trust in omens (birds' flight or cries, chance meetings, a victim's entrails), since the gods, not the bird, signify what is profitable.
- He advised friends to consult the oracle on matters whose outcome cannot be calculated. Examples: who will harvest a field one sows, who will live in the house one builds, whether a campaign will profit a general, whether a fine wife brings joy or sorrow, whether political connections will get a man cast out of his city.
- He held that "to suppose that all these matters lay within the scope of human judgment... was preternatural folly."
- The reverse was equally foolish. Anything learnable by "numbering, weighing, and measuring" (whether to hire an expert coachman or a landsman as skipper) should not be put to the gods, and asking was "a sort of profanity." His rule: "where we are permitted to work through our natural faculties, there let us by all means apply them. But in things which are hidden, let us seek to gain knowledge from above."
- He believed the gods know everything: words, deeds and the counsels "in the silent chambers of the heart." He thought they are present everywhere.
- He would no more disregard a divine sign than follow a blind man who didn't know the road. He scorned people who defied warnings to avoid disrepute among men.

chunks.heading: Why Socrates rejected speculation about the cosmos
chunks.text:
- He never discussed the nature of the Universe, how the "kosmos" came to be, or what forces cause celestial phenomena. He called it folly to trouble one's brain with these things.
- His questions to such thinkers:
  - Do they know human affairs well enough to move on to divine ones?
  - Do they hope to create winds, waters and seasons at will once they understand the causes, or only to know how things come about?
- He pointed to their disagreement as proof of futility: one says Being is one, another that it is infinite in number; one that all things flow, another that nothing can move; one that all is birth and death, another that nothing is born or dies. He compared them to madmen, who differ from one another in the same way.
- He discussed human topics constantly: piety and impiety, the beautiful and the ugly, the noble and the base, just and unjust, sobriety and madness, courage and cowardice, what a state, a statesman and a ruler are.
- He said knowing these answers "conferred a patent of nobility on the possessor," while those who lacked it "might deservedly be stigmatised as slaves."

chunks.heading: Piety in practice: law, prayer and modest sacrifice
chunks.text:
- He followed the Pythia's rule: "Act according to the law and custom of your state, and you will act piously." He called people who acted otherwise "busybodies and vain fellows."
- His prayer was simply "Give me that which is best for me," because the gods know best what is good. Praying for gold, silver or power is like praying for a particular dice throw or battle stake, with uncertain results.
- Small sacrifices from small means were no worse than large ones from ample means. If gods preferred large offerings, bad men's gifts would often outrank good men's, and life would not be worth living. The gods' joy "is greater in proportion to the holiness of the giver."
- He liked Hesiod's line "According to thine ability do sacrifice to the immortal gods," and applied "do according to your ability" to dealings with friends, strangers and life in general.
- As Council member under oath, he presided over the Assembly when it wanted to condemn the nine generals (Thrasyllus, Erasinides and others) by one inclusive vote. Despite the people's anger and threats from powerful citizens, he refused to put the question, valuing his oath over pleasing the crowd or protecting himself.

chunks.heading: The argument from design: Socrates and Aristodemus
chunks.text:
Socrates challenged Aristodemus "the little," who neither sacrificed nor consulted divination and mocked those who did.

- **Design vs. chance:** Aristodemus admired Homer, Melanippides, Sophocles, Polycleitus and Zeuxis. Socrates asked whether a maker of lifeless images or of living, intelligent creatures deserves more admiration. Aristodemus replied that it would be the latter, provided they came from design and not chance. Things serving an evident purpose are the work of design.
- **Evidence of foresight in the body:**
  - eyes, ears, nose and tongue, each matched to a use
  - eyelids as doors, lashes as screens, brows to stop sweat
  - front teeth to cut, molars to grind
  - the mouth placed near the nostrils and eyes, and waste passages kept far from the senses
  - the desire to beget, the mother's urge to rear her child, and the creature's love of life and fear of death
- **Mind in the universe:** Aristodemus has a small portion of earth and water in his body, yet supposes that only mind was snatched up by lucky chance. Not seeing the gods is no objection, since he cannot see his own soul, "the master agent of your body," either.
- **Gifts to humans:**
  - erect posture, which gives a wider view
  - hands
  - a tongue shaped for articulate speech
  - an appetite not limited to seasons
  - the best soul, able to recognise the gods and learn
  - his remark that a human mind in an ox's body, or hands without human wit, would be useless
- **Why care is plausible:** Aristodemus said he would believe if the gods sent him counsellors. Socrates answered that oracles, portents and warnings to Hellas are meant for him too. He added that:
  - the longest-lasting cities and peoples are the most god-fearing, and individuals grow more religious with age and judgment
  - as the mind rules the body and can think of Egypt or Sicily at once, divine wisdom can embrace all things at one instant
  - he should test the gods by acts of service, as he tests which friends will repay kindness and whose counsel is wise
- **Effect:** Xenophon says such talk made listeners avoid unholiness, baseness and injustice even in solitude, since no conduct escapes heaven.

chunks.heading: Self-control as the foundation of virtue
chunks.text:
- Socrates called self-restraint "the very corner-stone of virtue," to be laid as "the basis and foundation of his soul." Without it, nobody can absorb or practise a good lesson.
- He argued with analogies. In war we wouldn't choose a leader enslaved to belly, wine, lust or sleep. A dying man wouldn't entrust his sons, daughters and property to a libertine, and nobody would take an intemperate butler or errand boy even as a free gift.
- The intemperate man is worse off than the covetous one. The covetous enrich themselves by taking from others, but the intemperate wrecks his own body and soul, which is the greatest mischief. A guest who loves the wine more than his friends is unwelcome.
- His practice matched his words. He took only enough food that appetite served as sauce, drank only when thirsty, and advised avoiding foods that tempt you to eat when not hungry. On Circe's pigs: Odysseus "through his continency" did not turn into a swine. He also favoured moderate exercise and rejected both excess and neglect of the body.
- On beauty, he said to keep clear of attractive people: "once lay finger on these and it is not easy to keep a sound head and a sober mind." He teased Critobulus for kissing Alcibiades' son, warning Xenophon that it would cost his freedom, force him into hurtful spending, and leave no leisure for noble study. Beauty "wounds so far off," like Eros the archer, and is worse than the tarantula because no contact is needed. His advice was to "run helter-skelter for bare life" from fair forms, and Critobulus should "go abroad for a year" to heal.
- He declared himself immune: he found it easier to abstain from beauty's fullest bloom than others find it to avoid "weeds and garbage."
- Taking money from donors "sets up over himself a master" and binds one to "an abominable slavery."

chunks.heading: Defending a simple life and refusing fees: Socrates and Antiphon
chunks.text:
- **Antiphon's attack:** the sophist said Socrates lived wretchedly, with cheap food and drink, one cloak for both seasons, no shoes or shirt, no money-making. Socrates should call himself "professor of the art of wretchedness."
- **Reply on needs:**
  - Not charging means he need not talk to anyone but those he chooses.
  - Sharp hunger needs no sauce and thirst needs no exotic drink.
  - Clothes and shoes serve only against cold, heat and sore feet, and he doesn't stay indoors or fight for shade.
  - Training makes even a weak body outdo a neglected strong one.
- **Reply on happiness:** the best pleasure is the consciousness of "becoming better oneself, of acquiring better and better friends," not luxury. A man with few needs has more leisure for friends and country, serves as a soldier more easily, and holds out better in a siege. His creed: "To have no wants at all is... an attribute of Godhead; to have as few wants as possible the nearest approach to Godhead."
- **Fees:** Antiphon said Socrates must not value his wisdom, since he'd never give his cloak or house away free. Socrates answered that beauty and wisdom both have a fair way and a foul way to be disposed of.
  - Selling beauty to anyone is bad, but making a worthy lover a friend is sensible.
  - Selling wisdom to the first bidder makes a sophist, "a man who prostitutes his wisdom." Teaching a person of noble nature everything good and making him a friend is a good citizen's duty.
  - He compared taking pleasure in good friends to other men's pleasure in horses, hounds or fighting cocks. He teaches them whatever good he has, recommends them to others who can help, and reads the old wise men's books with them.
- **Politics:** Antiphon asked why he didn't enter politics himself. Socrates asked whether it was more statesmanlike to practise politics alone or to make many others fit for it.

chunks.heading: Honest virtue over false appearance
chunks.text:
- Socrates said the best route to renown is to become good at what you want to be thought good at.
- A pretender to flute-playing needs the equipment, the attendants and a bought claque, and can never perform without being exposed. He gets expense, bad reputation and mockery.
- A pretended general or pilot either fails to convince anyone, or succeeds and ruins the people who trusted him. Pretending to be rich, brave or strong fails the same way: you'll receive commands beyond your power "and the world will give you no commiseration."
- He called one who defrauds people of money a great cheat. "Of all imposters" the biggest is the one who persuades people he is fit to lead the state while worthless.

chunks.heading: Defence against the charges: corruption of youth, Critias and Alcibiades, and the laws
chunks.text:
- **Teaching by example:** Xenophon says Socrates never claimed to teach virtue, yet by being virtuous himself made companions hope to resemble him by imitation. He took no fees, which he thought protected his freedom, and called fee-takers "vendors of their own persons." He expected those who agreed with him to be true friends to him and each other for life.
- **Persuasion over violence:** to the charge that criticising election of officers by lot made the young violent, Xenophon replies that those who value wisdom prefer persuasion. Force breeds enmity and needs many allies, whereas persuasion wins "single-handed."
