- **Critias and Alcibiades:**
  - They sought him for his independent, disciplined life, not to learn civic virtue, and Xenophon thinks they would have chosen death over living as he did.
  - While with him they were temperate. They fell away once they thought themselves masters, and once he was no longer there to check them, as flattery, wealth and power corrupted them.
  - Virtue needs practice. Without it the soul forgets what it learned, as a long poem is forgotten without repetition. Hence the saying that the good are formed by good company and ruined by base company.
  - A teacher should not be blamed when a pupil fails under another, and praise would be due for earlier good conduct.
  - Socrates rebuked Critias for pursuing Euthydemus carnally, comparing him to a pig rubbing against stones. Critias resented this.
  - His real companions were Crito, Chaerephon, Chaerecrates, Hermogenes, Simmias, Cebes and Phaedondes, who wanted goodness of soul to do their duties to family, friends, fellow-citizens and the state.
- **Confronting the Thirty:** Socrates said a herdsman who thins his cattle is a poor herdsman, and a ruler who thins the citizens is worse. Critias and Charicles then banned him from talking to anyone under thirty. He asked whether he could buy goods or ask where Charicles lived from someone younger. They told him to drop his shoemakers, carpenters and coppersmiths, and the just and holy, "especially from cowherds."
- **Pericles and law:** Alcibiades, before twenty, questioned Pericles on what a law is. They agreed that anything forced on citizens without persuasion, whether by a tyrant, a minority or even a majority over the wealthy, is "violence rather than law."
- **Disputed teachings:**
  - He did say the sick depend on a doctor and the litigant on a lawyer, not on relatives. Likewise, friends are worth honouring only if they can be useful, because "lack of intelligence means lack of worth." His examples were burying a body once the soul has gone and trimming nails or hair, not disrespect to kin. His aim was that people become useful to those whose esteem they want.
  - On madness and ignorance: someone who may be justly confined for folly can't object to being kept in check by those who know more, and the ignorant should sit at the feet of those who know.
  - Hesiod's "No work is a disgrace" meant that only good work counts. He called dicers and gamblers "idle drones."
  - On Homer's Odysseus beating commoners, he said only that useless, insolent people who can't help the army, state or people should be restrained.
- Xenophon concludes that Socrates, a lover of the people who took no pay, harmed no one, and spent his life making others better, deserved honour rather than death.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Socrates urges self-control and voluntary hardship as the road to virtue (the Choice of Heracles), teaches gratitude to parents, mends quarrels between brothers by taking the first kind step, and treats friendship as the most valuable and most neglected possession. He insists friends are won by being good and useful, never by flattery or lies.

chunks.heading: Self-discipline is the training ground for anyone who wants to rule, and for anyone who wants to be happy
chunks.text:
- Socrates argues that whoever is educated to govern must be trained in self-control over food, drink, sleep and sexual desire, and in endurance of cold, heat, toil and pain. He asks Aristippus which of two boys, one raised to rule and one raised not to, should get this training. Aristippus answers that it must be the future ruler, "if we would not have affairs of state neglected."
- He compares people ruled by appetite to animals caught by their own greed. Fish and beasts are drawn to bait by hunger or thirst, and quails and partridges rush into the hunter's snare at the hen's cry. The adulterer, who knows the penalties and still plunges in, is "tormented by an evil spirit."
- He notes that war and agriculture are carried on in the open air, so a man who will lead must be able to bear cold and heat lightly. He ranks the self-disciplined as fit to rule and the rest as unfit.
- Voluntary hardship differs from forced hardship. The man who starves by choice can eat when he likes, and he faces the toil "gaily, buoyed on hope," like a hunter who finds the chase a pleasure. Those who toil for good friends, for victory over enemies, for a well-run household and for service to their country bear their sorrows lightly. They have their conscious virtue and the world's praise to support them.
- Indolence and fleeting pleasures build neither a healthy body nor a soul with worthwhile knowledge. Socrates cites Hesiod: wickedness is easy to take "wholesale," while "in front of virtue the immortal gods have placed toil and sweat." He also cites Epicharmus: "The gods sell us all good things in return for our labours."

chunks.heading: "Neither rule nor be ruled" is no safe path: freedom is not found by avoiding other people
chunks.text:
- Aristippus says he wants a middle path between rule and slavery, "through freedom," and that he will roam the world as a foreigner under no single state. He also says ruling is folly because rulers serve everyone else's wants and get blamed when they fall short.
- Socrates replies that this works only if the path could avoid human beings. Among people, the stronger make the weaker "sit on the stool of repentance," in public and in private. He gives examples: stronger neighbours cut down the crops and fruit trees of those who refuse to pay them court, and the powerful enslave the helpless and cowardly.
- Free citizens protect themselves with laws, friends, walls, armaments and foreign allies, and they still sometimes suffer injustice. A solitary foreigner has none of these protections and is an obvious target. He cannot count on a proclamation of safe conduct, or on being too poor a slave for anyone to want.
- He turns Aristippus's own treatment of slaves against him. Masters curb a wanton, thieving, idle servant with hunger, bolts and bars, bonds and the lash, and Aristippus admits he does the same ("I correct them with all the plagues"). Socrates uses this to show that a man with no self-discipline invites such treatment himself.

chunks.heading: The Choice of Heracles: Virtue and Vice offer two roads
Ingratitude to parents is the greatest wrongdoing, and a mother's sharp tongue is no excuse
chunks.text:
- Socrates reasons with his son Lamprocles, who is angry at his mother. They agree that ingratitude is wrongdoing whether the benefactor is a friend or a foe, and that the greater the benefit, the greater the wrong of failing to repay it. No benefit is greater than a parent's.
- He lays out what parents give. They bring a child into being and let it see and share all that the gods give man. A father chooses a wife to bear the finest children and stores up provision for them. A mother carries the child "with travail and pain, and at the risk of life itself," feeds and tends it for many months and expects nothing back. Parents then teach the child themselves or pay others to do it.
- Lamprocles says his mother's temper is worse than a wild beast's. Socrates points out that she has never bitten or kicked him. He also reminds him how much trouble he himself caused her since childhood, and how she nursed him when he was ill.
- He compares her scolding to an actor hearing abuse on stage, which is harmless because it is only words. The difference is that she means him no harm: she wishes him every blessing, nurses him when sick and prays and makes vows for him. "If you cannot away with such a mother, you cannot away with such blessings either."
- He adds practical consequences. Lamprocles already wants to please neighbours, travelling companions and rulers, so refusing a mother who loves him most makes no sense. The state punishes neglect of parents: the offender is struck off the roll and barred from the archonship, and neglect of parents' tombs is examined in the magistrates' scrutiny. The gods and men will treat an ungrateful son the same way, and he will find himself "in a desert devoid of friends."

chunks.heading: Brothers: be the first to show kindness, because brothers are made to work together
chunks.text:
- Socrates urges Chaerecrates, who is estranged from his brother Chaerephon, to value a brother above goods. Goods are senseless chattels needing protection, while a brother is a sensible being who can give it. People happily choose to live among many fellow citizens, yet they ignore the same logic about brothers. Brothers share a birth and a nurture, a natural start toward friendship, and a man with brothers commands more respect.
- Chaerecrates says his brother is pleasant to everyone else but hostile to him. Socrates answers that perhaps he is handling him ignorantly, as an unskilled rider is kicked by a horse. He observes that Chaerecrates already knows how to win people: to be invited to dinner, invite first; to get someone to mind his affairs, offer to mind theirs; to be sheltered abroad, offer shelter first. The same applies to his brother.
- He says the first move belongs to the younger brother, and "to you the final victory." Younger men already give way to their elders in the street and in seats, and "it is commonly held to redound to a man's praise to have outstripped an enemy in mischief or a friend in kindness."
- A proud and honour-loving nature "cannot be caught by a bribe"; it must be won by affection. At the worst Chaerecrates will have shown himself a good brother. More likely his brother will be "pricked on by emulous pride" to outdo him in kindness.
- He gives an image: brothers are like two hands or two feet made by God to help each other, which instead hinder one another. It is "insensate stupidity to use for injury what was meant for advantage." Hands, feet and eyes cannot reach more than a short distance, but "a pair of brothers, linked in bonds of amity, can work each for the other's good, though seas divide them."

chunks.heading: Friendship: the best possession, and the one people neglect most
chunks.text:
- Socrates notes that people say a good friend is the best possession, yet few try to acquire or keep friends. They work to get houses, fields, slaves, cattle and furniture. A man will fetch the doctor for a sick servant but ignore a sick friend, and he mourns the servant's death as a loss. Most people can count their goods but cannot list their friends, and may retract names once they try.
- A good friend is "kindlier and more constant than the faithfullest of slaves." He supplements what his friends lack in private and public affairs, helps them with money, energy, argument or force, gladdens them in success, and steadies them when they have nearly slipped. He does for a friend what the friend could not do himself.
- Socrates asks Antisthenes whether friends have market values like slaves, using Nicias's talent for a mine overseer as an example. Antisthenes says one friend he would prefer to two minae, another he would not value at half a mina, a third he would keep for ten, and a fourth he would not want at any cost.
- Socrates turns this into self-examination: "What after all may I chance to be worth to my friends?" Each person should try to be as dear as possible to friends, so they do not care to give him up. If a base slave is sold for what he will fetch, a base friend is likewise dropped when someone can profit by the exchange; good slaves and good friends are not so easily parted with.

chunks.heading: Choosing and winning a friend: test character by deeds, and be good yourself
chunks.text:
- Socrates tells Critobulus whom to avoid: the slave of belly, wine, lust, sleep or idleness; the spendthrift who begs from neighbours and hates them if refused; the money-grabber who is "glad enough to take in, but loath to pay out"; the man too absorbed in gain for anything else; the quarrelsome person who loads his friends with enemies; and the man who takes kindness and never returns it.
- The good friend is the opposite. He masters bodily pleasures, is kindly, upright in dealings and eager not to be outdone in kindness by his benefactors, and wants his friends to gain from knowing him.
- Test a man as you would a sculptor, by his earlier work and not by his talk. Kindness to older friends predicts kindness to new ones, as skill with horses predicts skill with more horses. Socrates adds that one should first ask whether Heaven approves the friendship.
- A friend cannot be captured by force, snares or fetters; those who are bound become foes. The spell is suited to the listener (the Sirens' call "Hither, come hither, thou famous man, Odysseus" was for souls athirst for fame and emulous of virtue). Flattery is hateful: telling a small, ugly, weak man he is tall and beautiful breeds repulsion.
- "To win the love of any good man we need to be good ourselves in speech and action." Service must be paid for with service, and a bad man cannot make good friends.
- He explains why even good men sometimes quarrel. "Seeds of love" are planted in us by nature, since men need, pity and help each other. There are also "seeds of war": rivalry over the same things thought beautiful or agreeable, more-having, avarice and envy. Good men still form bonds because they prefer scant means without pain to an empire won by war. They share food and drink and wealth, settle strife to the general advantage, check anger before it brings remorse, and treat each other's goods as common. Good men can also hold office together for the public good. A band of the best is stronger than rivals, and "one good man is better worth your benefiting than a dozen knaves," for with the base "the more you give them the more they ask for."
- On love of friends he says he demands to be loved in return and works to please whoever pleases him. He offers to tell the person Critobulus admires that Critobulus admires him, is kindly, is devoted to friends, takes joy in a good friend, takes pride in friends' deeds as in his own, and holds that virtue means outdoing friends in kindness and foes in hostility. But Aspasia taught him that matchmakers should report only what is true, since falsehood makes the deluded parties hate each other and the go-between.
- Praising a man falsely helps no one. If he is falsely called a good pilot, general or manager, he will be given a ship, a state or an estate to ruin. "In whatsoever you desire to be deemed good, endeavour to be good." Socrates adds that every virtue can be increased by learning and practice.

chunks.heading: Practical help for friends in need: put idle talents to work, find a defender, and buy friends cheaply
chunks.text:
- **Aristarchus and his household of relatives.** Aristarchus is crushed by the burden of fourteen free-born female relatives and has no income. Socrates asks why Ceramon, with slaves to feed, prospers. He points out that Nausicydes (barley meal), Cyrebus (bread), Demeas (cloaks), Menon (mantles) and the Megarians (vests) all live well from useful trades. He tells Aristarchus that the women know how to make these goods, and that they should not live in idleness. Idle people grow to resent each other, while shared useful work brings affection. Honest work is nothing shameful for them, and what we know best we do with ease and pleasure. Aristarchus borrows capital, buys wool, and the women work and smile. When they complain that he is the only drone, Socrates tells him the fable of the dog and the sheep: the dog is rightly fed from the master's table because he guards the flock.
- **Eutherus.** Eutherus lives by bodily labour that will fail with age. Socrates advises him to manage a large estate. When Eutherus says he cannot bear to be held to account, Socrates replies that every work involves accountability and some mistakes. Eutherus should "avoid censorious persons," attach himself to the kind, accept what he can do and decline what he cannot, and do each task "heart and soul" as his finest work. That silences fault-finders and secures his old age.
- **Crito and Archedemus.** Crito is harassed by blackmailing lawsuits. Socrates asks why he does not keep a watchman, as he keeps dogs against wolves, since a man like Crito is more pleasant to gratify than to quarrel with. Crito finds Archedemus, honest, clever and poor, and gives him gifts of corn, oil, wine and wool and invitations to feasts. Archedemus finds crimes in the informers and prosecutes one, winning a payment from him. Crito's friends then ask for his guardianship too. Archedemus replies to critics that it is less shameful to repay honest folk with kindness than to wrong gentlemen for scoundrels' favour.
- **Diodorus and Hermogenes.** Socrates asks Diodorus, who pays to recover a runaway slave and calls doctors for a sick one, why he would not help Hermogenes, a friend in want. A willing, kindly and trusty assistant with good judgement "is worth dozens of slaves," and "nowadays when times are so bad it is possible to get good friends exceedingly cheap." Hermogenes will be ashamed not to repay. When Diodorus asks Socrates to send Hermogenes to him, Socrates refuses: Diodorus is no better entitled to summon Hermogenes than to go himself, and the advantage is not more on Hermogenes's side. Diodorus goes and wins a friend whose one concern is to help and gladden him.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Xenophon's Book III shows Socrates testing ambitious men on whether they know the office they seek, from generalship to statecraft. He argues leadership means making the led happy, virtue is wisdom, and ignorance of oneself is near madness. He also teaches that good and beautiful mean useful for an end.

chunks.heading: Generals must know the whole job, not only tactics
chunks.text:
- Socrates argues that anyone seeking the office of Strategos who neglects to learn its duties deserves a fine, more than a charlatan who takes a contract to carve a statue without having learnt sculpture. The reason is that "the whole fortunes of the state are entrusted to the general during a war."
- He holds that the man without the science is no general or doctor "even if the whole world appointed him."
- Tactics is "only an infinitesimal part of generalship." A general must also supply the army and its provisions, be quick in devices and full of resource, and miss nothing. He must combine clemency and fierceness, be a watchman and a robber, be as open-handed as a spendthrift and as tight as a miser, and be impregnable in defence and daring in attack.
- Tactics is still worth having. He compares it to a heap of stones, bricks, wood and tiles, which is useless until it is arranged by principle into a dwelling.
- Arranging troops presupposes knowing good from bad. Piling coins "best at top and bottom" is no help unless you can first tell real from counterfeit.
- Arrangements must also suit the occasion. The same order of march or battle is out of place in countless circumstances.
- If a professor takes the pupil's money and sends him away without this, Socrates says he ought to blush.

chunks.heading: The leader's purpose is the happiness of those he leads
chunks.text:
- Socrates reads Homer's "shepherd of the peoples" to mean that a general must see his soldiers safe, supplied, and able to reach the aim of their soldiering. That aim is to beat the enemy and add to their own good fortune and happiness.
- "Warrior bold" and "good king" mean more than personal courage. The leader must inspire the whole host with prowess and be the source of happiness to those he rules.
- A king is not chosen "to take heed to himself, albeit nobly, but that those who chose him may attain to happiness through him."
- Men go soldiering to improve their lives and choose generals as guides to that goal. So he who takes the office must procure for them what they seek.
- Stripped of everything superficial, he says, the function of every leader is to make happy those he leads.

chunks.heading: A cavalry commander must improve horses and men, and win obedience through knowledge
chunks.text:
- Socrates asks a new hipparch what he is after. Riding at the head of the knights is no goal, and notoriety is "a fatal distinction." The real aim is to hand the cavalry to the state in better condition and be the cause of some good to Athens.
- He presses practical duties:
  - Check that horses are sound in feet and legs, well fed, well broken and steady in the ranks.
  - Make the men expert at mounting.
  - Drill on ground resembling a real battlefield, not the sandy practice ground.
  - Train them to shoot on horseback.
  - Whet their courage and kindle their rage to meet the enemy.
- Obedience is the crux: without it, "not one particle of good will you get, for all your horses and troopers so brave and so stout."
- People follow those they regard as adepts, such as the cleverest physician, the most skilful pilot or the best farmer. A commander must therefore prove himself the better man and show his troopers that obeying him brings greater glory and surer safety.
- Teaching that is far easier than teaching that bad things are better than good.
- The commander must be able to speak and argue. He says the noblest things we learn, and our knowledge of life itself, come through speech and reason, and the best teachers are those with the freest command of thought and language.
- Athens beats the world in choruses not through voice, stature or strength but through "ambition and that love of honour." Appeal to that, and the cavalry can also lead the world in arms, order and eager encounter.

chunks.heading: Management of a house and of an army are the same art
Reviving Athens: fear breeds order, inheritance breeds virtue
chunks.text:
- Talking with Pericles the younger, Socrates weighs Athens against Boeotia. Athens matches Boeotia in numbers and fine men and is more united and more jealous of honour, with a richer heritage of ancestors' deeds.
- Pericles points to the decline since the defeats at Lebadeia and Delium. Socrates replies that the state was never "so ripe for a really good leader." Boldness breeds carelessness and insubordination, while fear breeds application, obedience and order. He compares calm weather aboard ship, when disorder reigns, to the approach of a storm or an enemy, when crews hush and obey.
- To rekindle virtue, appeal to inheritance. Just as one stirs men to claim ancestral property, show them that headship combined with virtue is an old, honoured heritage that belongs to them above all. He cites Cecrops, Erechtheus, the Heraclidae, Theseus and the wars against Asia.
- Athens declined because "we are victims of our own success." Like an athlete grown lax through easy superiority, they neglected themselves. The cure is to rediscover the forefathers' institutions or to imitate and outdo today's leaders.
- Pericles lists Athenian failings: contempt for age, neglect of the body, defiance of magistrates, envy, litigiousness and quarrelling over common interests. Socrates urges him not to think the people incurably depraved. They obey well in naval matters, at gymnastic contests and in training choruses, and the Areopagus is a model of honour and justice.
- Where discipline fails, he suggests it is because the officers are the least knowledgeable. No one leads harpists, dancers or wrestlers without the requisite knowledge, yet "most generals are amateurs and improvisers." A leader should be able to say where he learned his craft, and should seek out those who know when he finds ignorance in himself, "sparing neither gifts nor gratitude."
- His practical proposal: hold the mountain barrier along Boeotia's border with a corps of young, lightly armed Athenians. They would be a thorn to the enemy and a bulwark for the country, as the Mysians and Pisidians do for the Persian king.

chunks.heading: Know what you propose to manage before seeking office
chunks.text:
- Socrates flatters the under-twenty Glaucon's ambition, then asks how he will benefit the state. Wealth is the obvious answer, and Glaucon cannot name the state's revenues or its expenditures.
- Socrates presses on further matters:
  - Enriching Athens from its enemies requires knowing both sides' land and naval forces. A statesman who knows his city is stronger can advise war, and one who knows it is weaker can advise caution.
  - Whether the outposts should be swept away rests on conjecture unless he has inspected them himself.
  - He has never visited the mines.
  - He does not know how long the corn supply lasts.
- "A man could not even manage his own house or his estate well, without, in the first place, knowing what he requires, and, in the second place, taking pains, item by item, to supply his wants." The city has more than ten thousand houses. If Glaucon cannot improve his own uncle's household, how could he persuade all Athens?
- "Do you not see how dangerous it is for a man to speak or act beyond the range of his knowledge?" People who exceed their knowledge gain blame, and those who enjoy admiration are the ones with the highest knowledge. The advice is to make sure of "the knowledge as far as in you lies of what you wish to do," and then the goal is reachable.
- Charmides, who gives sound private advice but shrinks from the Assembly, gets the opposite correction. A person who could win a crown and refuses to compete, or who could exalt his city and hangs back, is a coward.
- The Assembly is made of fullers, cobblers, carpenters, farmers and traders, not experts. Socrates compares fearing them to a man who beats trained athletes yet quails before amateurs. He closes: "do not be ignorant of yourself!" and urges Charmides not to rush to examine others while neglecting to examine himself.

chunks.heading: Good, beautiful and useful are measured by fitness for the end
chunks.text:
- When Aristippus asks if he knows anything good, Socrates asks whether he means good for fever, for sore eyes or for hunger. He says he neither knows nor wants to know of "any good thing which is good for nothing."
- Beautiful things can be unlike each other, like a runner versus a boxer, or a shield versus a javelin.
- "Relatively to the same standard all things are at once beautiful and good." The standard is what the thing is useful for, so a dung basket is beautiful for its use and a golden spear ugly for its.
- "Everything is good and beautiful when well adapted for the end in view, bad and ugly when ill adapted."
- Applying this to housebuilding, a house should be both pleasant and useful. A southern aspect with a higher south side catches winter sun, and the roof shades it in summer. A lower north side keeps out cold winds, and the whole should be a secure place to keep goods. Paintings and ornamental mouldings "deprive one of more joy than they confer."
- He advises placing temples and altars on a site visible from afar and untrodden by foot.
- He tests the corselet maker Pistias on "proportion." It means fit to the wearer, not an absolute measure. A fitting corselet distributes weight over collar-bone, shoulders, chest, back and belly and feels "like another natural integument." An ill-fitting one, however gilded or inlaid, is "a curiously-wrought and gilded nuisance." Since the body moves, the true fit is the corselet that does not gall the wearer in use.

chunks.heading: Courage, wisdom, virtue and rule rest on knowledge and practice
chunks.text:
- Courage: Souls differ by nature as bodies do, yet "by learning and practice the natural aptitude may always be strengthened towards courage." Scythians, Thracians and Lacedaemonians would each refuse to fight with the others' weapons. Natural differences are compensated by care and attention, so everyone should "learn and practise those things in which we would fain achieve distinction."
- Wisdom and temperance are not distinguished: one who recognises the beautiful and good well enough to live in them, and knows the base well enough to avoid it, is wise and sound of soul.
- Knowing right action but not doing it is not wisdom or self-control: "Every one... deliberately chooses what, within the limits open to him, he considers most conducive to his interest." Those who act crookedly are neither wise nor self-controlled.
- "Justice, and all other virtue is wisdom." Those who know what is beautiful and good will choose nothing else, and those who lack the knowledge cannot do it, even if they try.
- Madness is not simple ignorance but ignorance of oneself, "to imagine and suppose that he knows what he knows not." On a large scale, he says, this is called madness.
- Envy is pain felt only at the successes of friends, not at an enemy's fortune or a friend's misfortune. He calls it the condition of a silly mind.
- Leisure is the freedom to turn from something worse to something better. No one has leisure to turn from the better to the worse.
- Rulers: not those who merely hold the sceptre, are chosen by the crowd or by lot, or seize power by force or fraud, but "those who have the special knowledge how to rule." Ship, farm, sickness and athletics all show people obeying the expert, and women rule men in wool-spinning because they know the art. A tyrant who rejects wise counsel errs and is punished. Killing his best ally brings swift ruin.
- Success: the best pursuit is "successful conduct," doing a thing well through learning and practice. Fortune, success without seeking it, is the opposite. Those who do well in their calling, whether farming, healing or statecraft, are best and dearest to God.

chunks.heading: Learning from craftsmen, caring for the body, and modest living
chunks.text:
- With painters and sculptors: Socrates asks Parrhasius whether the soul's moods can be depicted. They are invisible, yet loving or hostile looks, relief or anxiety, nobility or servility show through the face, posture and movement, so they can be imitated. He tells Cleiton that statues seem alive through faithful copying of muscle tension, gesture and weight, and that the sculptor must also capture the soul's workings.
- Theodote: He treats the courtesan as a person with something to learn about friendship. She lives on friends, which he calls better property than flocks. Friends are won by kindness and pleasure, not force, and by acts of love rather than lip phrases. She should ask only what a well-wisher can grant without repenting, and requite in kind. Favours should come when appetite exists: "create hunger, and even coarser stuff seems honey-sweet." He tells her, "Seek and you will find means, if you truly need me," and declines to be drawn to her ("I wish you to come to me").
- Body: He tells the feeble Epigenes that a bad bodily habit leads to death in war, capture and slavery, disgrace, and impaired thought, including forgetfulness, despondency and "madness". A healthy body brings safety, honour and a better legacy. Because Athens does not train publicly, one should train privately. "It is a base thing for a man to wax old in careless self-neglect before he has lifted up his eyes and seen what manner of man he was made to be."
- Everyday corrections:
  - Do not rage at a man's rudeness when you would not rage at his poor health.
  - For a lost appetite, "stop eating."
  - Hot household water means a ready warm bath, and servants use it contentedly.
  - A master flogging a lazy slave should ask which deserves it more.
  - A journey to Olympia is just several ordinary walks strung together, so set off a day early.
  - A man too tired from a trip carrying only his cloak, while his slave carried the baggage, is a poor athlete.
- Banquets: Socrates has small and large food contributions pooled so the lavish stop catering for delicacies. He mocks eating many dishes at once as extravagant and destructive of the cook's art, and notes it makes a man feel starved when few dishes are served. "Making good cheer" means eating what troubles neither soul nor body, is easy to find, and fits a modest, orderly life.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Xenophon portrays Socrates exposing the pride of Euthydemus, who thinks books make him wise, and leading him to "Know thyself." Socrates argues that self-control is the root of freedom, that the ignorance to avoid is ignorance of the good and just, and that he lived by growing in goodness, so he faced death calmly.

chunks.heading: Educating the gifted, the rich and the self-satisfied
chunks.text:
- Socrates "fell in love" with young people whose souls showed promise: a readiness to learn what they attend to, a memory that retains lessons, and a passion for studies serving the good management of a house or state. Such people, educated, become happy themselves and able to make others happy.
- To those who trusted natural talent and despised learning, he argued that the most gifted nature needs the most training. A spirited colt properly broken in becomes superb; left unbroken it is intractable. A well-bred puppy trained becomes an excellent hunter; neglected, a stupid brute.
- The same holds for people. The strongest, most determined youth, if taught what is right, becomes superlatively useful. Left in ignorance, he does the worst on the grandest scale, because without knowledge of what is right his vehemence cannot be reined in.
- To those proud of wealth ("money makes the man"), he argued that without instruction a person cannot tell what is gainful from what is hurtful. Without that discrimination, wealth alone cannot get a man what he wants. Nor can wealth without true knowledge buy a reputation for excellence.
- He did not rush students toward skill in speech, action or invention without a foundation of self-control. Power without self-control, he believed, only makes men worse and more mischievous.

chunks.heading: Curing the proud scholar: Euthydemus and the saddler's shop
chunks.text:
- Euthydemus had collected a large library of poets and philosophers and believed he already out-topped his peers in wisdom. Socrates went to the saddler's shop where he sat, and first raised the point indirectly: it is naive to think minor arts need teachers while leading the state, the greatest concern, "drops into the lap of anybody."
- He mocked the self-taught politician with an imagined opening speech: "I have never learnt anything from anybody." He set it beside a candidate for state physician announcing he learned no medicine and will "acquire skill by experimenting on your persons." The listeners laughed.
- He observed that people will sit at the feet of the best teachers to learn harp, flute or riding, yet some expect to master politics, the harder field with more competitors and fewer successes, "by inspiration" with no preparation.
- Once Euthydemus was listening, Socrates spoke with him alone. He praised him for prizing wisdom over gold and silver, then asked what he wanted the books for. Euthydemus ruled out doctor, architect, mathematician, astronomer and rhapsodist. He wanted statesmanship, which Socrates called "the noblest of virtues and the greatest of the arts," the "royal" art.
- After being refuted (see the next section), Euthydemus left in despair. Many of Socrates's refuted interlocutors never returned, and he judged them dullards. Euthydemus instead saw that his best course was to stay close to Socrates and imitate him. Socrates then taught him plainly and simply what is needful to know and practise.

chunks.heading: Testing justice: the R and W columns
chunks.text:
- Socrates asked whether anyone can be a good statesman without justice. Euthydemus said no and claimed he could "hold his own against all comers as an upright man."
- Socrates proposed writing R (right) and W (wrong) on two sides and sorting actions. Lying, deceit, mischief and enslaving free men all went to W.
- He then tested the sorting with cases:
  - A general who enslaves a wicked, hostile city, or deceives and plunders an enemy, does right.
  - A general who invents a story of reinforcements to revive demoralised troops does right.
  - A father who deceives a sick son into taking medicine does right.
  - Taking a knife from a despairing friend who might kill himself is right.
- Each case forced Euthydemus to revise the rule. Deceit is not simply wrong; what matters is its object and effect. He withdrew his claim that one must always be straightforward with friends.
- Socrates pressed further: is voluntary or involuntary deception worse? Euthydemus said voluntary. Socrates compared it to the man who misspells on purpose, who is more literate than the one who errs from ignorance. If justice is a science like letters, the intentional wrongdoer would then be more just. Euthydemus saw the absurdity but could not resolve it.
- Socrates's test for knowing: a man who says the road is east and then west, or whose sums keep changing, "does not know what he thought he knew."
- Slavishness, he said, is not ignorance of smithing or carpentry (many skilled craftsmen are "little better than slaves"). It is ignorance of "the beautiful, the good, the just," and everyone should strain every nerve to avoid it.

chunks.heading: Know thyself, and the questionable goods
chunks.text:
- Socrates asked Euthydemus whether he had heeded the Delphic inscription "Know thyself." Euthydemus said he assumed he knew himself, since otherwise he would know nothing.
- Socrates rejected knowing only your name. A man buying a horse tests whether it is tractable or stubborn, strong or weak, quick or slow, for its use. Likewise a man must examine his own nature and capacities for what a man needs.
- Benefits of self-knowledge:
  - He knows what is advantageous to himself and discerns the limits of his powers.
  - He does what he knows and avoids what he does not, so he makes fewer mistakes.
  - He gains fame and honour, and friends and neighbours seek his counsel.
- Costs of ignorance of self: a man neither knows what he wants, what he is doing, nor the people he deals with. He fails, loses reputation, and ends in contempt.
- States are the same: one that ignorantly wars against a stronger state is uprooted or enslaved.
- Applying this, Socrates showed that commonly named goods are not unconditionally good:
  - Health and strength can kill those who sail or fight while the weak stay safe.
  - Wisdom did not save Daedalus and Palamedes from slavery and murder.
  - Beauty, strength, wealth, reputation and political power are among "the commonest sources of mischief": beauty draws ruinous admirers, strength tempts men beyond their powers, wealth softens and invites plots.
- A thing that sometimes benefits and sometimes harms should not be called strictly good or evil.
- He also showed the vagueness of "rich" and "poor": some with a pittance find it enough and save, while kings driven by want act like paupers. So good economists with little can be wealthy and rulers can be poor.

chunks.heading: The gods' care and honouring them
chunks.text:
- Socrates's first aim with companions was a wise spirit toward the gods. With Euthydemus he listed divine provision for man: light, night for rest, stars and moon to mark time, crops and seasons, water, fire ("nothing serviceable to the life of man worth speaking of but owes its fabrication to fire"), and the sun's gradual approach and retreat so we are neither scorched nor frozen.
- He added animals that serve man for food, commerce, and work and war, and man's own gifts: senses matching nature's variety, reasoning and memory, and speech for teaching, forming societies and laws. Divination helps where human foresight fails.
- The gods themselves are unseen, so one must "behold their works" and honour their authors. Their ministers are hidden too: thunderbolt, winds, and the soul of man, which shares in the divine yet is invisible.
- To Euthydemus's worry that no one can repay the gods enough, he cited Delphi: honour the gods "according to the law and custom of your city," with offerings according to one's ability. The best honour is doing what they bid, without falling short of one's ability.
- The reasoning: expect great blessings from those able to help most, by pleasing them with the amplest obedience.
- This teaching made companions "more devout and more virtuous."

chunks.heading: Justice as lawfulness: Socrates and Hippias
chunks.text:
- Socrates showed justice in deed: he refused an unconstitutional vote as president of the assembly, refused the Thirty when they forbade him to talk to the young and ordered him to help arrest a man for execution, and at his trial refused the customary flattery and pleading even though bending slightly would have won acquittal. He "preferred to abide by the laws and die rather than transgress them and live."
- He told Hippias it is strange that people know where to send a horse or ox to be trained, yet cannot tell where to find a teacher of right. Hippias complained he repeats the same old talk; Socrates replied that on a settled subject one says the same thing, just as one always spells a name the same way.
- Challenged to say what justice is, he first pointed to his conduct: never bearing false witness, informing maliciously, stirring strife or doing wrong. Hippias objected that this says only what the just man avoids. Socrates then defined "the lawful is the just."
- Arguments that law-abidingness is just:
  - Laws are enactments citizens agree on, so the lawful citizen does what is just.
  - Laws being repealed no more discredits obedience than the fact that war ends in peace discredits discipline in war.
  - Lycurgus made Sparta distinguished chiefly by instilling obedience to the laws.
  - Concord, the greatest blessing of a state, is sworn across Hellas. It means obedience to laws, not shared tastes in choruses, flute-players or poets.
  - The law-loving man is protected from penalty, wins honours and is trusted with deposits, command and treaties by friends, allies and even enemies. Hatred and hostility melt before him.
- He then added the unwritten laws, which Hippias said must come from the gods since they hold everywhere: worship of the gods, honour to parents, and returning kindness for kindness. Their transgression carries its own penalty (the ungrateful man ends isolated; incest brings ill-begotten offspring), pointing to a higher than human legislator.
- Hippias agreed the gods' laws are just, so the gods are pleased that "the lawful" and "the just" coincide.

chunks.heading: Self-control as the root of freedom and pleasure
chunks.text:
- Socrates told Euthydemus that freedom is the noblest possession of a man or a state. A person ruled by bodily pleasures, hindered from the best and driven to the shameful, is not free but enslaved to "the worst of masters."
- Incontinence shuts out wisdom, drags men to the pleasant, and makes them choose the worse even when they know good from evil. It undermines modesty and carefulness. Self-control, its opposite, is the best thing a man can have.
- It also yields more pleasure. Only those who can endure hunger, thirst, sexual appetite and lack of sleep until each is at its height get the full joy of eating, drinking, love and rest. The incontinent are tied to the nearest pleasure and miss the joy of learning what is good, of managing body and household well, and of serving friends and state.
- A man who gives up aiming high and only gratifies pleasure is no better than "the silliest of cattle."
- The self-controlled discover hidden treasures, choosing the good and rejecting the evil. He derived "dialegesthai" (discussion) from "dialegein," picking things out by kinds, so the self-controlled become best at reasoning and debate and fittest to lead.

chunks.heading: Definitions by stepwise agreement
chunks.text:
- Socrates held that whoever knows what each thing is can explain it, and that those who do not will stumble and cause others to stumble. So he constantly inquired into the nature of things.
- Definitions reached with Euthydemus:
  - Piety: knowing the laws about honouring the gods and honouring them accordingly. A man honours the gods only as he thinks he ought.
  - Justice: knowing the lawful dealings among men. Nobody obeys laws without knowing them, and nobody who knows what he ought to do does otherwise.
  - Wisdom: knowledge. Each man is wise only in what he knows, and no one can be all-wise.
  - Good and beautiful: relative. The good is the beneficial to whom it benefits, and the useful is beautiful for the use it is applied to.
  - Courage: not mere fearlessness, since madmen who do not know dangers would count. It is knowing how to meet terrors and dangers well. Those who fail utterly are cowards.
- Governments: a kingdom rules willing subjects by law; a tyranny rules unwilling subjects by the ruler's whims. Aristocracy has offices filled from those who meet legal requirements, plutocracy by property, democracy by all citizens.
- When a disputant merely asserted that a person he admired was wiser or a better citizen, Socrates returned to the underlying question. He asked what a good citizen's work is: increasing the state's resources while lightening expense, winning wars, making friends from enemies abroad, and ending party strife at home.
- His method: advance step by step from points of general agreement. "Herein lay the real security of reasoning." He admired Homer's praise of Odysseus as a safe orator for leading discussion from one accepted opinion to another.

chunks.heading: Useful learning only, and the examined life
chunks.text:
- Socrates sought to find what each companion really knew and taught gentleman's knowledge himself or sent them to those who knew.
- Geometry: enough to measure, divide or take over land. He disapproved of pursuing intricate diagrams, which would wear out a lifetime and crowd out more useful studies.
- Astronomy: enough to tell the hour of the night and the season for travel, march and watches, which night hunters and pilots can teach. He opposed studying planets, distances and causes.
- He opposed trying to work out how the gods produce celestial phenomena: it is beyond human power and displeasing to the gods. He cited Anaxagoras, who claimed the sun is a red-hot stone and lost his head over it, ignoring that we can look at fire but not at the sun and that plants grow in sunlight but are parched by fire.
- He urged study of reasoning only up to the limit of utility.
- He urged attention to health: learn from experts, but also observe yourself for a lifetime to find the food, drink and work that suit you.
- For help beyond human wisdom, he counselled turning to divination.

chunks.heading: Facing death and the judgment of his life
chunks.text:
- The "divine sign" opposed Socrates each time he tried to prepare a defence. He told Hermogenes that his whole life had been his defence, spent "distinguishing between what is just and what is unjust" and doing right.
- He considered his death timely: no one had spent a better or happier life than his. "Theirs I regard as the best of lives who study best to become as good as may be, and theirs the happiest who have the liveliest sense of growth in goodness."
- He reasoned that old age would bring dimmer senses, weaker intellect and forgetfulness, and a life with consciousness of such decline would be "a death in life."
- If put to death unjustly, the shame belongs to those who slay him, since injustice is base. Posterity will judge him differently from his killers: "I never at any time did wrong to any man, or made him a worse man, but ever tried to make those better who were with me."
- He lived the thirty days before execution, delayed by the Delian embassy, with the same cheerfulness and calm.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In Xenophon's account, Socrates refuses to rehearse a defence because he believes a lifetime of acting justly is the only real preparation. He sees death as preferable to the decay of old age, rejects servile pleading, and regards an unjust conviction as the shame of his accusers, not himself.

chunks.heading: Why Socrates did not rehearse a defence and welcomed death
chunks.text:
- Asked by Hermogenes why he was not preparing his defence, Socrates answered: "What! do I not seem to you to have spent my whole life in meditating my defence?"
- His reasoning: "By a lifelong persistence in doing nothing wrong, and that I take to be the finest practice for his defence which a man could devise."
- Hermogenes warned that Athenian juries often kill the innocent and acquit the guilty, swayed by pity or a charming phrase. Socrates still would not craft a plea.
- He said twice he began to consider his defence and twice his divine sign (the "divinity") hindered him. He took this to mean it seemed better to God that he die at once.
- He claimed no man had lived better than he had: "what can exceed the pleasure, which has been mine, of knowing that my whole life has been spent holily and justly?" His friends' opinion of him echoed this self-approval.

chunks.heading: Old age as the evil that death spares him
chunks.text:
- If his life were prolonged, he expected the penalties of age: dimmer sight, duller hearing, slower learning, faster forgetting.
- He added the "sting of self-reproach" of conscious failing powers, and asked what joy in living would remain.
- He read the divine hindrance as kindness: God letting him close his life "in the ripeness of age, and by the gentlest of deaths."
- Had he secured acquittal, he would have prepared for himself not release but an end "wasted by disease, or by old age, on which a confluent stream of evil things most alien to joyousness converges."

chunks.heading: How a good death benefits friends
chunks.text:
- Socrates held that a death by sentence is the easiest kind and gives friends the least trouble.
- It also produces the deepest longing for the departed. A man is remembered with regret and longing when he leaves nothing unseemly behind, but, "sound of body, and his soul still capable of friendly repose, fades tranquilly away."

chunks.heading: Refusing to beg for life
chunks.text:
- He would display no ardent zeal for acquittal. If openly stating the blessings he owed to gods and men, and his honest opinion of himself, wearied the court, he would "choose death rather than supplicate in servile sort for leave to live a little longer merely to gain a life impoverished in place of death."
- When asked to name a counter-penalty, he refused and would not let friends do it, saying that proposing one is like a confession of guilt.
- When friends planned to steal him out of prison, he treated it as a jest, asking whether they knew "some place outside Attica where death was forbidden to set foot?"

chunks.heading: Answering the charge of impiety and the divine voice
chunks.text:
- On not recognising the state's gods: he was regularly seen sacrificing at common festivals and public altars.
- On "novel divinities": his divine voice is no more novel than birds' cries, human utterances, thunder or the priestess at Pytho. All are voices through which the god, who has foreknowledge, premonishes whom he will.
- He says he speaks "of a divinity" more exactly and reverentially than those who ascribe the power to birds.
- His proof: though he reported heaven's counsels to many friends, he was never shown to be "a deceiver or deceived."
- He cited Apollo's oracle through Chaerephon (no man more liberal, upright or temperate), and urged the jury to test it point by point rather than accept it on the god's word.

chunks.heading: The evidence he offers for his own virtue
chunks.text:
- Least enslaved to bodily appetites; takes no gifts or pay, so more independent of spirit.
- Most just, being so content with what he has that others' possessions excite no craving.
- Wise, because from the time he understood speech he never stopped inquiring into and learning every good thing in his power.
- Many citizens pursuing virtue, and many strangers, choose his company, and many give gifts though he cannot repay them. Many acknowledge debts of gratitude to him and none dun him.
- During the siege he lived no worse than in the city's prosperity, and he has the "dainties of the soul more sweet" than market delicacies, procured without expense.

chunks.heading: Answering the charge of corrupting the young
chunks.text:
- He challenged Meletus to name anyone changed under his influence from religious to irreligious, sober to prodigal, moderate to drunkard, or hardworking to effeminate.
- Meletus said he persuaded young men to obey him over their fathers. Socrates admitted it for education, which he has made his study.
- His analogies: a man obeys his doctor over his parents in health, the assembly obeys the wisest arguments over relatives, and generals are chosen for military wisdom, not kinship.
- He found it strange that the best get exclusive preference everywhere else, yet he is prosecuted on a capital charge for being chosen as an adept in education, "the greatest treasure men possess."

chunks.heading: After the verdict: serenity, and who is the real loser
chunks.text:
- He did not hold his head lower: nothing proved he sacrificed to novel gods or swore by other gods. Habituating the young to "manliness and frugality" could not corrupt them, and no accuser alleged a capital crime like temple robbery or betrayal of the state.
- Dying innocent is "a blot not upon me but upon those who condemned me." Perjurers and those who heeded them must be conscious of deep impiety and injustice.
- He took consolation in Palamedes, a nobler theme of song than Odysseus who wrongly killed him, and expected time to testify that he "never wronged another at any time or ever made a worse man of him," teaching gratuitously every good thing he could.
- To weeping followers: "Do you not know that for many a long day, ever since I was born, sentence of death was passed upon me by nature?" If he dies prematurely amid life's blessings, grief is fitting, but dying on the eve of troubles is good fortune to rejoice in.
- To Apollodorus ("hardest to see you put to death unjustly"): "Would you have been better pleased, my dear one, to see me put to death for some just reason rather than unjustly?"
- Of Anytus: whichever of the two "has achieved what is best and noblest for all future time is the real victor in this suit." He prophesied, as the dying do in Homer, that Anytus's son would not stay in his father's tanning trade and would fall into base passion without a guardian.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: At a dinner party Socrates mixes jokes with serious teaching. He holds that love of the soul outlasts love of the body, that friendship is the basis of any worthwhile society, and that a lover must himself be virtuous to make the beloved good. He also keeps company with the good, and stresses genuine virtue over reputation.

chunks.heading: Socrates on the Fragrance of True Nobility and Learning Virtue from Good Company
chunks.text:
- Socrates argues that perfume suits women but not men, because scents blur the difference between a free man and a slave. The scent of a free man comes from the toils he loves, from habit and time.
- Asked by Lycon where older men whose gymnastic days are over can find fragrance, he answers: "Why, that of true nobility, of course." Asked where one gets it, he says not from sellers of perfumes and unguents.
- He cites Theognis: "From the good thou shalt learn good things, but if with the evil Thou holdest converse, thou shalt lose the wit that is in thee."
- He says a young man who wants to excel, as Autolycus did in the pankration, should take counsel to find the fittest friend to help him, and associate with that friend.
- When the guests ask whether such wisdom can be taught or only learnt, he treats the question as debatable and defers it.

chunks.heading: Socrates on Women's Nature, Courage and Choosing a Difficult Wife
chunks.text:
- Watching the dancing-girl throw hoops in perfect time, he says her skill is one proof among many that "woman's nature is nowise inferior to man's". Women lack only strength and judgment.
- He urges husbands to teach their wives whatever they want them to know as associates.
- Antisthenes asks why Socrates does not tutor his own shrewish wife, Xanthippe. He answers with the rider who wants to become an expert horseman and so avoids soft-mouthed, docile animals: "the horse for me to own must show some spirit".
- His reasoning: he wishes to deal with human beings in general. He knows that if he can tolerate her spirit, he can "with ease attach myself to every human being else".
- When the girl somersaults into a ring of upright swords, he says none present can again deny that courage can be taught. If a woman rushes so boldly into the midst of swords, courage looks like something that can be trained.

chunks.heading: Socrates on Exercise, Dancing and Moderate Drinking
chunks.text:
- He asks the Syracusan to teach him to dance, and defends this with a serious face. Dancing exercises every part of the body, giving an even balance, unlike the long-race runner's muscular legs and leaner shoulders or the boxer's thick chest at the expense of the legs.
- Benefits he lists: better health, enjoying food more, sleeping better, and reducing "a paunch a trifle too rotund". He can do it indoors in a "seven-sofa'd chamber" without stripping in public in the training school.
- He approves of drinking in moderation. Wine "moistens the soul of man" and "lulls at once all cares to sleep", like mandragora, and kindles light-hearted thoughts as oil does a flame.
- His analogy is to plants. Too much rain keeps them from lifting their heads, while the right amount lets them stand erect and bear fruit.
- Over-large draughts make the legs reel and thoughts falter. His prescription is a "frequent mizzle of small glasses" (borrowing Gorgias's language), which leads to "sportive levity" and not drunkenness.

chunks.heading: Socrates on Wisdom, the Soul and Pandering (the Art of the Go-Between)
chunks.text:
- At Callias's challenge that each guest name what he is proudest of, Socrates answers "On pandering", with a solemn face. He says he could make a fortune at it if he chose.
- His step-by-step argument, each step agreed by the company ("Without a doubt"):
  - A good go-between makes the person he works on agreeable to others.
  - One step towards agreeableness is a becoming fashion of hair and dress.
  - The same eyes can dart a look of love or hate, and the same tongue can speak with modesty or boastfulness.
  - Some words carry hate and some tend to friendliness, so the good go-between teaches only what conduces to agreeableness.
  - The better go-between makes clients pleasing to many people, and one who could make them pleasing to the whole community would be an arch-go-between.
- He then names Antisthenes as the master of this art, since Antisthenes had introduced Callias to Prodicus and Hippias of Elis, and had brought Socrates and others together by praising each to the other.
- His conclusion: a man who can see two natures made to be of service to each other, and make them mutually enamoured, is the sort who "should weld together states in friendship; cement alliances". Such a person is "a treasure worth possessing" to friends, intimates and partisans in war.
- On the gods: asked by Hermogenes' account of divine friendship what service he pays them, Socrates approves his answer (thanks, speaking well of them, never falsifying an oath). He says: "the gods themselves, it would appear, delight in nobleness of soul."

chunks.heading: Socrates on Beauty as Fitness for Function
chunks.text:
- In the mock beauty contest with Critobulus, Socrates questions him first. Critobulus agrees that beauty belongs not only to people but to horses, oxen, shields, swords and spears.
- The shared test they reach: things are beautiful "if well constructed by the hand of man to suit the sort of work for which we got them, or if naturally adapted to satisfy some want".
- Socrates applies this test to his own features:
  - Eyes serve vision, and his prominent eyes see aslant as well as straight ahead, so they are more beautiful than Critobulus's. By the same reasoning the crab has the loveliest eyes, being the toughest.
  - His wide, flat nostrils welcome scents from every quarter, while Critobulus's nostrils point to the earth.
  - A snub nose does not act as a barrier between the eyes, while a towering nose is "an insulting wall of partition".
  - His thick lips give a softer kiss.
- The jury votes in secret and every vote goes to Critobulus. Socrates remarks that Critobulus's beauty, unlike Callias's money, "can corrupt both judge and jury".

chunks.heading: Socrates on Kissing, Desire and Self-Mastery
chunks.text:
- Socrates says that Critobulus caught the fever of love for Cleinias at school, and that Critobulus's father consigned him to Socrates hoping Socrates could do something for him. He reports Critobulus's condition has improved.
- He suspects a kiss is the root of the worst of it, "than which love's flame asks no fiercer fuel", calling it insatiable and suggestive of mad fantasy.
- His advice: "let every one who wishes to be master of himself and sound of soul abstain from kisses imprinted on fair lips."
- Charmides teases that Socrates once sat head to head and shoulder to shoulder with Critobulus over a book. Socrates answers in jest that his shoulder ached for five days, like a bite from a wild beast, and that he felt a "scraping at the heart". He warns Critobulus not to touch him again until he has as thick a beard as head of hair.

chunks.heading: Socrates on Heavenly Love, Friendship and Love of the Soul
chunks.text:
- Socrates calls Love a divinity as old as the everlasting gods yet youngest in form, whose shrine is in the soul. He says: "I cannot name the time at which I have not been in love with some one."
- He distinguishes two Aphrodites, whom he treats as separate in nature, with separate altars, shrines and sacrifices:
  - The earthly (common) Aphrodite is lighter and laxer, and sends the bodily loves.
  - The heavenly Aphrodite (Ourania) is purer and holier, and sends loves that "feed upon the soul, on friendship and on noble deeds".
- He tells Callias his love for Autolycus appears to be of the heavenly kind. He bases this on Autolycus's strength, hardihood, courage and sobriety of soul, and on the fact that Callias invites the boy's father to share in their company, hiding nothing from him.
- Why love of soul beats love of body:
  - Without friendship there is no society of any worth. Friendship based on admiration of the inner disposition is "a sweet and voluntary compulsion".
  - Bodily beauty reaches its prime quickly, then withers, and the affection based on it withers with it.
  - Bodily enjoyment brings surfeit, as meat does through repletion, but "the soul, with every step she makes in her onward course towards deeper wisdom, grows ever worthier of love". Its attachment, being pure, "knows no satiety".
  - The beloved cannot hate a lover who thinks him beautiful and good and cares more for his welfare than for selfish joys. Such a pair will share trust, forethought, joy in success and burdens in misfortune, and be more attentive when apart than when together.
  - The bodily lover gives himself what he wants and offers the beloved only reproach. He separates the beloved from his nearest friends. If he uses persuasion and not force, he corrupts the soul of the one who yields, and that is a deeper reason for loathing.
  - "Nothing harsh was ever yet engendered by attachment based on moral qualities", while shameless intercourse has been the source of countless hateful deeds.
  - A true educator who trains another in virtue deserves honour, as Cheiron and Phoenix were honoured by Achilles. The bodily suitor, always begging a kiss or caress, ends up treated as a beggar.
- His farm analogy: the lover of outward beauty is like a man on a short lease, who tries to take the largest crops without improving the land. The lover of the soul is like an owner of his own farmstead, who scours the world to find what will improve the value of his beloved.
- On the effect on the beloved: one who knows his beauty is enough to enthrall his lover grows careless and wanton. One who knows he must himself be truly good to keep affection becomes more studious of virtue.
- The lover who tries to make his beloved good is bound to practise virtue himself: "how can he hope to make his comrade good, if he himself works wickedness?"
- Myth as evidence: Zeus left the women he wed for their bodies mortal, but raised to immortality the heroes whose souls he admired (Heracles, the Dioscuri). Ganymede was taken to Olympus for his mind, as his name ("joy" and "counsel") suggests.
- Achilles avenged Patroclus as a comrade, and Orestes and Pylades, Theseus and Peirithous are celebrated for common great deeds done out of mutual admiration.
- He disputes Pausanias's claim that an army of lovers and beloved would be invincible. He asks how men who ignore censure and behave shamelessly to one another would feel more shame at shameful deeds. He says Thebans and Eleians pairing lovers in battle seems to suggest mistrust. The Spartans, by contrast, forbid lustful touching, so their young men are moulded to such virtue that they will not desert even foreign comrades, because Sparta worships "Reverence", not "Shamelessness".
- His closing test: ask to whom you would entrust money, your children, or a favour. Even a lover of outward beauty would entrust his precious things to the one with inward beauty of the soul.

chunks.heading: Socrates on Education for Public Virtue and Genuine Reputation
chunks.text:
- Speaking to Callias about Autolycus, Socrates says the boy's ambition could be turned to benefiting friends and the fatherland, and to being remembered among Hellenes and barbarians. Such a boy would honour the one he regards as his bravest fellow-worker.
- To please him, Callias should study what made great statesmen great. He lists Themistocles' knowledge in freeing Hellas, Pericles' wit as the best adviser of his country, Solon's wisdom in framing Athens' laws, and the training that made the Spartans the best leaders.
- He admits his tone may be more serious than the wine-cup suits, but says "It has long been my wont to share our city's passion for noble-natured souls, alert and emulous in pursuit of virtue."
- When Callias asks Socrates, as go-between, to introduce him to the state, Socrates replies it will work if people see his loyalty to virtue is genuine and not "mere repute".
- His reasoning: "A false renown indeed is quickly seen for what it is worth, being tested; but true courage... perpetually amidst the storm and stress of circumstance pours forth a brighter glory."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Socrates tells Critobulus that wealth is only what one knows how to use well, and that the true masters of men are unseen vices like idleness, luxury and lust. He then recommends learning from those who succeed, praises husbandry as a school of justice, bravery and friendship, and sets out to find the truly "beautiful and good" man.

chunks.heading: Wealth is what you know how to use
chunks.text:
- Socrates defines wealth through use. A possession counts as wealth only if it benefits its owner, and "the same things... are wealth or not wealth, according as a man knows or does not know the use to make of them."
- His examples: a horse is no wealth to a man who is thrown each time he mounts. Land is no wealth if tilling it brings only loss. Sheep and cattle are no wealth to an owner who loses by them. A flute is "no better than the stones we tread under our feet" to someone who cannot play it, unless he sells it.
- Selling does not fix this. If the owner sells the flute for something he cannot use, the sale does not turn it into wealth.
- Money is included. Money spent on a mistress, to the harm of "body and soul and whole estate", is not wealth. Socrates would have such money "banished to the remote corners of the earth rather than be reckoned as wealth."
- Friends are wealth if a man knows how to use them, more truly than cattle are. Even enemies can be turned to profit by one who knows how, and many estates have grown through war.
- Economy is therefore a branch of knowledge. It lets a man enhance his house or estate, meaning all his useful possessions. A skilled man can manage another's estate as well as his own and earn a salary for it.

chunks.heading: Hidden masters: passions that enslave
chunks.text:
- Socrates says some people with the knowledge and capital to prosper still do nothing, because they are ruled by unseen masters. The masters are "idleness and effeminacy and reckless negligence", plus false pleasures such as "dicings and profitless associations among men". These look innocent but turn out to be "pains tricked out and decked with pleasures."
- Others work hard yet wear out their substance. They are slaves to "luxury and lechery, intemperance and the wine-cup along with many a fond and ruinous ambition."
- These masters take a man's labour while he is strong and spend it on their own lusts. When he is old and cannot work they abandon him "to his gray hairs and misery" and seize new victims.
- Socrates says to "wage ceaseless war" on these passions "for very freedom's sake", as if they were armed enemies. Even a conquering enemy can improve the conquered by chastening them. These tyrants only torment body, soul and substance.

chunks.heading: Rich is relative to needs: Socrates and Critobulus compared
Knowing teachers: what Socrates says he can and cannot teach
chunks.text:
- Socrates says he cannot teach economy from experience. He never owned the "instrument of the science", which is wealth, so he never went through a pupil stage. He compares himself to a man who never owned a flute and cannot learn it unlent.
- He warns that a learner may spoil the instrument, so practising on Critobulus's estate could ruin it.
- His method is to direct a seeker to better teachers, as one would send a man to another house for fire or water, or to a more skilful music teacher.
- He had long studied who in Athens is most expert in each field. He was amazed that among people doing identical work, half are destitute and half rich.
- When he investigated, he found "it all happened very naturally". Those who ran their affairs haphazardly "were punished by their losses". Those who "kept their wits upon the stretch and paid attention" were rewarded with greater ease and profit.
- He tells Critobulus to learn from the second group and says that, "unless the will of God oppose", he can become a clever man of business.

chunks.heading: Order, discipline and the wife as partner
chunks.text:
- Socrates names several contrasts that mark the essentials of economy:
  - Two men build houses, one spending heavily on useless ones, the other building cheaper homes with everything needed.
  - Some households own plenty of furniture but cannot find any when needed, which torments the family and servants. Others have everything ready at once, because each thing has "that to which it naturally belongs", not just the first place it lands.
  - Some slaves are fettered and keep running away. Others are loosed, yet choose to work and stay loyal.
  - Two farmers work alike farms: one says agriculture ruined him, the other has abundance from the same art. Socrates also means those who claim to be farmers but lack money for the real needs of the business.
  - Some men grow poor with horses and others rich.
- He tells Critobulus to come and look, and to test himself. Critobulus will rise at cock-crow and trek far to see a comedy, yet never invites Socrates to see such cases. Socrates says that is "far more ridiculous to yourself".
- He says Critobulus watches people as a theatre-goer watches actors, entertained but not aiming to be a poet. When circumstances force him to deal with horses, it is foolish not to avoid being "a mere amateur."
- On wives, Socrates says some husbands gain true helpmates in their wives, and others suffer disaster. He compares this to shepherds and riders: blame falls on the keeper.
- If a wife was taught and still does wrong, she may be to blame. If her husband "never tried to teach her the first principles of 'fair and noble' conduct", then the husband is to blame.
- Critobulus admits he entrusts important matters to his wife more than anyone, yet talks with her less than almost anyone. She married very young with little knowledge of the world. Socrates says it would be more astonishing if she knew how to speak and act well than if she went astray.
- A good wife, he says, is the husband's "counterpoise and counterpart for good". The husband brings goods into the house, but the wife's thrift checks most of the expenditure, and on that depends whether the estate grows or shrinks.
- He offers to introduce Critobulus to Aspasia, who can explain this "in a far more scientific way".

chunks.heading: Which occupations suit a free citizen
chunks.text:
- Socrates says the "base mechanic arts" have a bad name and are rightly held in ill repute by civilised communities. They ruin the bodies of workers and overseers who must sit at the loom or crouch before a furnace. Weakened bodies bring weakened souls.
- Such work leaves no leisure for friendship and the state, so those engaged in it are "sorry friends and ill defenders of the fatherland". Some warlike states bar citizens from any mechanical craft.
- He recommends the two arts the Persian king honours most, husbandry and war, and says the king takes a close interest in both.
- Socrates's evidence:
  - Governors must keep set numbers of cavalry, archers, slingers and targeteers. The king reviews troops each year, in person or by trusted proxies.
  - He honours officers whose forces are complete and well equipped, and punishes and replaces those who neglect or profit from their posts.
  - On royal progresses he inspects land. He rewards governors whose districts are thickly populated and fully cultivated, and removes those whose land lies idle through harshness, insolence or neglect.
  - Civil governors, who oversee the population and the farmers, and military commandants, who guard the land, can accuse each other. A badly tilled land cannot support its garrisons or pay tribute. A satrap holds both roles.
  - The king keeps "paradises" (orchards and gardens) wherever he lives and spends his days there when the season allows.
- Gifts go first to brave warriors, "since all the ploughing in the world were but small gain in the absence of those who should protect the fields", and next to those who made their lands productive. Cyrus said he deserved gifts of both kinds, since he excelled at stocking the country and protecting it.
- Socrates takes it as proof of a ruler's worth that followers follow him freely. Not one man deserted Cyrus for his brother the king, while tens of thousands went the other way. When Cyrus died, his friends died fighting around his body.
- In the story told by Lysander, Cyrus showed him his paradise at Sardis, with trees planted in straight, regular rows. Cyrus said he had measured and arranged it himself and planted some trees with his own hands. He added: "when in ordinary health I never dream of sitting down to supper without first practising some exercise of war or husbandry in the sweat of my brow". Lysander replied: "Cyrus, you have indeed good right to be a happy man, since you are happy in being a good man."

chunks.heading: Why husbandry is the noblest livelihood
chunks.text:
- Socrates calls agriculture "thrice blest". It gives a sense of luxury, the satisfaction of an improved estate, and the physical training of a free man.
- The earth freely provides necessities and many luxuries, including flowers and incense for altars, food, and animals for sacrifice. She does not let her gifts be received effeminately, but trains men to endure summer's heat and winter's cold.
- Those who labour with their hands gain strength, and those who oversee and think are made "more manly", rising at cock-crow and making long journeys.
- It supports public service. Farming lets a man keep a warhorse for cavalry, builds a foot-soldier's robustness, and supplies the hunt and hounds. Horses and dogs repay the farm: the horse carries the master to work, and the dog guards flocks.
- It trains for war. Men are fitted "to run, and hurl the spear, and leap with the best".
- It also builds justice and mutual help. Earth "gives lessons in justice and uprightness": "the nobler the service of devotion rendered, the ampler the riches of her recompense."
- If invaders seize the work of their hands, men raised on husbandry are strong enough to take supplies from the enemy, and in war it is often safer to seek food "with sword and buckler than with all the instruments of husbandry".
- The husbandman must create enthusiasm and ready obedience in his workers, as a general does with gifts for the brave and punishment for the disorderly. Both need seasons of exhortation, and slaves as well as free men need "the lure of hope and happy expectation".
- He endorses the saying that husbandry is "the mother and nurse of all the arts". When the land lies desert, "the spring that feeds the other arts is dried up."
- He sums it up with a rural image: a generous hostess who keeps open house, with a warm bath and fire in winter and cool streams and shade in summer. She is a favourite of the good wife and the children and welcomes the master's friends.

chunks.heading: Husbandry lies in the gods' hands: piety and the search for a "beautiful and good" man
chunks.text:
- When Critobulus objects that most farming outcomes are beyond human control (hail, frost, drought, flood, mildew, murrain), Socrates answers that farming and war alike lie "in the hands of the gods".
- Men about to fight seek divine favour with sacrifices and omens. Farmers should do the same: "the wise and prudent will pay service to the gods" for crops, cattle, horses, sheep, goats, and all possessions, "great and small, without exception."
- In his summary, Socrates restates the agreed points: husbandry is the noblest employment for a gentleman, a "beautiful and good" man. It is the easiest to learn and the pleasantest to follow. It gives the body beauty and hardihood and leaves the soul leisure for friendship and civic duty.
- It also makes men brave, because the crops grow outside the city walls. It is held in highest repute by statesmen and states for producing the best citizens.
- To test the different attitudes, he suggests seating farmers and artisans apart and asking whether to defend the fields or guard the walls. Farmers would vote to defend the land. Artisans, trained to sit still, would vote not to fight.
- Socrates describes how he sought a model. He quickly examined carpenters, bronze-workers, painters and sculptors, but wanted to know what justified the title "beautiful and good".
- He first approached beautiful people, hoping to find "good" joined to beauty, but found some who were outwardly beautiful and inwardly "the veriest knaves". He then set aside outward beauty and sought out Ischomachus, whom everyone called "beautiful and good". Their conversation fills the later chapters.
